text:
I declare open this meeting of the Senate Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Legislation Committee. I want to begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we are meeting today and paying my respects to their elders past and present. The Senate has referred to the committee the particulars of the proposed expenditure for the year 2026-27 and other related documents for the Foreign Affairs and Trade portfolio and the Defence portfolio. The committee has set 5 November 2026 as the deadline for senators to submit written questions on notice. The committee has set 17 December as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice.

Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session, and this includes answers to questions on notice. I want to remind all witnesses that, in giving evidence to the committee, they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence to a committee. The Senate has resolved the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings: any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in the estimates are relevant questions for the purpose of estimates hearings. I want to remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has a discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise.

The Senate has resolved that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked to superior officers or to a minister. This resolution prohibits only questions asking for opinions on matters of policy and does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. I draw the attention of witnesses to an order of the Senate of 13 May 2009 specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised, which I now incorporate into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

(Extract, Senate Standing Orders)

Witnesses are specifically reminded that a statement claiming that information or a document is confidential or consists of advice to government is not a statement that meets this requirement of the 2009 order. Instead, witnesses are required to articulate the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or the document.

I remind senators of their obligations under the Behaviour Code for Australian Parliamentarians to treat all witnesses with dignity, courtesy, fairness and respect. I ask members of the media to follow the established media guidelines and instructions of the committee secretariat. I remind everyone in the gallery they are not permitted to speak or interfere with proceedings or with any witness at any point during the hearing. Witnesses and senators who are seeking to table a document during the Senate committee hearing are requested to provide an electronic copy of those documents to the secretariat so that the documents can be circulated electronically during the hearing.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Minister, do you have an opening statements?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
I do, Chair, thank you. Colleagues, since we last met in June, the world has only become less certain. Conflict is taking a devastating human toll, strategic competition continues to sharpen and the global economy is deteriorating. Disruption to vital shipping routes is pushing up fuel and fertiliser costs as well as inflation around the world, including for Australians. We cannot isolate ourselves from these pressures, but we can act to shield Australians from the worst impacts, and that is what we are doing. The Albanese Labor government keeps focusing on our region, strengthening our relationships, upholding the rules that protect us all and fortifying Australia's resilience. As I've said many times, it is in our region where our interests are most at stake.

In June, we signed the Nakamal Agreement with Vanuatu, supporting its development ambitions, economic transformation and our shared security. In July, we signed the Vuvale Union and the Ocean of Peace Alliance, which will establish Fiji's first mutual defence alliance and Australia's fourth. The Pukpuk Treaty entered into force, making Papua New Guinea our newest alliance partner. At last week's Australia-Papua New Guinea Ministerial Forum, we advanced cooperation on health, security, telecommunications and economic opportunity. We continue to progress a new comprehensive treaty with Solomon Islands. These partnerships are guided by Pacific priorities, mutual respect and trust.

In South-East Asia, we are deepening security cooperation with Indonesia under our Treaty on Common Security. I was pleased to meet Indonesia's new foreign minister, Minister Nasir, last week. Also last week, we announced more than $60 million to strengthen Timor-Leste's security resilience and regional engagement. And with Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Brunei, Malaysia and Indonesia, we are working to secure essential supplies, including petrol, diesel and fertiliser. In July, we welcomed India's Prime Minister Modi to Australia, formalising cooperation in tech and maritime security, diversifying supply chains and enhancing Indian Ocean stability.

Chair, since we last met, catastrophic floods along Nepal's border with China have caused immense devastation and loss of life. Thirty-four Australians remain unaccounted for. My thoughts are with their families, their loved ones and all those affected by this tragedy. Australia deployed 49 officials and specialists to support search, rescue and recovery efforts, and we have committed $26 million in humanitarian and recovery assistance to help Nepal rebuild. The Prime Minister and I have met with our Nepali counterparts, and the government continues to work with Nepali and Chinese authorities to seek information. We will continue to do all we can to seek answers for families and stand with the people of Nepal as they recover.

The Albanese government is also acting globally to uphold the rules that protect us all. At the UN High-level Week, the Prime Minister launched Australia's bid for a Security Council seat for 2029-30. We seek that seat because we believe a safer world is governed by rules, not power and force alone. Should we be successful, our purpose and our approach will be consistent with how we conduct ourselves. We will listen with respect, we will partner as equals, and we will protect what matters most. Australia ratified the landmark High Seas Biodiversity Treaty, and the Prime Minister joined more than 20 world leaders calling for stronger international control of frontier artificial intelligence.

Colleagues, Ukraine shows why rules matter. Russia, a permanent Security Council member, continues its unjustified and illegal invasion. At the United Nations, the Prime Minister and President Zelenskyy signed the Australia-Ukraine Bilateral Security Agreement, providing for enduring defence and security cooperation. We also announced a further $60 million in support of Ukraine, including Australian Defence Force equipment. We stand with Ukraine because its people have a right to determine their future and because the Security Council veto must never be a licence to violate the charter.

These rules also include international humanitarian law. In honour of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom, killed by the Israeli defence forces alongside her World Central Kitchen colleagues, Australia led the Declaration for the Protection of Humanitarian Personnel. One year on, more than two-thirds of the UN has signed on. With Jordan, I co-chaired the inaugural meeting of signatories, taking forward practical steps to improve protection and accountability. We committed a further $10 million for stronger protection measures, including security training, evidence collection and assistance to victims and families. I continue to work with Zomi's family as we press Israel for accountability and for justice. In Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan and conflict zones everywhere, humanitarians dedicate their lives to protecting others. This work should never cost them their own.

In the Middle East, we have committed new assistance for Palestinian recovery and institutional reform as we work with partners to keep the hope of a two-state solution alive. We believe this is the only way to secure lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians. We continue to call for de-escalation and for an end to the conflict in Iran. At the UN, Australia joined the EU No Fees**/**No Tolls pledge against coercion at sea. Alongside 80 nations, we called for the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and condemned Houthi attacks. Tomorrow, I will travel to the United States for the third Quad Foreign Ministers Meeting this year and the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, continuing our work for Australia's security and prosperity. I thank the Chair and the committee for moving the day of this hearing to accommodate this travel.

Can I also take this opportunity to thank the secretary and all of the personnel at DFAT, both here and abroad, for all their ongoing work to protect and advance Australia's interests. Deteriorating international circumstances will continue to confront us, but they will not confound us. We will continue to take the world as it is, and we will continue our work to shape it for the better in the interests of the Australian people. Thank you.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
Yes, thank you, Chair. Chair and senators, since I last appeared before you, DFAT has continued to deliver. At a time of volatility and increased global contest, we are strengthening Australia's security and prosperity, providing trusted services and responding effectively to crises. Most recently, DFAT led Australia's response to the devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet, China—floods that left more Australians missing overseas, 34, than any single incident in over a decade. We brought together Australian agencies to tailor support for the families of missing Australians, who are experiencing unimaginable grief; and to support the search and rescue and humanitarian effort.

Senators, we want to ensure a favourable strategic balance for Australia and for a peaceful, stable and prosperous Indo-Pacific. Since the committee last met, we have delivered significant outcomes for Australia's partnerships in the Pacific. We signed the Nakamal Agreement with Vanuatu and the Vuvale Union and Ocean of Peace Alliance with Fiji. We are advancing agreements with the Solomon Islands and with Tonga. Our Pukpuk Treaty with Papua New Guinea has taken the relationship to the next level, as demonstrated last week at the ministerial forum, with 27 ministers participating. We want all countries of our region to have the freedom to develop and shape their futures. To do this, our engagements in regional institutions are more crucial than ever. That is why we amplified Pacific voices at the pre-COP leaders meeting and backed in new security and gender equality initiatives at the Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting in Palau.

On the fifth anniversary of the ASEAN-Australia Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, we remain committed to ASEAN centrality and the ASEAN-led architecture; and to deepening our bilateral relationships, demonstrating that Australia is a steadfast and reliable partner. We have increased support for maritime and security cooperation with the Philippines. We have bolstered the security of essential supplies with Singapore. Minister Wong launched the next phase of our flagship economic governance program with Indonesia's new foreign minister in Jakarta last week.

Recent visits by world leaders to Australia, including India's Prime Minister Modi, Thailand's Prime Minister Anutin, and Vietnam's General Secretary and State President To Lam, among others, underscore our reputation for addressing shared challenges with partners. The purpose of our international engagement is to make Australia stronger, safer and more prosperous. We are investing in our relationships with Japan, Korea, the United Kingdom, the United States and others to build resilience, including through the Quad. Earlier this month, I participated in the inaugural Australia-Japan Leadership Dialogue, announced by the Prime Minister and Prime Minister Takaichi in May, and in strategic consultations with my Japanese counterpart. I had the opportunity to reiterate to Japanese officials, as I have done before this committee, that Australia supports Japan's efforts to maintain dialogue with China to de-escalate tensions in support of regional stability and international law, while also opposing economic coercion. Australia also continues to engage China on the full range of Australia's interests.

More broadly, DFAT is reinforcing our economic security by working to preserve and improve open rules-based trade. We pushed for practical change in multilateral fora in the WTO, the G20, OECD, APEC and the UN, where Australia's bid for a seat on the Security Council is underway, centred on our commitment to protection, oceans and climate and digital futures. Stepping up to the table, not vacating it for others, gives Australia a stronger voice in the decisions that affect us and our region. At UN High-level Week, in front of the largest annual gathering of world leaders, Australia showed its credentials for promoting international peace and security through the rule of law. Minister Wong led more than 130 countries in strengthening global commitment to the protection of humanitarian personnel. We signed a bilateral security agreement with Ukraine and announced more than 100 new sanctions against Russia. And we helped set up cross-regional coalitions on a range of critical issues, including AI and protecting children online.

As Australians travel overseas in increasing numbers, DFAT's global network is invaluable. We issue more than 100,000 travel documents yearly. We handle almost 30,000 consular cases each year. We're also seeing a growing number of complex consular cases, including mental health, financial hardship, welfare concerns, child custody and legal issues, often requiring sustained support. Last year we managed more than 3,700 welfare and other serious matter cases globally—a 27 per cent increase on the previous year. Staff at DFAT take pride in serving Australians and advancing Australia's interests around the world. I'm proud of the fact that our passport and consular services are consistently top-ranked as the most trusted among government agencies according to the Australian Public Service Commission survey. DFAT staff are also working in Kyiv, Riyadh and other locations affected by conflict and dangerous and demanding conditions, and I would like to take this opportunity to thank them for their remarkable dedication. Thank you, Chair.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Minister, I want to start with the public reporting yesterday around what appears to be a targeted hack, attributed to Iran, of an Australian journalist and political commentator, Sharri Markson, journalist at News24; and Michael Kroger, political commentator. I should disclose I'm a regular guest on Sharri's program and I've known Michael Kroger for 20 years. I'm raising it not because I know them but because it's a concerning report. Are you familiar with this issue?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Only through the media at this point, Senator, obviously.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes. Just to recap for everyone's benefit, a former administration official in the United States had one of their accounts compromised and reached out to Ms Markson to set up a meeting. As a result of that process, her personal data was compromised. Mike Burgess has made some public comments attributing this to the Islamic Republic of Iran, and I believe the IRGC specifically. How concerning is it that this regime appears to be targeting Australian nationals?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This is obviously a matter for Home Affairs, but I'm happy to make some general comments. I think you would be aware that this government took unprecedented action in expelling the Iranian ambassador after having had continuous diplomatic relations for decades. It was the first decision by government of this nature since the end of World War II. We did that because of the evidence and the advice from agencies about the work of the IRGC in Australia and their links to the antisemitic attacks on Australian soil. That is unacceptable. I think we are very aware of the way in which the IRGC has operated in Australia and in other countries. On the specifics of this, as you correctly identified, Ms Markson was, as I understand through the media, advised by the Director-General of ASIO. This would be a matter for Home Affairs rather than for DFAT.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sure, yes. I'm interested in the diplomatic implications of it, which is why I'm asking about it here. This is continued malign conduct from a malign regime. And we now have a journalist and a political commentator who've been targeted by this regime and had, in one instance, their personal data compromised. My understanding from the reporting is that the attempts to disrupt Mr Kroger's personal data were not successful, but a journalist has had their personal data stolen by a foreign authoritarian regime that has launched what the Australian government assesses to be terror attacks on Australian soil. In his public comments about it, Mr Burgess said he's concerned that the regime is capable of and may have the intent to carry out further acts of violence in Australia. So the question is: what are the implications for the diplomatic relationship and any further steps that the government would consider taking in response to this?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, first I would make the general proposition that Australia will not and does not tolerate attempts by Iranian agents to surveil, harass or intimidate individuals in Australia, whether they are members of the Iranian diaspora or journalists conducting their work or political individuals—full stop. Secondly, we'll obviously take advice always from security agencies about particular matters, including more generally, but we have already expelled the Iranian ambassador.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: A third Australian contacted me overnight after having seen the reporting and recognised the pattern of behaviour. They believe they too have been a victim of this attack. They are now—I won't reveal their identity; it's not appropriate—dealing with our agencies to assess whether or not that's correct. And that has to be assessed by our agencies. It's up to them to make a judgement. But if it is the case that it wasn't just these two people and that other Australians have also been targeted—that a wider group of people may be targeted in these operations—how concerning would that be?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, I've given you our principal view, which is that we do not tolerate attempts by Iran to behave towards Australians or on Australian soil in the way you've outlined. I am reluctant to get drawn into responding on a threat which is, as you said, already before the security agencies. The government has made its position clear. We do not tolerate the harassment or intimidation or surveillance of Australians or individuals in Australia; and we have taken the strongest possible action against Iran, including the expulsion of the ambassador. I would make the point, as I've made previously in this hearing, that we have taken stronger action against Iran than any previous Australian government.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's true, isn't it, that our embassy in Tehran is closed currently—is that right?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, the embassy has currently suspended operations. It's no longer operating there.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That's right. And that was done after the Australian government's decision to expel the Iranian ambassador and also to list the IRGC as a terrorist organisation?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's been raised with me by members of the Iranian Australian diaspora that it's, of course, very welcome that the Iranian ambassador to Australia has been expelled but that Iran's embassy continues to operate here in Australia. What is the government's thinking about continuing to permit that embassy to operate on our soil?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, the view is that we have retained a formal channel to make clear, and to continue to make clear, our concerns about Iranian actions and to pursue our national interests. The embassy in Canberra serves as a conduit for that purpose. We do regularly communicate with them, including our views on Iran's destabilising actions and our complete rejection of their interference in our affairs.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I do understand that argument, but a similar argument was made prior to our decision to expel the ambassador and prior to our decision to list the IRGC as a terrorist organisation. When I and other members of parliament advocated for both of those things, we were told that would shut down channels of communication, that the bilateral relationship was important and that we shouldn't do that. So—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The threshold of IRGC on Australian soil being part of organising attacks against Australians on Australian soil in order to foment fear and division—obviously, there is a threshold where the government took unprecedented action to expel the ambassador. Also, I would make the point that we have imposed, I think, some 230 sanctions on some 230 Iranian-linked persons, including more than 100 IRGC-linked individuals and entities. We have also listed, as you said, the IRGC as a state sponsor of terrorism. So we have taken action, Senator.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No-one's suggesting otherwise.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, in fact, if I may, far more action than the government that you were part of ever took.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Is there any threshold which the regime could cross? To your point, Minister, a threshold was crossed, I agree, when they were sponsoring terror attacks on Australian soil. Is there any threshold that they could cross that would lead to the embassy in Canberra being closed down?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I have to differ with my officers here. The decision to keep open the embassy was primarily because there are still visa and passport services and other essential paperwork that Iranian Australians require.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So it's not about—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: With respect to Dr King, I don't regard the embassy primarily as the way we communicate to the Iranians. I think that was communicated by our sanctions, the listing as a terrorist organisation and the expulsion of the ambassador—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Indeed, and we can make public statements at any time—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sorry, may I?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. They are lower level staff for the purposes of practical engagement that some Iranian Australians still need.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We obviously have do not travel advice—very strong do not travel advice—for Iran for very good reasons. Certainly my perception, based on the feedback that I've received from Iranian Australians, is that a very large number of them—I couldn't assess whether it's the majority; I haven't done a poll—are very concerned about the continuing operations of the embassy. They feel threatened by that, and they are concerned that it could be used against their interests. At what point does that convenience of visa processing and document access become less important than the safety of the Iranian Australian diaspora and also our journalists and other public figures?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The safety of Iranian Australians is always front of mind, Senator, and we would take advice from security agencies on those issues.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So you would be willing, on advice, to close the Iranian embassy if necessary?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm not going to speculate on advice from security agencies.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm not asking you to speculate on what their advice might be. I'm asking you to tell me what the government's thinking is on whether there are any circumstances or any activity that the regime could engage in that would lead to the embassy being closed.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The safety of Australians is our first priority. That's the answer I would give you.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I think these questions are reasonable because when opposition senators, me included, asked, 'Could we list the IRGC as a terrorist organisation?' we were told no. When we asked, 'Could the ambassador be expelled?' we were told no. Subsequently, the government did both of those things, and we strongly support that and welcome that. So I think it is reasonable to test whether something that currently is not contemplated could be contemplated in the future if the threshold is crossed.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And I think I've answered that by saying what our first priority is, which is the safety of Australians.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The answer is yes, there are circumstances—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, I'm not going to be drawn on hypotheticals—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sorry, Minister. I apologise for interrupting you before, but you're interrupting me now. I'd like to ask my question.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I haven't finished my answer.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I was asking a question.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I haven't finished my answer. I have answered your question by saying the first priority is the safety of Australians—full stop. I'm not going to get into speculating—particularly in this forum, and you understand that—on what the advice of security agencies might or might not be. I'm not going to do that and I'm not going to get into hypotheticals. But, when it comes to the safety of Australians, that is our first priority. We would make any decisions that we thought and were advised were necessary to protect the security of Australians, as we have done.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay, so I interpret from that there are circumstances under which you would be willing to close the embassy, and I think that is an important statement. Chair, I have other topics to move on to, but if you need to rotate the call I'm happy to come back.

text:
If I may, Senator, we work very closely with the United Kingdom. I've worked now with, I think, five British foreign secretaries, including, obviously, Secretary Miliband, who was recently appointed. We have engaged on reform and on the recognition of Palestine; we've engaged on the sanctioning of ministers Smotrich and Ben-Gvir. We've engaged and coordinated on many of the statements—as you know, one has been—and I know your party has been dismissive of this. We have moved Australia's position in international fora on the issue of two states and on the issue of what is occurring in Gaza and what is occurring in West Bank very substantially over the period of this government. We have often done that—not always—in coordination with the United Kingdom. There have been points where we have moved first; there have been points where the UK have moved first over this period.

I do note that the Israeli election, obviously, has occurred over the last 24 hours. We are all grappling with how you deal with the Netanyahu government's policies—in particular, on this issue in the West Bank—which are inconsistent with the prospect of two states. We do believe—and I know that there are others who have different views—and have a very clear view that the only way to secure peace and security for both Israelis and Palestinians is for there to be two states. When we came to government, we made decisions in relation to these issues, including nomenclature, and reversed the decision of the previous government in relation to Jerusalem.

We have made clear our continued opposition to the settlements. We have been clear about our view as to settler violence and we have sanctioned settler entities and individuals who are involved in perpetrating violence or inciting others against Palestinians in the West Bank. We are all grappling with the decision by the Netanyahu government to accelerate settlement activity and, of course, there are discussions and have been discussions about what is the best way to respond, including over a period of time with different—under the Starmer government as well as under the Burnham government.

I can go where you want to go. Why did we not join this statement? I think I'd refer you to what I said in the parliament. We are moving in the same direction. That doesn't mean we do precisely everything at the same time. I indicated we would look at targeted sanctions rather than a blanket ban, and I would note that the UK has as yet not implemented, although it has announced, such a ban.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: When was the decision not to participate communicated to the United Kingdom?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It was communicated to them before the statement was released.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: How much before?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I don't have that detail.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Who was responsible for overseeing the communications between the United Kingdom and Australia in relation to this? Was that in your wheelhouse, Dr Webster?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It was in my wheelhouse, but it is often done through our high commission in London.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It was an important matter, I assume?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Very important, yes.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'll ask you again: when was the decision communicated to the UK that Australia would not participate in the statement?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As I said, it was communicated before the statement was released.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: When?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I don't have that detail, I'm afraid.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, will you provide it on notice, please.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Certainly.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Did Australia raise specific objections to the proposed measures during negotiations? Were there elements that Australia objects to? If so, what were they?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, I think I'd refer you to what I said in the Senate. I don't think it's right to describe this as—it's not a negotiation in the way that you might be implying. We have worked together on multiple statements. There have been so many occasions in which CANZ or sometimes CANZUK—CANZ is Canada, Australia and New Zealand; sometimes it's Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the UK. Sometimes we've had Japan and Korea join. I think on some of the statements we had Japan but not the United Kingdom. There have been a group of countries which are all trying to deal with the horrific situation we have seen in Gaza and the actions of the Netanyahu government in the West Bank. There are discussions which might occur Canberra to London and might occur in London, but we were very clear. With what the UK was proposing, the judgement that the government had to make was whether we would go down the path of agreeing ahead of time to an announcement of blanket bans or whether we would look at an alternative of more targeted measures. The government made a decision to do the latter.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Was the decision to not sign on to the statement made by you, Minister? Was it made by the Prime Minister? Was it made by cabinet?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's a decision of senior ministers.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Which senior ministers?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm not going to go—these are matters of government. It's a decision of the government.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, was it a decision of you and the Prime Minister?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I've just said it's a decision of the government.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, you said 'which senior ministers'—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, you said 'which'.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You said 'senior ministers', and I'm asking you which senior ministers.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's a decision of the government.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Did it go to cabinet?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm not going to comment on cabinet processes.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm not asking you to comment on what the discussions in cabinet were. I'm asking whether or not this was a decision of cabinet. It's an incredibly important decision. You've set out that there's been a long history of working with the United Kingdom. This is an occasion where Australia has not followed what is broadly seen as a very welcome move by the United Kingdom. Did such an important deviation from previous practice go to cabinet?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'd make two points. The first is there have been occasions where we have been ahead of the United Kingdom, if you want to put it that way, in terms of our willingness to make certain statements. In fact, through this conflict, the original grouping of Canada, Australia and New Zealand was because we wanted to go further than the United Kingdom at that point in relation to the conflict. So I don't think it's—I just wanted to make sure that dynamic was clear. It is the case, Senator, that disclosure of whether an item goes to cabinet is disclosure of that fact. There's a longstanding convention that we don't comment on that, but this was a decision of the government.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
The rationale for rejecting this call was—and I think this is from you, Minister—apparently:

We are concerned blanket import bans present practical challenges, including how to ensure they do not inadvertently harm Palestinian businesses, workers and livelihoods.

Minister, has any Palestinian or human rights group raised these concerns with you and said that they share those concerns? If so, please tell me who.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, can I just make this point. I would ask you—and I'm sure you won't recognise this because that is the nature of political debate. We have already sanctioned entities for actions in the West Bank. We have already sanctioned extremist settlers and entities that are responsible for violence and human rights abuses. Already Australians cannot trade with these entities. Already, Australian law bans buying, importing or transporting goods from sanctioned individuals and entities. We have already done that. The UK has announced that it will do a blanket ban. As yet, it has not implemented it, and we certainly will look at and engage with them about how they are going to construct that and whether they are going to ban all products from settlements or whether they are going to exempt any products from it.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Minister, my question was about—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, it's an issue—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: whether any Palestinian or human rights—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, the minister is responding.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, why is it you feel—I would like to finish my answer.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'd like the question answered.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The minister is answering.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We will look at what the UK does. In answer to your question, I have already engaged not on this issue but on the broader issue of progress towards implementation of the peace plan with the Palestinian authority. I would anticipate that we would engage—particularly post what the UK does—with them as well to gain any insights that they have.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Minister, there is not a single Palestinian group or human rights group that in any way supports your rationale for not implementing a blanket import ban. They are almost to a person offended that the rationale for not putting a blanket ban on illegal Israeli settlements on occupied Palestinian land is allegedly to not cause inadvertent harm to Palestinian businesses, workers and livelihoods. The harm that is being caused to Palestinians in the occupied West Bank is because of the illegal settlements. It's because of the violence directed at Palestinians. It's because of the fact that the Israeli state doesn't prevent that violence. When they see you say the reason your government won't put a blanket ban on illegal Israeli settlements is that you're trying to protect Palestinians, they've been, to a person, offended by that from the communications I've seen. Have you not heard that? Have you not heard that call from the Palestinian community and from human rights groups?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, the thing that you said with which I do agree, and with which the government agrees—and our policy position reflects that—is that we disagree with and oppose the former Netanyahu government's policy and the consequences of that policy in relation to the West Bank. We believe the actions that have been taken by individuals and the actions and policy of certain government ministers are the opposite of peace and have compromised the human rights of Palestinians in the West Bank. We do believe that, which is why we have implemented sanctions, why we have taken the action we have taken and why we will take further action.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On that note—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'll come back and try again next time.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I will share the call around. Senator Dowling, I'll give you a block, and then I'll come back to Senator Paterson.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As we approach another year of schoolies, we reflect on the tragic deaths of Bianca Jones and Holly Bowles in Laos in November 2024 due to methanol poisoning. I want to ask the government: with schoolies approaching, what is the government doing to improve travel safety for young Australians?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sorry, is that to me?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, it is, Minister.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
Can I start by again saying I think all Australians were shocked and distressed by the news of the deaths of Holly and Bianca. What happened to Bianca and Holly and the four other young travellers in Vang Vieng should never have happened. I've had the privilege of engaging with the families, and I know that this tragedy weighs so heavily on them. They're in our thoughts.

We have advocated at every level for a thorough and transparent investigation in Laos and for those responsible to be held to account. We've engaged repeatedly at officer level but also at the highest level of the Laos government. I've raised this with the Laos deputy prime minister and foreign minister. We will continue and do continue to press for justice. I know that this has been such a hard road for the Morton-Bowles and Jones families, how deeply painful this has been and how bitterly disappointing this legal process has been for them. At the same time, we have been working to ensure that more young people are aware of the dangers that can await them overseas. I was really honoured to be invited by Bianca's parents to Mentone Girls' Grammar for that reason—it was last month or earlier this month.

We are approaching schoolies season, as you rightly point out, and many young Australians embark on some exciting adventures—many for the first time abroad. What we want is to make sure they are aware of potential dangers. I did spend that evening with parents, teachers and students who were pretty excited about what the future might hold, but the message I shared was this: have a plan, know where the nearest hospital is and keep the DFAT emergency consular number saved in your phone. I also said make sure you write it down somewhere in case you lose your phone. Stick with your mates; don't leave anyone behind. Do not drink from unlabelled bottles. Don't accept free shots or drinks that are unusually cheap. Drink from trusted brands and sealed bottles if you're drinking because methanol can be in a free shot or that unmarked bottle and, as you know, you can't smell it, you can't taste it and you can't see it. In the hours after, it can feel like a bad night. We talked about what you do if you have a friend who's in trouble. If you notice a friend has got blurred vision or has trouble breathing or feels sicker than the number of drinks that they've had, that's an emergency. Don't try to wait and sleep it off. Get medical help straightaway.

I'm sure that's good advice. I have to say it's advice that, even as a young person when I was travelling overseas, I didn't know. Given we're assuming that most school leavers aren't watching Senate estimates, I'll let the committee know that we are partnering with DrinkWise and we're partnering with Red Frogs so young Australians can carry that knowledge with them. We've also put a TravelSmarts test online so school leavers can do a practical kind of test that asks them what they would do in certain situations to check their knowledge so they can have fun and stay safe. I would say this to every young person out there. Do go and see the world. Say goodbye to your parents at the airport and send lots of photos, but look after yourself, look after your mates and come home safely.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you for that insight, Minister. I think, as you point out, many young kids probably aren't watching these hearings right now, so maybe I could ask the department to share some of the channels you're using through digital and others. Obviously, most will be very aware of Smartraveller, but I understand there's a partying safely hub and there are a range of other measures now to try to reach younger audiences.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
Yes. We do use a range of channels to get these messages out to young travellers. What I would say is that our approach from Smartraveller is always practical, and it's evidence based. We want to help young Australians to understand alcohol related risks and to make safer choices overseas, so we take a broad approach to partying safely. We look at how we can strengthen the approach as well, so we work with other agencies—particularly, this year, we've worked with the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing on how we can expand our alcohol safety messaging. What that messaging emphasises is that young people do not need to drink to enjoy schoolies and that choosing not to drink is also an option and may be the safest choice. But we also continue to provide practical harm minimisation advice for those who do choose to drink.

To the channels that we use, we have the partying safely hub, which is the central source of practical safety information for young people heading overseas. That was launched by the Foreign minister on 10 September 2025, and it brings together advice on alcohol safety, methanol poisoning, drink spiking, drugs, travel insurance and other risks, as well as resources for young travellers, parents, schools and universities. That hub supports a broader communications effort. We use social media, we use digital advertising and we go to schools. That DrinkWise event was part of that effort. The airports—we work with them, travel providers and partners. All of that messaging is effectively reaching young people where they are and directing them to trusted Australian government advice. To give you some numbers, since its launch, the hub has been viewed nearly 20,000 times by over 14,000 Australians and their parents. We're continuing to update that hub as we go. It has a range of resources there. It has research. It has partner materials. In 2026, as the minister mentioned, we also launched TravelSmarts, which is a scenario based, 'choose your own adventure' style learning tool. It's really fun, it's interactive and it's educational.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Great. Thank you. You reflected on it being evidence based. Where do you get the evidence to suggest what you should be advising and what works? Do you have particular performance targets or metrics you're trying to achieve through the Smartraveller or the party safely hub?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
We do a range of market research to examine how that messaging is going and to make sure that it's effective. We take an evidence led approach to all of that. It involves audience research, testing, tracking and evaluation as well. Under the Smartraveller advertising campaign, that research that we undertake informs our target audience, our message framing, our creative development and also our channel selection. We test concepts with the target audience before the launch. We track performance during the campaign, and we formally evaluate the results to refine our approach. For example, the 2025 schoolies campaign with DrinkWise included pre- and post-campaign research to understand young travellers' behaviours and to assess whether those messages reached the intended audience and supported safer decision-making. We supplemented that with targeted research to gain deeper insights into specific audiences and emerging trends.

Recent studies have explored gen Z behaviour and the use of AI in travel planning, which is increasing. We've also looked at travel behaviours, information needs and preferred communication channels of culturally and linguistically diverse young Australians. Our results have confirmed that this evidence led approach that we're taking is quite effective. Our evaluation of the current 'Know before you go' campaign found 49 per cent campaign recall, and 83 per cent reported taking a key action after having viewed that campaign, such as visiting Smartraveller or preparing more thoroughly for travel. The schoolies evaluation found that 72 per cent of international schoolies attendees surveyed considered the campaign messages were important and 68 per cent said the campaign would help attendees make better choices. So I think we have some numbers there to back up that this campaign is cutting through to the right audiences.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's great to hear how effective that campaign is. Thank you.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator Paterson.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I have some questions on recognition of Palestinian statehood for relevant officials. When the government announced recognition of Palestinian statehood in August last year, it said that there are a number of preconditions to that recognition. Could you remind me what those preconditions were.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: When we recognised the State of Palestine, we took into account the commitments of the PA to the following: reform governance, terminate prisoner payments, institute schooling reforms, demilitarise and hold general elections.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And what was DFAT's advice to government at the time about the prospects of those reforms?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As my colleague's just said, those commitments are given by the Palestinian Authority. We made them clear. We have continued to make clear to the Palestinian Authority that we hold them to account and that we are monitoring, as are other partners, their progress on these reforms.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The PA saying that they're going to do something is one thing, but DFAT is capable of making an independent assessment of how likely those are. So what was DFAT's advice at the time about the prospects for each of those preconditions?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, the key element, as I understand it, in the recognition of Palestine was to keep the two-state solution alive. We did that with partners. That was the primary motivation for recognising Palestine at that time. I'm unaware of the assessment made with specific regard for reforms, except for the fact that we have remained in touch with the Palestinian Authority to hold them to account, and we are satisfied they are making progress on that basis.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So DFAT didn't do an assessment of how likely it was that the PA would deliver?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I am unaware of that, and I would have to get back to you on that, Senator.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You weren't in a substantive role at the time, or there was another official?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: If I can just answer—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: PSM, Secretary

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Please.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Obviously, we don't go into details in this committee and detailed advice from the department to the minister on policy issues that inform government decisions.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: PSM, Secretary

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, as you know, Ms Adams, from your experience in this committee, we don't accept advice to government as an excuse not to answer a question. There has to be a public interest immunity claim, and advice to government has never been accepted by the Senate as a reason not to answer a question. Did DFAT provide this advice or not?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I think what has already been said is the key point. The decision took into account the commitments of the PA to those elements and made clear that we would continue to press the PA to implement those commitments.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: PSM, Secretary

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But if Australia's making—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Can I just intervene—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sure.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: if I may, because it's not fair to officials for you to set up a hard binary, which is not quite the way we articulated it. Australia's position is predicated on the commitments we have received from the PA. We will continue to work with the international community to hold the Palestinian Authority to its commitments and to encourage normalised relations between Israel and its neighbours. I think the point is, and I can attest, I can say to you that something we have engaged particularly with the United Kingdom and Canada about, but more broadly with others who are part of the recognition shift—and, as you know, the overwhelming majority of our like-minded partners have now recognised Palestine—was that this would require work, whether it is work on governance, education reform or a range of other areas, as well as the election process, which you've discussed. We also know that if we're serious about two states, and I appreciate you have a different view about two states—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That's not—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sorry, you have a different view about whether Australia should contribute to it.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, no.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, you do. You want to wait and see if it happens.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Don't verbal me, because that's—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sorry, I apologise. I thought that was the conservatives' position.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The opposition's—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The opposition's position.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The opposition's position's not relevant to the question, but you're putting words in our mouths.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I think what I would say to you is we have worked with, for example, Indonesia and the PA in relation to progress on some of those issues, and Dr King or Dr Webster—everyone's a doctor—can take you through some of the programs we have engaged in, including our trilateral work.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I will get them to do that in a minute. But, just before we get to that, you said just then that the government's position is predicated on the commitments. So, if something is predicated on the commitments, then we need to know how likely it is that those commitments are going to be fulfilled, and, if they're not fulfilled, we need to know what the consequences are. That's why I asked. If something is predicated on commitments, what assessment was made at the time about the likelihood of the Palestinian Authority's ability to honour those commitments?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I don't think we've got much further to add. As the minister said, everybody knows that there's work to be done.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: PSM, Secretary

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
Senator, this is the problem with your position—continued tests, thresholds, for the Palestinian people that you keep setting before you all go to a two-state process. Meanwhile, thousands of people, including children, are displaced; human rights abuses continue to occur in the West Bank; and the former Israeli government continues to build settlements which, on the ground, render a two-state solution impossible or highly unlikely. So your position is we sit back and say, 'They're not good enough, and we're not going to do anything about it, whilst we allow the only prospect of peace in the Middle East to be rendered impossible.' I do not think that's responsible, and I do not think that's in our interests.

We have a different view. We have recognised. We are working with the PA on how to progress those commitments, and what I've also said is we would link further practical steps on recognition by Australia with those commitments. I've made that public.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The opposition's position is interesting, and I look forward to debating that another time in another forum. But you're the government and this is Senate estimates, and this is where we ask about the government's policy.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And I'm happy to talk about that. I accept that. I'm making a slightly different point. I'm actually making a philosophical point, a policy point, with you, because the position you're asserting is the same position, I think, that others have asserted for many years, which is 'We're not going to have progress towards two states; it's got to be between the parties, and the Palestinians have to do A, B and C.' That ignores the reality of what the Netanyahu government sought to do, which was to make a two-state solution impossible on the ground. And so, in the face of that, the theoretical proposition that we're just going to wait for the Palestinians to do all these things means you accept the removal of the possibility of two states by inaction.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm actually not—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's a fundamental foreign policy distinction.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Minister, I'm actually not asserting anything this morning. I'm just asking questions about how the government's policy is working in reality.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes. And I—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That's what I'm interested in—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sure. And—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: and I think that's reasonable in Senate estimates.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Of course it is, Senator. But I'm saying to you we start from a different position. You're saying you shouldn't do anything because you should just wait for all these things to happen. I'm saying, if we do that, there is no Palestine left to recognise.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Winston Churchill—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: If I may, there is no Palestine left to recognise if we just wait.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, and—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And that is the same position that the United Kingdom took. It's the same position that Canada took. It's the same position that France has taken. It is the same position that so many of our like-mindeds have taken—that we cannot simply sit back and wait and watch the reality of a Palestinian state be removed.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sure. I'm paraphrasing, but Winston Churchill once said, no matter how good the intentions are, occasionally we should check the results. So what I'm trying to do today is check the results on your good intentions.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And the results of your position, of an alternative position—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We're the opposition, Minister. You are the government. This is—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator Paterson, I'm not trying to set up an opposition political debate.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sort of seems like it.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, no, I'm actually making a point, which is: it depends what your policy position is. If your policy—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, and I just want to assess how your policy is going. How is it working out, Minister, is what I'm trying to get to.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You are critical of this. I accept that you're entitled to be. But the alternative position—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I haven't even been critical yet. I'm just asking questions about how it's going.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Can I just finish? The alternative is that we sit back, the UK sits back, Canada sits back, all of Europe sits back, and we just wait for the continuation of a whole range of activities which we know on the ground mean that there will never be a Palestinian state, and we're not prepared to do that.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Minister, as we all know, you won the election. You're the government.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Your policy has been implemented. I'm just trying to see how that's going in practice.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sure.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So let's try and get to that, if we can. We set out five areas that our commitment was predicated on and that the Palestinian Authority gave us assurances about. Sorry, can you run through them again for me? Governance?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sorry, could you just restate the question?
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Could you set out those five preconditions again for me? There was governance.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes. Reform governance, terminate prisoner payments, institute schooling reforms, demilitarise and hold general elections.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. Let's go through them one by one. How are governance reforms going in the Palestinian Authority?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Before I do that, just going to the Foreign Minister's point, both the Prime Minister and the Foreign Minister have underscored to their counterparts in the Palestinian Authority the importance of following through on their commitments.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Good.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Most recently, the Foreign Minister spoke to the Palestinian foreign minister on 10 August, and we have made very clear that further Australian steps on recognition, such as establishing diplomatic relations, will be considered once the PA makes further reform progress. That is the overall posture.

text: No, I don't think I did ask that question. I'm asking how governance reforms are going.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Fine. In this case, we assess that the PA has made significant progress on its reform commitments along the metrics in social payments. We believe they've instituted a needs based system for social payments. They've substantially delivered on this. This is replacing the 'pay for slay' arrangements.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

We have provided $5 million over 2024 to 2027 to build Palestinian Authority capacity. witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: To clarify, I'm not asking about what Australia has done to assist the Palestinian Authority. I'm asking what progress the Palestinian Authority has made against each of these objectives. What is our assessment of the progress the Palestinian Authority has made on governance?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Starting with governance—what progress has been made on governance?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, two points. This is a hard and long process, and that is recognised by the fact that President Trump's peace plan, which also talks about progress on a range of governance fronts, is still being implemented. Obviously, this is a process of reform which many parties, including the United States but also Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom, are engaged in. It's not a tick-a-box process, and, if it were, we probably would have peace in the Middle East. It is relevant, what we are doing—because your political proposition, which is very obvious, is about whether it's been achieved. These are still a work in progress, and it is important to see what we are doing. Now, I think Dr King indicated that there had been progress in—what were the payments? How did you describe the payments?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The social payments.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thanks, Minister. I have limited time. There are other senators who might wish to ask different questions, but it's not up to you to tell me which questions I should ask in this forum.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Perhaps there are other senators—perhaps a government senator—willing to ask a question that's not my question. My question is: what progress has been made on governance? I haven't heard any answer about any progress made on governance. So, if there is nothing to add because there has been no progress, we can move on to payments. But I just want to be clear that we don't have any assessment of progress on governance before we move on to payments.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We will get you an assessment on that.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. Let's move on to payments. What is your assessment about the improvement on payments?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On the payments reform, Australia is working with partners to hold the PA to account on its reform commitments, including on prisoner payments. As part of the PA's reform agenda, President Abbas committed publicly to repealing the law regarding payments to families of prisoners and martyrs and the implementation of a non-discriminatory social security system that is open to international audit. The July 2026 report by a US firm, Alvarez and Marsal, assessed that the social payment reform, the so-called pay for slay, has been substantially delivered. The PA has enacted new laws that apply the same eligibility standards to all families in need of social welfare assistance and has revoked previous laws and regulations related to the system of paying financial allowances to the families of prisoners, martyrs and the wounded. The new system has been implemented by the Palestinian National Economic Empowerment Institution. On 10 November 2025, President Abbas dismissed PA finance minister Omar Bitar after an internal investigation showed that he'd authorised payments to Palestinian prisoners outside the guidelines of the new system. In January 2026, the PA completed an audit of databases and beneficiary eligibility documentation to ensure that all parts of the Palestinian government were complying with the new system.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I have just a couple of follow-up questions there. I noticed you used the word 'martyr'. Is that terminology the Australian government uses?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, it is not.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That was a quote.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It was a quote.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Right. That's why I asked. You said also that President Abbas committed to repealing the scheme. Has it actually been repealed?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes. He's enacted new laws.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So it's not just a commitment to repeal; the legislation has been repealed?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, and the assessment from the consultants that Dr Webster mentioned says it has been substantially delivered. There's a new system in place called Tamkeen.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So there are no payments being made to people who've been convicted of terrorism?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That is our understanding.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So you would say that has been delivered?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
