witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: 'Substantially' leaves a bit of room. So what aspects of it have not been delivered, then?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I can't go into the details of that, but we are pleased that new laws have been enacted and that there is a commitment to stand by those laws and their implementation.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sorry, can you just clarify why you can't go into the detail of what 'substantially delivered' constitutes?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Because we're not—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I don't have the—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This is a report from the United States entity. So, obviously, we're relying on their report. I'd again make the point these are reforms that are discussed in the Trump peace plan. So, obviously, there are a lot of international eyes on this. We've been removed from Ramallah by the Israeli government. So we actually don't have personnel on the ground to do this. We rely on the work of others.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So we concur with that assessment that it's been substantially delivered?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We believe it's a reliable source document, I think.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And no payments are being made?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, we're relying on what an American entity has ascertained.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Moving on to the schooling reforms, what's our assessment of progress on schooling?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On education reform, the Palestinian Authority is developing a new curriculum in line with UNESCO standards, and they're partnering with the European Union on that initiative. From 16 to 27 April this year, Australia and Indonesia jointly delivered an education dialogue with the Palestinian Ministry of Education and Higher Education and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The program focused on integrating national curriculum into religious schools and strengthening teacher training and professional development. It showcased Indonesia's approach to education reforms and how Australia has supported those reforms through our development partnership.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Can I just add to that? This was very important. I really wanted us to work with Indonesia on something associated with the PA reform process. There are a number of reasons for that. One amongst them is, obviously, they have a very different relationship with the Palestinians. They are very close to and have worked with the Palestinian Authority over many years. So, if we're really trying to support reform and therefore peace in the Middle East, it is a very good partnership to work with Indonesia. It also goes to the closeness we have with Indonesia that we are trusted enough to work with them on this. So that was a measure that I encouraged former foreign minister Sugiono to agree to because I thought it was a good thing in terms of our relationship with Indonesia but also in terms of the effectiveness of the engagement with the Palestinian Authority.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: One of the contentious issues in this space has been the incitement in educational materials—dehumanisation of Jews and advocacy of violence. So is it our assessment that those classroom materials, including textbooks and other teaching materials, are no longer being taught in Palestinian Authority schools?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's our assessment that there are very few instances of that. The Palestinian Authority is working with the European Union on an initiative to deliver curriculum on UNESCO standards. We believe the instances of offensive material are very minor.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Could you expand on what you mean by 'very minor'?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I would have to check the figures, but there are very limited instances, to the best of our understanding.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It has previously been rife. We've all seen horrific examples of the textbooks provided to kids depicting Jews as devils and glorifying so-called martyrs, terrorists. So that's not currently prevalent in the Palestinian school system?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That is not currently prevalent. They're working very seriously with the European Union and with UNESCO on this.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. Moving on to demilitarisation, what's our assessment of the progress on demilitarisation?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That is a work in progress. To get a detailed response, we'd have to come back to you on that. But it is obviously a challenge because of the Hamas factor.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Could you expand on that, please. Saying it's a challenge is probably an understatement.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The PA security authority has worked very closely with the Israeli authorities and their security partners on this. But to get you a detailed assessment on progress on that, I'd have to come back to you.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This is part of President Trump's peace plan. This is not a bilateral issue about what Australia can do.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Minister, to be clear, I'm not holding you responsible.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, but I'm making a slightly broader point, actually. This is all of the countries, including, obviously, the US, but also the Arab and Muslim countries who were central to negotiating that peace plan. We were not part of that negotiating group, obviously, but we, like the rest of the world, supported it after it had been agreed. But this is one of the challenges for implementing that peace plan that has to be met.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sure. I'm not saying the Australian government is responsible for delivering this, but the Australian government said its recognition was predicated on these things. So I'm just trying to understand to what extent they've been delivered. It doesn't sound like we're particularly optimistic about that.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: About which?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: About the delivery of demilitarisation.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's very central.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's central to whether or not there can be two states.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Indeed.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And that is a challenge for the whole world.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Moving on to elections, I think President Abbas is 21 years into his four-year term. How are we going on elections?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The minister joined other minister counterparts in expressing our disappointment at the postponement of the elections. We've called on them in Ramallah to ensure that elections take place without delay. It was part of their commitment, as we said before, and we continue to make clear our expectations on that matter.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Were we surprised that we've had yet another delay in Palestinian Authority elections?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As the minister said, we were disappointed in it.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: 'Disappointed' doesn't seem all that strong. It's one of the core commitments. This is not the first time.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: To be clear, we expressed deep disappointment in it, yes.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: 'Deep disappointment'? That's a bit stronger. Why should we anticipate that there will ever be elections for the Palestinian Authority, given how often they have now been delayed?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I think that's asking Dr King for an opinion.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Not on a matter of policy.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It is an opinion. You're not—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Minister, as you know, the standing orders only prevent—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Am I allowed to finish my answer?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You are, Minister; you are.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. I'll start again. I think you're asking Dr King to express an opinion. The way I would respond to you is this. Credible elections are an important element of what the Palestinian Authority has committed to the whole of the international community, not just to Australia, and on reform, democratic renewal and governance. What I've also said is that we see this as linked to further practical steps on recognition, such as the establishment of reciprocal embassies.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So, to be clear, the standing orders prevent senators from asking officials for an opinion on a matter of policy. I'm not asking Dr King or any other official for an opinion on a matter of policy. I'm asking for the department's assessment about the likelihood of Palestinian elections occurring given that the Australian government's policy is predicated on elections being held.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I think that is the definition of a question about an opinion—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm not—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You're saying, 'What do you think will happen?'

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, Minister—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You can't ask him that.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Minister, you know the purpose of the standing orders. It is to prevent the officials being put in a difficult position to express a view about the desirability of government policy, because they're apolitical. I'm not asking Dr King or anyone else to say if the government's policy is good or bad. I'm asking Dr King, or anyone else who's got the expertise and can assist me, how likely it is that the Palestinian Authority is going to hold elections given they've delayed them so many times.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I've answered the question.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You haven't, actually.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, I've responded—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What's your assessment then, Minister, if you won't let the officials answer? What's your assessment? How many more times will President Abbas be allowed to delay elections before we recognise that maybe he does not intend on holding them at all?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'll respond to you by saying that that's like asking you, 'When will Israel stop building settlements that prevent a Palestinian state?' We are not—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm not the government. It's not my policy.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You misunderstand. That wasn't actually a partisan point. We're not in control of what happens in the Middle East. All we can do is establish principle policy parameters that Australia operates within and that Australia seeks to make a contribution to. I've explained to you how that is. I've put a view about the elections. That is a view shared by the ministers with whom I made that statement, which I think was Canada, UK and France. We have put that view. You're asking Australian officials, as I remind you, with limited representation in country to make an assessment about something that so many countries are seeking to have happen.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Look—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I don't think that's a fair question for Dr King.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I've responded in the way I think is appropriate. You can make a political comment about that, but—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I don't need to make a political comment. I'll ask a final question, and then the chair wants to rotate the call.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sure.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Your government's policy on Palestinian statehood recognition is predicated on the delivery of these key issues, including elections. So my question to you, Minister, on government policy, is: if the Palestinian Authority continues to delay elections and doesn't deliver on its commitment to the Australian government and the international community, are there any circumstances under which the government will revoke the recognition of Palestinian statehood?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No. We have recognised the state of Palestine.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's not a precondition then, is it?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, we have recognised the state of Palestine, and that is a contribution to peace in the Middle East, because there is no peace—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So they don't have to adhere to these—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: May I finish? There is no peace without two states. What I have done is done where we are able. And we're not the central player here. We're not the key player, but where we are able to make a contribution to that reform, we are doing so. And I've made clear a number of the steps on recognition. In relation to recognition, we are linked to the observance of the delivery of those commitments.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But you've just said that it doesn't matter whether they deliver on these or not; we will not change our policy. We'll continue to recognise Palestinian statehood even if they don't deliver on those preconditions, Minister.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, as the Minister has said, we recognise the state of Palestine. What we made clear at the time was that further steps, including the establishment of diplomatic relations and the opening of embassies, would be considered as the Palestinian Authority makes progress on its commitments to reform. So the recognition has happened, but further steps are contingent on these.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. So, Minister, why would the Palestinian Authority feel any need to deliver on these commitments, given that you won't change your policy? You will allow them to flout these and not change your policy.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: They're your words. I disagree with them. And, really, the Palestinian people want a state.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sure.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Let's be clear—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's a legitimate aspiration.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, I do need to move the call.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Oh, my goodness. You just won't let me finish, will you?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Minister, conclude, and I'll have to move the call around.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The Palestinian people want a state, and we want to see those commitments delivered. And we want to see them delivered because we want to see progress towards two states, which is also why we have taken the view we have about the actions of the Netanyahu government in the West Bank.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On that note, I'll hand the call over to Senator Hodgins-May.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Minister, today we learned that two—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sorry. Can we just get the area?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes. It's in relation to the UN rapporteurs on climate writing to the Australian government.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Climate.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, but it's relating to DFAT too.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That's fine. I'll just try and get—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We're just going to get the appropriate officials up to the table. I think that's what the minister is trying to indicate.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Pacific or global?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Global.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Minister, today we learned that two UN special rapporteurs have formally put allegations to the Australian government about your coal and gas expansion, subsidies to fossil fuel companies, lobbying and influence from these companies and the consequences for young people. This follows a formal complaint lodged by nine brave young Australians with the UN special rapporteur on climate and human rights. I've had the privilege of meeting with those young people today. Minister, are you, or the department, able to share when you first became aware of the UN special rapporteur's letter?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm not sure we are aware of that letter, but this would be a lead, as I understand it, of the Department of Climate Change, Environment, Energy and Water.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Climate Change Division, and Ambassador for Climate Change

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But the government has responded to this letter and it is with the United Nations. Is that not something that you're aware of?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We are aware that we received that communication, and it is with the department of climate change to respond to that. We haven't seen the letter today, but this would be the responsibility of the department of climate change.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Multilateral Policy and Human Rights Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I note that it was signed by the ambassador and deputy permanent representative to the UN, Ms Roper, last week, but DFAT didn't have any involvement?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Our permanent mission in Geneva is often the conduit for these communications. They represent the entire Australian Government. In this case, it was a communication by that department. But they certainly represent all government agencies and transmit those communications to the UN.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Multilateral Policy and Human Rights Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So the minister had no involvement in this letter or the consideration behind the input into that letter?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Not that I'm aware of, but we can take that on notice.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Multilateral Policy and Human Rights Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And the department, DFAT, didn't have any involvement in that?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: My division is aware of the communications as they come in. We often make sure the relevant agency is then aware of it and is actioning it. We can remind them of the due dates—
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Multilateral Policy and Human Rights Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But you didn't have any input.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: but we're not responsible for the content.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Multilateral Policy and Human Rights Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And no input?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I can double-check for you that we didn't have. We certainly are aware of communications as they come in and track them, but very often—in fact, mostly—we're not the responsible agency for the content.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Multilateral Policy and Human Rights Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. I will note that the response which I've read today doesn't actually address any of the UN's allegations. It makes no commitment to stopping approving new coal and gas projects, ending fossil fuel subsidies or preventing lobbyists from influencing climate policy. In fact, it doesn't even mention young people once, despite it being 11 pages long. Has DFAT assessed whether the government's continued approval of coal and gas is consistent with our human rights obligations?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Not in my division. It is for other areas of government to look at that issue.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Multilateral Policy and Human Rights Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: By your division, you mean all DFAT?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Do you think it's appropriate for Australia to be co-hosting the COP international climate conference when we have the UN special rapporteurs—not one, but two special rapporteurs—telling us that we are failing young people on climate?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: He could give a version. Senator, I understand your party's position on this. You've been consistent on it, and I think I've responded to some of your questions. What I would say about the pre-COP is that, for many years, including when I was climate minister and Ms Adams was my Ambassador for Climate Change many years ago, we have always sought to try and elevate the Pacific's perspective and their issues in the Conference of the Parties process. In Copenhagen, for example, I remember redrafting the elements of the Copenhagen Accord with the Pacific. This is part of what I think Australian foreign policy should be. So I see the pre-COP in the Pacific as being very much in line with that responsibility and partnership that we have with the Pacific, as a member of the Pacific family. We want to try and work with them to do as they seek in international fora, and that is what they wanted, so we respected and backed their desire to have more leaders and more senior ministers see what their lived experience is. What was interesting for me is that, in my bilateral recently, I think with the Nepali foreign minister—he's from a country that has experienced such devastation, but a very different country; I think he was one that went to Tuvalu—he said, 'Here I am from a mountain country, and I see climate change in this way. But in Tuvalu, I saw it through their eyes as well.' So that is very important. You're entitled to your position on the resources sector. We understand that. agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you for that adjudication, Chair. I want to ask a different set of questions to officials dealing with the devastating flash flooding around the Nepal-China border. Just at the outset, I'm interested in getting an update from officials on the situation on the ground in the affected areas, including the current status of operations.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
The Foreign minister just referred to meeting her Nepali counterpart in Melbourne on 8 October, where she made clear that we stand with Nepal as part of its very long journey on a protracted recovery. In terms of the latest situation on the ground, two months after this very unprecedented and devastating landslide affected Nepal, reconstruction and recovery continues. The immense scale of the disaster remains very significant. There are still well over 5,000 people missing, including 34 Australians; my colleague from the consular division can give you an update on that, if you wish.

On the ground, the scale of the disaster has limited access to some of the affected area, impacting relief efforts and local emergency services. Secondly, some isolated areas still rely on air support, with damaged roads and poor weather continuing to disrupt delivery of relief and recovery supplies. Thirdly, shelter remains a key challenge, particularly as the weather worsens, and, as the Nepali foreign minister advised our minister, some locations are fundamentally unsafe to resettle. We're shifting towards supporting its long-term recovery, particularly as the Nepal government has announced a transition from search and rescue to longer-term recovery and identification.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, South and Central Asia Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. In relation to the Australians that are missing, I think there are still 34 missing Australians. Can you confirm that and what efforts the government is making to support families of those missing Australians, and what services and supports are available.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
There are 34 missing Australians from that devastating flooding event in Nepal and China. Our first priority has been to support families through an extraordinarily distressing and prolonged period of uncertainty for them. That support began in the acute response phase and is continuing to this day as the focus shifts to recovery, identification, coronial and longer-term missing-person processes. By 1 September, each affected family group had a dedicated, experienced DFAT consular case officer as its primary point of contact, and that provided them with continuity and regular telephone and written updates. Those DFAT case officers have worked alongside AFP family investigative liaison officers and Services Australia social workers to provide coordinated support to families, including to explain disaster-victim-identification and coronial processes and to connect those families with practical and psychological support.

The Australian government family support hub commenced in Kathmandu on 7 September, providing a dedicated place for families in Nepal to receive briefings and meet with consular staff and social workers. DFAT convened a whole-of-government virtual family meeting on 9 October with AFP, Services Australia, Home Affairs, NEMA and Health. The virtual meeting provided updates, enabled direct questions to responsible agencies and identified a range of follow-up actions, which we are completing. There's been a family centred, trauma informed engagement plan that coordinates continuing support across government, which DFAT has led. This covers proactive contact with families, which is tailored to their preferences. It covers recovery and identification processes, repatriation and coronial matters, practical and financial issues, wellbeing referrals and longer-term family needs. Eligible Australians affected by the crisis can also access Australian government disaster recovery payments. NEMA and DFAT are continuing to engage financial institutions, insurers and relevant industry bodies on difficulties arising from unresolved missing-persons cases, and we will continue to support those families for as long as is needed.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. In terms of the search and rescue operations themselves, how do you decide as an agency what specialist services, officials or capabilities to send? I understand that in this case there might have been specialist drone operators. What's the decision-making process there, and what were some of the capabilities sent to the rescue efforts?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
The first important point to make is that we respond to the requests from the Nepali government—so what is the nature of the assistance they want? Very early on, I think on day 2, the Foreign minister had a call with her counterpart, and we made the full offer of all our urban search and rescue capability. At that time, they weren't ready to receive large urban search and rescue teams, but, as the situation evolved, eventually on 2 September they realised they did need some more specialised search and rescue capability through the provision of drones and drone support—so, like I said, that took a few days.

By 4 September we had sent, that evening, a 15-person DART team, which is our disaster assistance response capability; this sits within the fire and rescue services departments of Queensland and New South Wales as a combined team—15 drone operators, a team lead, some logistics support and two types of drones. There were small drones that could access structures, and they were specifically used to support some of the tunnel work, if you remember, that was going on. A lot of the hydro tunnels got flooded. There were a lot of workers still trapped in there. They were able to access those tunnels and provide some imagery and support to the teams working on those operations. There were larger drones that could do aerial surveillance, and they were able to search parts of the valley, including some of the places which were the last known locations of many of the Australians and other people that went missing in those floods.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Humanitarian and Civil Society Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. Finally, moving from search and rescue to the recovery and resilience package and the $15 million announcement earlier this month, can you give some insight into what that will deliver and how that is different from the initial support that was provided.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
As mentioned, that recovery process is going to be extremely protracted. Nepal's own rapid damage and needs assessment puts recovery needs at around A$7.7 billion. As mentioned, the Foreign minister met her Nepali counterpart in Melbourne on 8 October and announced a $15 million recovery and resilience package. That follows on from the $11 million in increments in immediate humanitarian support that Mr Scott has referred to.

That recovery component is broken into two parts. The first is around $5 million for recovery. That will support climate resilient infrastructure that restores essential services. We intend to work through international organisations in line with Nepal's priorities, and this will focus on rebuilding and restoring disaster affected education, health, water and sanitation infrastructure, and restoring access to essential services. It will also provide technical advice on infrastructure investments that incorporate climate resilience and disaster-risk-reduction best practice. Secondly, the resilience component, which will make around $10 million, will help address the risk of future flooding through early warning, water management and disaster resilient planning and management. This will be done through existing partnerships—and the minister has mentioned just how appreciative the Nepali Foreign minister was to attend the pre-COP meeting in Tuvalu and to make the connection between melting glaciers and rising sea levels.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, South and Central Asia Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Can I just add one thing on Nepal. One of the things we did was to announce and publicise—and I think the media organisations have also assisted with this—the Emergency Action Alliance appeal, which is essentially a platform of multiple NGOs that come together to encourage Australians to donate and provide a platform for Australians to donate. I announced that we would match it. Australians donated from their own pockets more than $20 million—is that right?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, that's right.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, South and Central Asia Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That's right.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Humanitarian and Civil Society Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Which was at a time when we know the cost-of-living pressures that people are experiencing. If you want something that makes you feel more optimistic, for me that was heartwarming—to see the response from the Australian community to that appeal. The government was happy to just slightly more than match that contribution.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator Paterson.

text: I just want to get through some consular cases, now that we have the opportunity. I'll preface these questions by saying there'll be some cases that we won't ask about today; it's due not to a lack of interest in any particular case but advice about the sensitivities involved and the best interests of those people. Senator Smith, my colleague, will come and ask some specific questions about a specific case; I'll leave that to him. If we could start with Dr Yang Jun.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We remain appalled by Dr Yang's suspended death sentence. We're continuing to raise with China our longstanding, principled and bipartisan opposition to the death penalty, including at the highest levels, and we're continuing to advocate for Dr Yang's interests and wellbeing.

witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you; I'll leave it there. Could you give me an update on Mr Gordon Ng, please.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On Mr Gordon Ng, we remain deeply concerned about his case and the broad application of national security legislation in Hong Kong. We continue to advocate for his interests and welfare, including through repeated senior level representations to Hong Kong and China mainland authorities. We remain in contact with Mr Ng's family and will continue to monitor his welfare and pursue consular access to him, which we do not have.

witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. And an update on Mr Oscar Jenkins, please.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On Mr Jenkins, the Australian government is appalled at the sham trial and the 13-year sentence given to Mr Oscar Jenkins. As a full serving member of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Mr Jenkins is a prisoner of war. We've made clear to Russia our expectation that it comply with its obligations under international humanitarian law, including with respect to prisoners of war. We're providing consular support to Mr Jenkins's family, who have requested privacy.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. That's all the cases I had. As I said, Senator Smith will raise a specific case later today.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Given our earlier discussion around multiple special rapporteurs contacting the Australian government in relation to our rights and responsibilities with respect to climate change, do you think it's appropriate that DFAT is engaging in fossil fuel sponsorship arrangements?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As I said, I was not the minister primarily involved in the development of the pavilion at the expo, so I feel—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But more broadly speaking.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I think you always have to be aware of the implications of sponsorship, and I'm sure that the minister and department considered that. Our policy positions remain the same. It is a good thing for us to promote Australia through the expo. As I said, I understand a lot of people visited, and I'm sure we can provide some further information on notice or later in the hearing.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Looking at DFAT annual reports over the last five years, it looks like DFAT has accepted fossil fuel sponsorships for events like Australia Day celebrations in Mexico and Japan from companies like Woodside, Chevron and IMPEX. At a time when we're debating energy security and gas policy and when the UN itself has expressed concerns around the influence of fossil fuels on government, it's really puzzling that DFAT can justify accepting this sort of corporate sponsorship, or corporate investment, from corporations that are actively lobbying to protect their profits. Do you think that creates a potential conflict of interest, Minister?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You've asked similar questions previously, and the point I would make is we take decisions which we believe are the right decisions for the country. We make decisions, including those which are opposed or which members of the sector have concerns about. We have said, for example, we would implement a gas reservation scheme—which I think is currently in the Senate; is that right?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Not yet, but it will be.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's in the House. Parts of industry have expressed their views about that. We've done that because it's the right thing to do.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I suppose it's more the conflict of interest that I'm trying to home in on.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, you continue to interrupt me, and I'm trying to be polite and not interrupt your questions.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm trying to be specific though.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But I'm entitled to answer it as I wish. You can ask a follow-up question. The proposition that your party continues to put—and Senator Milne put it to me, so it is a continued position of your party—is somehow because people give us sponsorship. We have a position that we think is right.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So they are doing this out of the goodness of their heart?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, excuse me—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Profit driven corporations are investing $1 million—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Hang on, Senator. We take—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: out of goodwill for this country.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Please, come on.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Please, let me finish.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's mind-boggling.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, I'm trying to be polite. Could you please be polite?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I will try.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. Could you just not interrupt me every time I speak?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Please keep it specific. We get 10-minute blocks—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, you don't get to decide how I answer a question. You get to follow up—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senators, come on.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: but I get to speak my words. What I'm saying is we make decisions that are in the national interest. You seem to assume that people don't agree with you are somehow corrupt. That is not the case. We just don't—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You're putting words in my mouth.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We just don't agree. We have a different view about what is right. In terms of the management of conflicts of interest, I'm sure others in the department can speak to about how they are dealt with, and I'm happy for them to deal with that. But the fundamental political proposition that you continue to assert is that somehow government makes decisions that are not in the national interest but only in the interests of particular companies. You are wrong.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Why do you think these corporations make these investments?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You are wrong.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Minister, why do you think that Santos would put $1 million in towards a convention like this? I'm genuinely curious to understand how you think that is appropriate and why these corporations would make those sorts of contributions.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: If I could provide some background, for hosting a big undertaking like an exhibition pavilion at a global expo—in this case with a very important partner, Japan—it's very standard practice for government to seek sponsorship.

text: DFAT sought sponsorship from Australian companies with something to add to themes of the expo and who were involved in the relationship with Japan. I reiterate what the minister said about how our policy decision-making process is not affected by those particular sponsorship arrangements in any way. We were very pleased to have around three million visitors through the Australian pavilion. It had universal acclaim, and we were very pleased to participate in Japan's important expo. I still don't really, to my satisfaction, have an answer about why these corporations would invest that money and what they are getting in return and whether this government thinks it genuinely passes the pub test, the public interest test—for massive multinational exporters of gas making huge mint off our resources to get to make these types of investments. text: You just made a political point, so I'm going to respond, Senator.

text: You chose to do that. These are the same gas companies we are opposing a reservation on for the Australian people.
