text: This has nothing to do with that. I turn up every time asking these questions on corporate capture.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But what I would say to you is we have a clear view about what we believe is in the national interest. You're entitled to have a different view. We are proceeding with the gas reservation, which will deliver cheaper gas for Australians. That obviously has a financial effect on the companies. I understand you have a different position. You're entitled to that. That is the position that we are seeking to proceed with through the Senate, and I look forward to your party voting for a gas reservation, which would enable Australians to have access to cheaper gas.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We've been very clear that the Australian people—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Look forward to it.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: want to make revenue off this. I'd like to request on notice an outline of all sponsorship agreements entered into by DFAT with fossil fuel companies over the past decade and if any risk assessment was completed for each.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm not doing it over the last decade.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Let's say five years.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, I will see if—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Since you've been in government then, let's do that.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I will consider the resource implications of that, but I'm certainly not doing it for previous governments.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: For your government, I will rephrase.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We'll have a look at that, absolutely.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And also if any risk assessment was completed for each, any conflicts of interest identified, as well as DFAT sponsorship policy or guidelines, if that exists. Thank you.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We are always aware of conflicts of interest. And this comes back to the same point you made, which is, I think, the implication that the government changes policy because we get $1 million for an expo. This is a multibillion, multidecadal generational reform.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's not just me who thinks this.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's really an extraordinary proposition.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Alright. Senator Paterson.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I have some questions about the Foreign minister's speech to the United Nations in September. Dr King, did the department provide an initial draft of the speech to the Foreign minister's office?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, we did.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Was the speech then edited by the Foreign minister's office before delivery, or was it delivered as drafted?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: My understanding is it was delivered as drafted.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: In the draft provided to the Foreign minister's office, what number was used in relation to children displaced as a result of settler violence in the West Bank?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The figure was over 15,000.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What's the source of that claim?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The source of that is an OCHA document. We use reports by UN OCHA, the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, because their figures are widely relied on in the humanitarian system, reflecting their central role in coordinating data analysis and response. In this instance, the figure given was for the wrong period.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Could you table that document.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I certainly could.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: When you say it was for the wrong period, what does that mean?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It means it was for an 18-month period rather than a six-month period. To be specific, it was for the period of January 2025 until July 2026. That's something for which I accept responsibility. It was provided in error.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The speech referred to the number of displaced people over a six-month period, but the figure was actually over an 18-month period.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That is correct. The figure was from UN OCHA, and it said, 'Over 41,000 Palestinians, including over 15,000 children, were displaced in the West Bank over 18 months as a consequence of settler violence, security operations and a range of punitive measures.' So, yes, you're right, and I take responsibility for the error.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's very good of you to do that. Was it just a transposition error? How did it occur?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, believe me, I'd like to know, but I take responsibility for it.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We are all human and we all make mistakes. It's very decent of you to take that responsibility. I note that there are UNICEF figures which are similar, in that they say between January and June of this year, 1,500 children were displaced. But you're saying it was a different dataset. It wasn't the UNICEF dataset.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That is correct.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: When did you realise the error occurred?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: After, unfortunately, the minister had delivered it.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As I understand it, the speech is on the DFAT website. Has the number been updated, or the time period been updated, to reflect the accurate data?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The speeches on the website are as delivered.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So you haven't added a note or anything to clarify it?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Not as far as I understand.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, International Security, Legal and Consular Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Has this been communicated or clarified by any other means—on the X account of the department or any other platform?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: If I could make a couple of comments about this, as you indicated, the 15,000 displaced children, in fact, should have been between January 2025 and July 2026. I think you would agree that's also not acceptable. That 15,000—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: However many it is, indeed.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: However many, over whatever period. Obviously, the website reflects what I said. I'm very conscious that there has also been criticism of other ministers for so-called doctoring of transcripts. It's a record of what I said. I think we were contacted by the media. I don't remember how many days after, sorry. We corrected the figure then, or the underlying timeframe for the figure. And we've done so again today.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Corrected it how? Corrected it where? To the media?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, to the media. We got a media inquiry, and we indicated to them what the underlying timeframe should have been for the figure.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There was an article by Matthew Knott on 30 September—that might be the one you're recalling, Minister.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm sorry, so much has happened these last few weeks.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Indeed.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, that may be the one, but I know that when asked, we explained what had occurred.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'll stand to be corrected, but I don't recall, having read that article, there being a correction in it. I think the journalist surmised that an error might have been made, but it certainly didn't say that the government or the Foreign minister or the department had conceded there was an error.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I think we indicated what the time period should have been. I haven't got the article in front of me, but that's my recollection. The relevant fact is not the 15,000 figure; it's the timeframe.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I take your word on that; I accept that evidence. I don't have the other dataset with me, but I accept that. Israel's foreign ministry has publicly asked where this data came from and for it to be corrected. Have you had any engagement with the Israeli foreign ministry or the embassy or any other arm of the Israeli government to clarify the remarks?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It hasn't been communicated with me directly that I know of; it hasn't been raised with me. Senator, can I also say to you—I'm advised by the office, by the way, that we did indicate to the journalist there had been an error. I don't have the article in front of me. We can have a discussion about timeframes, and I accept what was in the speech should have had a different timeframe. I accept that was an error. But we are talking about the context of 15,000 children being displaced over a very short period of time. I'm sure you would agree it's not acceptable.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I do agree. There's no debate about that. But it's also important that, when the Foreign Minister speaks, particularly at high-profile international forums like the United Nations, it's accurate and that, if an error is made, it's promptly, clearly and transparently acknowledged. This evidence to me today is the first I've heard of it being very clearly clarified on the public record. Particularly given a foreign government has asked for it to be publicly clarified, was there any consideration of either clarifying it with the Israeli government or clarifying it publicly prior to now?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, as I said, we did correct the record when asked by the media.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
Well, I'm not sure. Certainly, it was not clear to me, and I don't think it was clear to others, that that correction had been made. There's no on-the-record comment from you in this story, I'm advised. Perhaps your staff provided something on background to the journalist. The article simply states:

Wong is believed to have mistakenly used a figure referring to a longer time frame and more causes of displacement.

Clarifying to a journalist on background the source of the error is not the same as publicly identifying the mistake, because it's not just a journalist that's interested in these things; other people are interested in these things.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I think that's a political comment. What do you want me to—the officials have indicated what occurred, I've indicated what occurred. When a journalist asked us, we indicated what occurred. I mean, I think that's pretty transparent.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, there's a factual error on a speech on the department's website that has not been notified in any way. I've made errors before in interviews. Typically what we do is we put parentheses around it or an asterisk and have the updated figure so that anyone who comes to look at the website later and looks at it can and see what the original version of it was but also that the error is acknowledged. As I say, we're all human, we all make errors. But, in this instance, a visitor to the DFAT website would be none the wiser that the information in that speech is not correct.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I think Dr King has indicated what occurred. I think you've conceded it is 15,000 children displaced. It should have been over 18 months, not a six-month period. When we were asked about it, we indicated that the error had been made and indicated what it should have been.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We're in agreement that, whatever the number, it's not acceptable. Just to clarify, when we do say it was over 18 months, is it 15,000 displaced in the West Bank, or does it include Gaza as well?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: West Bank.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Middle East and Africa Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: West Bank only. Thank you, Chair.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'll keep rotating the call around. Senator Payman, I understand you've got some questions.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, thank you. Good morning. Does DFAT maintain an explicit position of non-engagement with the military junta?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: In Myanmar?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: In Myanmar, sorry.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There are a few in the world.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: My bad.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Even in some political parties too! Anyway.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Australia has consistently condemned the Myanmar regime's brutal and ongoing atrocities against the people of Myanmar. We have very limited engagement with the regime, and always in the national interest, in advocating or pursuing our national interests.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, South and Southeast Asia Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What steps is the Australian government taking to encourage ASEAN to maintain restrictions on the attendance of Myanmar military leaders at regional summits until meaningful progress towards fulfilment of the five-point consensus is made?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The Australian government supports ASEAN's leading role in trying to resolve the very bleak situation in Myanmar. Our participation in ASEAN led forums is critical to Australia's security and prosperity. Myanmar, of course, is a member of ASEAN. The Australian government, ministers, the Prime Minister, officials, refer to our concerns about the situation in Myanmar in depth when we meet ASEAN counterparts. It is very common, in fact, at all engagements that we have with ASEAN as a grouping, that we will outline our concerns about the situation in Myanmar and urge all efforts towards implementation of the five-point consensus.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, South and Southeast Asia Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Advocates within Myanmar have raised concerns with me about an upcoming ASEAN Regional Forum sponsored workshop on unmanned aircraft systems as part of the counterterrorism cooperation framework. I understand that Australia is a co-chair of this workshop with Singapore and the USA. Is that correct?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We're just checking that for you, Senator.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, South and Southeast Asia Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That's fine.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Australia is not co-sponsoring an ASEAN Regional Forum workshop on the use of unmanned aircraft systems.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting First Assistant Secretary, Southeast Asia Regional and Mainland Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Are we co-chairing any workshop in that regional forum?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We co-chair other work streams within the ASEAN Regional Forum. We are going to be co-chairing one on maritime security. I'm just trying to find—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting First Assistant Secretary, Southeast Asia Regional and Mainland Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: While the official is looking, you started your questions with, 'What is our framework in terms of engagement with the junta?' It would be useful, I think, just so you're aware, I did, as part of the advocacy for Sean Turnell to be released, engage with a representative from the military junta. You would also know, I hope, that we have continued to engage with the NUG. Obviously, we recognise states, not government. I met again with the National Unity Government's foreign minister last month, and also with Daw Aung San Suu Kyi's son.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: In 2026, Australia co-chaired two ASEAN Regional Forum officials-level meetings and one ASEAN Regional Forum experts and eminent persons meeting.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting First Assistant Secretary, Southeast Asia Regional and Mainland Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Can you confirm that the military junta in Myanmar would not be invited to participate in any of those workshops?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Consistent with ASEAN policies and processes, co-chairs invited all ASEAN Regional Forum members, including Myanmar. Australia did not provide funding support, and these meetings were not held in Australia.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting First Assistant Secretary, Southeast Asia Regional and Mainland Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Has Australia had any contact with other participants in relation to this issue around the engagement or involvement of the military junta participating?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: If I could just make a broader point, our engagement with ASEAN as a grouping, of course, is fundamental to Australia's security and prosperity, as I mentioned. It is a key regional grouping with which we engage. ASEAN leaders, after the 2021 coup, made a decision not to allow political-level representation at their summit meetings, meetings of leaders, and also in their Foreign Ministers' Meetings. That remains their position today. At ASEAN Foreign Ministers' Meetings and at the summits that are usually held twice a year, they do not take part at that level. It has been the practice that Myanmar is represented by an official.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, South and Southeast Asia Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you, Ms Chan. Thank you, Chair.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator Roberts, I understand you've got some questions on Japan.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I have, thank you, Chair. Thank you for appearing today. These questions, Senator Wong, are follow-ups from earlier questions regarding child support issues where children have been taken—stolen, rather—from a parent to now reside in Japan. I respect and admire the Japanese people. This is a difficult issue, and I understand it's sensitive, Senator Wong. We've discussed that in the past. What's changed, and what remains proposed in Australian child support law related to stolen children resident in Japan?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I don't think we can speak to child support legislation here. What we can speak to is the work we've done to advocate for the consideration of joint custody arrangements. I think that's the term that was used. The child support agency is not part of this portfolio.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Is someone going to speak to that?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We recognise the profound and continuing impact of parent-child separation on Australian families. This is a very difficult and sensitive issue, as you note. We have been working with Japan for a number of years now on their joint custody reforms. They have been in effect since 1 April this year. They're a very important step forward for Japan. They will not automatically change existing sole custody arrangements or resolve all legacy cases. What we have done, are doing and will continue to do is provide consular assistance to affected families. We're also advocating that the reforms be implemented in a way that supports children having relationships with both parents where that is in the best interests of the child.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator Wong, do you or the department give advice regarding changes of laws in this country on this matter?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sorry, changes of Australian law or changes of Japanese law?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Changes of Australian law, initially. What risks and representations aren't being considered?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm sorry, Senator, I don't quite understand. Is this adoption or is this joint custody?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Joint custody.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That would be a matter for the individuals in consultation with their lawyers. We do not provide legal advice as part of our consular service.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Are you giving advice in regard to the Australian government to change laws in Australia?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Oh, I see. Sorry. I thought you meant to individuals.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, that would be a matter for the portfolio, probably DSS.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Wouldn't they consult with you?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That would be a matter for Services Australia.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Surely they'd need to understand the situation in Japan. Surely you'd be giving them advice.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, I don't quite understand. I'm sorry, I don't quite understand the point you're making. What we have contributed to—I've raised it with a number of foreign ministers and we really appreciate the way in which Japan has progressed this—is we have spoken about our approach of joint custody. My recollection is that we had a Family Court judge go to Japan to talk through our legislative framework et cetera What are you asking? What are you saying should occur here in Australia?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What we've seen, Senator Wong, is wrongful removal or retention of children, unfulfilled return orders and prolonged obstruction of safe contact. Are these being assessed in reform designed in Australia? Our laws. Are you giving advice on these?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We don't give advice on child support laws. The usual practice of government is that if the department responsible believes it needs to engage with another portfolio, then that is done. I don't have personal knowledge of where the DSS has done that. Are you suggesting that the child support laws should be changed? Is that the assertion?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I just want to know if anything is being considered in regard to that, Senator Wong.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, that is a matter for the Department of Social Services.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You've had no interaction with Australian lawmakers on this topic?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, I am an Australian lawmaker—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I know that, but on this topic.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: and so are you. But I don't have knowledge of a reform where we've engaged on this.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. Thank you, that's all I wanted to know. What representations came from Japan or other foreign governments, and how are they being considered?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On what issue?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On the abduction of Australian children who now reside in Japan.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I think the way I'd approach that is, again, to go back to what I've spoken to you about before and that I referenced just then. Japan had a very different legal system in relation to this issue. That obviously meant that we had parents in Australia, or Australian parents, who were separated from their children and that was extremely distressing. We've advocated consistently and we've sought to provide consular support. We've spoken to them about legislative reform and we welcome their reforms from April 2026. We contributed by sharing our experience and our expertise in family law and dispute resolution. I don't know that I can add to that. I don't know if officials have anything further on that?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I think only to say that we've raised this at the very highest levels of the Japanese system over a number of years.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Will you continue to be doing that to advance the cause?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Which?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Because there's a sense that these reforms are minor. They're welcome, but they're minor.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We'll continue to advocate and we'll also continue to provide consular support to affected families. We're currently assisting 16 parents in relation to 23 children. Since 2004—that's how far back this assistance goes—we've assisted parents in relation to 90 children.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Are you able to tell me how big the issue is? For example, numbers of children affected, number of families affected, the amounts presumably collected for child custody payments?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I refer to my previous answer: we're currently assisting 16 parents in relation to 23 children and we've assisted parents in relation to 90 children since 2004. So we provide that consular assistance. We continue to advocate for the implementation of the reforms in the best interests of the affected children in these cases.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. How do disputed care determinations, qualifying contact costs, adjustments and direct payment credits operate internationally, including after interim protections expire?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator—
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Does that vary from country to country?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Custody and access decisions are matters for the Japanese courts. I would imagine that the situation varies for different countries, so I wouldn't speak to the broader global picture.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What mechanisms support safe contact and enforcement of relevant orders, and with what outcomes?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, again, they would be matters for the courts.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Have you considered proposed departure restrictions—assessing necessary child contact travel here in Japan as distinct from debt evasion—and what exemptions or review would be available? Are these matters you can influence?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, again, those are matters for the courts. And, in terms of Australian laws, they're matters for other agencies.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator Wong, the last time we spoke on this difficult issue, it was indicated that you had limited knowledge about seminars run in Brisbane for Japanese parents about taking children to live in Japan. One such seminar was held on 16 February 2024 at the Consulate-General of Japan in Brisbane. Attendees included Phoenix Law & Associates and an official from the Hague Convention Division in Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs. A representative of an organisation called 'International Social Security Australia' had been invited but pulled out beforehand. I'm just passing on advice because you had no information.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This was a Japanese government event in 2024?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Held at the Japanese consulate-general with representatives from Japan.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: A couple of years ago.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On 16 February 2024. Can you tell us any more about the April 2026 joint custody reforms in Japan? I know it's not long ago—only six months. Can you give parents hope?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, those reforms did come into effect on 1 April. As noted previously, we have done a lot of work with Japan both prior to that date, sharing expertise in terms of our experience in this very complex area. They are an important step. But now, of course, implementation lies ahead. We'll continue to work with Japan on that process. As noted previously, it will not automatically change existing sole-custody arrangements or resolve all legacy cases. But we are continuing to support Japan in this process to make sure that implementation occurs in a way that supports children having relationships with both parents, where it is in their interests.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. How will you assess the impact of these changes on Australian children and parents once more time elapses?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We welcome all feedback on our consular assistance. There are channels through which that feedback can be collected, including through our posts overseas and the Smartraveller website, as well as the conversations that we have with our clients. Through those channels, we will continue to gather information on the experience of our clients and use that to inform our engagement with Japanese authorities. That includes through regular consultations that we have with Japan on consular issues as well as other bilateral engagements that we have.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. Maybe we can liaise through the Minister's office to make sure you have the right details. Thank you. I might ask about preparedness for El Nino and what we're doing to support our neighbours. What's the department's assessment of the humanitarian risks associated with the 2026-27 El Nino in the Pacific and Timor-Leste?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
Yes, we are monitoring and tracking the El Nino very closely, and we see that the Bureau of Meteorology is estimating that those conditions will worsen in coming months. We expect there to be a peak between October—now—and December of this year, with the worst conditions in Papua New Guinea, Timor-Leste and Indonesia. Then we think that it will move eastwards into the first half of 2027 and we'll see more impact in Vanuatu, Tonga and Fiji, for example. We're tracking weather conditions that are affecting things like water shortages and reduced agricultural production, obviously, leading to food security issues, impacts on public health and impacts on hydroelectric generation and power supply.

Of course we're also aware that these things can be drivers of community tensions, conflict and violence as well. Some of this is compounded, too, by the Middle East conflict and the impact on fuel and energy supply in the region. The UN estimates that El Nino could result in an additional 8.2 million people facing acute food insecurity in Asia and the Pacific. So in our development program and our preparedness through the humanitarian program, we're looking at how we can adapt to these evolving circumstances. We've got flexibility built into many of our programs so that we can adjust to the situation as we discuss what's happening with partner countries and organisations in those countries. To date, we've committed more than $26 million to build community resilience and to respond to the impacts of El Nino. We can go into more detail about that, if you'd like it.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'd like to ask about the Foreign Arrangements Scheme—Research Security. Minister, the PJCIS warned in paragraph 3.21 of its August report that researcher-to-researcher arrangements are not captured by the Foreign Arrangements Scheme and can carry material risk. In your original bill on the foreign relations amendment, these types of arrangements weren't included. Why was that?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The scheme, originally, as conceived in 2020, covers enterprise-level arrangements, arrangements at the university between universities and foreign government partners. It doesn't cover individuals. As part of the legislative amendments that were just passed, it now includes researcher-to-researcher arrangements. Basically, the legislation now imposes an obligation on universities to identify research projects that are in place between researchers, employees of a university and foreign researchers, to have in place procedures and policies to identify the risks, to manage the risks and, essentially, to make sure that they implement those. Those were part of the amendments just passed.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Why weren't they included originally?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Back in 2020—I can't actually answer why individual arrangements weren't covered—essentially, the Foreign Arrangements Scheme, as originally conceived, was focused on the regulated community. Covered by the scheme were universities, so university-level arrangements; state and territory governments; and local governments. Those were the regulated community covered by the legislation, not individuals.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm not talking about the 2020 Foreign Arrangements Scheme, but the original bill, the Foreign Relations (State and Territory) Amendment Bill earlier this year.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The amendments flowed on from the independent review that was undertaken by Dr Rosemary Huxtable. The legislation reflects the recommendations made as part of that independent review. There were 23 recommendations. All of them were accepted or accepted in principle, by the government and implemented. There was no recommendation in that review relating to individual-level arrangements. As I said, the original scheme covered enterprise-level arrangements.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Was there no assessment that there was a risk there?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There are many risks in relation to foreign interference and other issues in the Australian environment. Not all of them are covered in legislation for which this agency is responsible.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As I understand it, there was a bill, and then there was amendment to that later on. Why in the original bill put forward by the government was there not the researcher-to-researcher arrangement covered?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, Senator—
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The amendment I agreed with Ted—you're complaining it wasn't in the original bill. Is that the political proposition?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm just asking questions. I'm just trying to work through—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, I'm just trying to understand what the point is. So, your complaint is—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, I'm just asking a question.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Why did the original bill not—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm not complaining, I'm asking questions.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Your complaint is, why did the original bill not include the amendment that I eventually suggested and agreed with your shadow, correct?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm asking, yes, why wasn't it in the original?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, Ted raised it. Ted raised with me your views, the opposition's views. I suggested to him this amendment was a way to deal with that, so then there was bipartisan support. I think it's an example of the legislature doing a good job.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I am going to get to that part of the process soon, and I'm just trying to understand why it wasn't in the original. Earlier this year, The Australian exposed collaborations involving researchers from the University of Sydney, UNSW and Adelaide University with Iranian scientists on drone technology. There are also more recent reports on research collaborations involving UNSW academics and scientists linked to China's PLA. Are you 100 per cent confident that comparable arrangements will now be captured and stopped under your amended legislation, if the university was not a party to the agreement?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Foreign Arrangements Scheme and the work that we do under it is just part of a whole-of-government piece of work that happens with universities to look at research security at universities, including researcher-to-researcher engagement. As part of the Foreign Arrangements Scheme, my team spent a lot of time talking to universities and working with universities to lift general awareness of risks and to lift due diligence, and capability, and we do so in combination with our agencies across the whole of government. That includes the Department of Education, which is responsible for universities. It includes the Department of Home Affairs, and it includes the intelligence and security agencies. Quite a bit of this discussion happens in UFIT, the Universities Foreign Interference Taskforce, which is a collaboration between government and universities to specifically look at risks. Now, that work has been going on for some time. Whole of government has been working with universities to actually identify risks, to manage risks, to do due diligence and to work on them. Foreign Arrangements Scheme is a very important part of that. This new provision that, as the minister said, was a bipartisan outcome of the legislative reform process that has just undertaken will be part of that work going forward. We continue to engage closely with universities on how that will be used to actually identify ongoing risks.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: DFAT has assessed whether these specific types of collaborations would be captured?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, we haven't made an assessment as to whether the particular one that you have identified would be captured. We will be working with and we are currently working with universities to look at what are those policies and procedures that universities will put in place. How do they manage them? What do they need to do to identify and assess risks? It is a new piece of legislation, a new obligation, quite a far-reaching obligation on universities, and it will be the subject of a lot of work. We haven't actually individually assessed some of these things that have appeared in the media as to whether they will fall within this. We are looking at how will we roll this out with universities to ensure that it is effective and that it is impactful, and to look at what it captures and how it captures them.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So the obligation is on the universities. Minister, will you have the power to cancel these individual researcher-to-researcher relationships?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
I will make a couple of points. I think the way in which the scheme envisages that is that the universities have the duty, not the government. In part, that is ensuring that the people who actually know about it can do something about it from the start. First, this is legislation that was brought forward in 2020. I thought at the time it was a bit rushed and the department doesn't have to respond to this. It was part of the Morrison government's attempt to promulgate its national security. That's probably a bit unfair. We were critical of it. I think we supported the legislation. I retained concerns about how they did it because it was, I thought, both not broad enough in remit but also very administratively problematic. That's why we asked Rosemary Huxtable, who is a distinguished public servant and a former secretary of finance, to do a comprehensive and independent review. I think the proper answer to why it wasn't included in the bill is, as I think Ms Heckscher said, because we followed the independent review's recommendations. We have consistently made clear that universities have to play their role in managing risks. That's what the legislation does. We would encourage universities to do that.

The point here is that national resilience—the resilience of the democracy and the resilience of particular parts of our polity, parts of the community and parts of government et cetera—is not only done by the government administering the scheme. It is also by Australians in leadership positions and in institutions like universities being risk aware and risk engaging, with recognition of the risks and making informed choices about what sort of engagement and with whom and making sure that is what they implement as policy and process inside their institutions. Canberra itself cannot regulate all that. We have thousands of researchers and thousands of employees at universities. We want the universities to discharge their obligation. We are prepared to, and we do, engage with them so they are aware of some of the risks.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I understand that. I am trying to understand the level of accountability and, I guess, the powers afforded to the government to be able to terminate any researcher-to-researcher relationships and whether it is actually captured in the legislation now or whether it is solely on the universities.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
I think, Senator, I am happy to answer that question at the next estimates. It will have given us time to actually implement this provision. It's very new. We're discussing it with universities now. I will follow up the minister's point. This legislation has actually been very effective. We have had over 23,000 notifications, 84 per cent of which have come from universities. We have a lot of visibility now of what is actually happening at universities than we did in the past. DFAT is working closely with other agencies, particularly Education and Home Affairs, which also have a role in this, to really work with universities and to actually strengthen their resilience. As the minister said, the situation is evolving. Risks appear in all sorts of different ways—in new and problematic ways—for universities. This has to be a collaborative and cooperative exercise with universities, and it is. If we actually don't do it that way and if universities aren't actually managing the risks, risks will pop up in ways that we don't expect and aren't covered by the legislation.

We are working currently with Education and universities to work through how we will implement and how they will implement this new obligation on their part. Feel free to ask me at the next estimates how we're doing with it once it's actually in force. The provision is not yet actually in force, though we hope it will be shortly.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. There aren't really any enforcement provisions, correct? As I understand it, this amendment has no real teeth to it. It's just an obligation. The onus is on the universities to oversee and manage the risk and terminate any researcher-to-researcher relationship. Put it this way: I have done 10½ years at university, and 6½ of them were postgraduate. I have seen the links that you have. I have seen the conferences that you go to across Australia and internationally. People come from everywhere. The people-to-people links are very strong around the world. It is very easy for many of these relationships to go unnoticed. You are putting the onus of that on universities, of which we have many. You mentioned before that we have thousands and thousands of people working at these universities. It is a very difficult thing to manage. Minister Wong, you wrote to universities in 2023.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Hang on. Take that to its logical conclusion. You are saying that, because there are so many, universities can't possibly be aware of them both. To that I would say: how is a bureaucrat or public servant in Canberra therefore aware of them?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm asking for the legislation.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You've got to work out how you make sure that we actually make the right decisions on these engagements. I don't think you do that by assuming that someone who is in Canberra can be aware if the university itself is not aware. The point is that the universities themselves need to make sure that their processes and procedures and how they tick off on researcher-to-researcher arrangements, what they expect of their staff, are fit for purpose. That's what that provision does. The bill was amended by the PJSC I think when it first went through. There were changes proposed by the PJSC when the first bill was proposed. We've amended it again as a consequence of both engagement with Mr O'Brien but also primarily from Ms Huxtable's report. I've no doubt in the future there may well be changes, where we think, 'Okay, this is not working well. This is working really well. We want to make these changes.' I'm open to that. I don't think this is closed. But your point doesn't make Australia safer because it assumes that Ms Heckscher, who works very hard, is going to be across every researcher-to-researcher arrangement that every university in Australia is engaging in.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And nor should she be, Minister. What I am suggesting is that perhaps the amendment needs some more teeth and some enforcement. You did write to universities in 2023, Minister, calling for an end to research collaboration with Iranian institutions. Further warnings were issued to 26 universities between March and June this year. Why does the government have to keep repeating these instructions?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I can actually say that, from a foreign arrangements perspective, when we took a good look at how many arrangements were actually still in place between Australian universities and Iranian counterparts, we found that we had none left in operation that fell outside the exception that was provided in the minister's original letter, which was for some student arrangements. That doesn't answer your question about the broader potential research partnerships between individuals at Australian universities and individuals in Iran. This provision gets us along that pathway. I would also note, going back to your earlier question, that we are very conscious that the Department of Education is responsible for universities. We are working very closely with the Department of Education to make sure that we are well linked in with the Department of Education and its administration of universities. What we don't want is conflicting messages—which there aren't—or conflicting or overlapping obligations. Hopefully, between us and the Department of Education, we will make sure that our respective responsibilities and legislative provisions are actually well-synced.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: How many universities were found to have continued collaborations after the original warning?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: In relation to Iran?
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So, as I just said, after the minister's original letter, in 2024, we went back to universities and asked about the individual enterprise level arrangements they had with Iranian institutions. We found none still in operation that fell outside the small exception that had been provided at the time in relation to some individual students. That is the enterprise level arrangements which to date are the arrangements covered by the foreign arrangement scheme.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Was there any enforcement action taken beyond sending further letters?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There were no foreign arrangements still in place.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What would we have enforced if they had already complied?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I am asking before that. There were repeated letters, weren't there? That's my understanding. Was it just letters?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But universities weren't not complying. In relation to Russia, for example, we did the same thing with Russia and Belarus. We sent a similar letter after the invasion of the Ukraine asking that there be no further engagement with institutions in Russia and Belarus.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: In late 2025, the minister made a rule that specifically brought institutions in Russia and Belarus within the scheme as institutions that would be covered formally by the scheme. We again checked whether there were any arrangements still in force. We found that there were no arrangements with Russian or Belarusian institutions that hadn't been terminated, expired or suspended et cetera. So there was nothing still on foot at that point. Two proposals were made to enter into arrangements with institutions in Russia and Belarus earlier this year. The minister issued prohibitions on those arrangements being entered into. Just as an example, we find that the scheme has been incredibly effective in giving us visibility of arrangements that our universities are entering into and providing a pathway for us to engage with universities and either turn them off as we need to, as the minister did earlier this year, or, alternatively, to work with universities to ensure that the arrangements are not on foot.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. What enforcement pathways or options are available if, for example, a university hadn't complied with it?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The enforcement pathway is under the legislation. There is an injunction pathway, which we haven't had to use to date. There is, frankly, cancellation and variation powers. As you would be aware, the cancellation and prohibition powers have been used by the minister under the legislation. We find that, as the minister said earlier, we need to actually harden the resilience of the whole sector and, in fact, local governments as well as state and territory governments and universities. One of the most effective things of the scheme is the way that we have done enormous amounts of outreach with universities at all different levels and with local governments and state and territory governments. We have worked with them on building their own capabilities and awareness of foreign policy risks and national interests and supporting them in making decisions that are in Australia's foreign policy and national interests.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Just to confirm, that is university to university. If it is researcher to researcher, the same powers—the injunction, the cancellation and variation powers—are not available to the minister?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: For researcher to researcher? That's right.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: For researcher to researcher, that's not available. You raised before, Minister, I guess, the bipartisan process in coming to this amendment. The coalition did propose an amendment to bring significant researcher-to-researcher arrangements within the scheme. The government rejected it, arguing that the existing national security laws were sufficient. Just a day later, the government introduced its own amendment recognising the same risk. Can you explain to us what changed within those 24 hours, please?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Did Mr O'Brien want you to ask these questions?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Pardon?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Did Mr O'Brien want you to ask these questions?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This is not an appropriate question to ask, I don't think.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: He is the shadow. I dealt with him. I would have thought he doesn't really want all our discussions aired in estimates.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm just trying to understand.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I can tell you this.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: If they're similar amendments, what changed in those 24 hours?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, I thought your original amendment let the universities off the hook and was administratively unachievable. First, I think universities should be obliged to do what we have outlined in the amendment. They are responsible for the people they employ, and they should ensure that the national interest is served and observed in those arrangements. Secondly, I don't think Ms Heckscher could actually keep on top of all the arrangements throughout the Australian tertiary education system, researcher to researcher. I had some engagement and my office had engagement with Mr O'Brien's office. This was the compromise position that we thought dealt with my concerns but also put in a legislative duty which has not existed before in this way on universities. So it's quite a big—I don't want to use the word 'stick', but we often do in the context of legislation. It's quite a substantial legal obligation on them now. We thought that was a reasonable compromise position to deal with some of the issues that Mr O'Brien had raised but also deal with the issues I had raised. I think it was a good example of the legislature working as it should.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: To follow up—this is not going to be easy for universities. We've had a number of webinars, and we've got another one. My team is having a webinar with universities and local governments later this week. There are already something like 400 individual registrations to participate in that discussion. Our universities are very engaged on working through what this looks like, how they deliver it, how they recognise foreign policy risks and how they manage it. This is really just to emphasise that there have been 23,000 notifications since 2020. Eighty-four per cent of them are from universities. That is just the enterprise-level arrangements. We would have had tens of thousands coming to us if we had captured under the notification obligation. I expect tens and tens of thousands would have been the impact. It would have been quite hard for us to focus on the high-risk arrangements with that volume coming to us. The universities will have to actually work very hard to make sure they have procedures and policies in place to identify and to manage risks relating to these arrangements. It's not going to be easy. It is a significant obligation on the part of universities.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This is my final question, Chair. The scheme as it stands today, as you mentioned just a few moments ago, wouldn't guarantee that the researcher-to-researcher arrangements, such as on drone technology or drone research in Iran, would be captured. We both can see that this is an issue. Does it not make it clear that we need to go further on this?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, I'm not sure that's what I just said. I think my answer was that we hadn't actually specifically gone back and looked at all of these individual ones to see if they would fall within the new provisions. We're focusing on making sure that we can implement these new provisions with universities in an effective way. They probably are covered by them. That will be something moving forward. I think I can say to you that universities and the government—DFAT, Education and Home Affairs—are committed to working with universities to actually make sure this is effective and that we can work with universities to manage risks, including researcher-to-researcher risks. UFIT, the University Foreign Interference Taskforce, which is a collaboration with the universities, plays a really important part in that as well.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Regulatory and Legal Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I look forward to following up at the next estimates. Thank you, Ms Heckscher.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I have a couple of questions with respect to the recent Pacific developments. I will start with you, Minister, in terms of how the government is strengthening our security and advancing our national interests in the Pacific given your and the government's recent time in the Pacific and the region.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
The first comment I would make is that the task of ensuring or assuring a safe and more secure region is never finished. It is ongoing. We have to work, and we are working, to continue to strengthen our relationships across the region. That means ensuring we build trust and remain a partner of choice. We turn up, we listen with respect, and we work with the Pacific to advance Pacific priorities. We are, of course, the Pacific's largest and most comprehensive development partner. There has been sustained engagement across the government from the Prime Minister to obviously myself, cabinet ministers and other members of the executive as well as members of parliament. I said I think in the first video I did just after we were sworn in that I talked to the Pacific about how we would engage with them. I have sought to keep faith with that.

I think that foundation of respect, of Australia being a better, more engaged member of the Pacific family, has enabled a change in Australia's relationships with the Pacific Islands Forum members. You see the result of some of that in some of the agreements that I went through in my opening. So there is the Pukpuk alliance with Papua New Guinea; the Ocean of Peace Alliance with the Vuvale Union; with Fiji; Nakamal with Vanuatu; Falepili with Tuvalu; and, of course, the Nauru-Australia Treaty. These are major achievements that wouldn't have been thinkable before the government changed. I think, to be very pragmatic about it, this is something we have to keep working every day to do—to advance Australia's interest and to strengthen our relationships in the region.

I think I mentioned the PNG-Australia ministerial forum. I appreciate all my colleagues who went as well. It was led by the Deputy Prime Minister. The co-leads were me and foreign minister Tkatchenko. We have an alliance. We have a very strong development and a comprehensive partnership. We focused on how we translate that into benefits for both our countries and our region. The officers can talk in more detail about that.

I want to make two points before I throw to them. One, we can never be complacent about what I've described as a permanent contest for influence in our region. Secondly, again I will say that Australia's interests are the Pacific's interests. Australia's interests are in a Pacific that is peaceful, stable, prosperous and sovereign. What do I mean by sovereign? It's that we can all make decisions for ourselves and for our people.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I will follow up from that and your opening statement. What would you say would be the main developments in terms of our engagement over the last five or six months?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I might turn to Ms Peak and ask if she can perhaps fill out a bit more detail on some of the agreements that I've gone through, if that's alright.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sure, thanks.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
In addition to the very helpful outline the minister gave in relation to Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu and Fiji, I will fill out the developments. We've also been working very hard with the Solomon Islands, including the Prime Minister traveling to the Solomon Islands and being the first leader from another country to ever give an address on Solomon Islands independence day. We are progressing the comprehensive treaty that our two Prime Ministers agreed that we would start negotiating. We have been working with Tonga on the Kaume'a Ofi agreement. We haven't forgotten Micronesia. We have been delighted to host PIF chair President Whipps, who opened Palau's embassy here in Canberra. That follows high-level visits from President Heine from the Marshall Islands and President Simina from the Federated States of Micronesia, who also opened an embassy earlier this year. So it has been a comprehensive effort. On top of that, the foreign minister attended the Pacific Island Forum foreign ministers meeting. The Prime Minister, Minister Bowen and Minister Conroy attended the PIF leaders meeting in Palau. So it has been a busy few months. I think it is exemplifying the fact that we are working hard to secure our region to have a safer and more prosperous region for our people.

In terms of some of the details of the agreements that the foreign minister spoke about, they are significant agreements. Indeed, in relation to the Ocean of Peace Alliance and the Vuvale Union, the Prime Minister described it as one of the most significant endeavours that Australia has undertaken with any country. The way that we worked with Fiji to come to that resolve is one of following its priorities. Prime Minister Rabuka requested those two treaties, which have provided and inked an alliance and provided a multidecadal effort between our two countries.

One point I want to highlight in that treaty is that the cultural component had been essential to progressing that. Our First Nations people, the Yolngu people in the Northern Territory, gifted the name 'bukmak' to one of the major committees that will take this relationship forward into the future. Cultural exchange is a fundamental part of continuing to operate with respect.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary and Head, Office of the Pacific

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. I will ask a few more questions about the details of the agreements specifically. Before I do that, I want to ask this. With these recent agreements that both you and the minister have just outlined with our Pacific friends and partners, how has that changed the way that we as a country work with them?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That is a really good question, Senator. The treaties do something important, which is establish architecture to take our relationships forward. That includes the proactive parts of our relationships in implementing the treaties. Perhaps even more importantly, they provide a culturally appropriate place to have some of the difficult conversations that are sometimes needed. I mentioned the bukmak forum in the Vuvale Union. Similarly, with the Nakamal Agreement, there is a Nakamal committee which, at its heart, has a philosophy of engaging with respect and in a spirit of consensus. So it's really changed the typical way that we would work as diplomats, taking into account the ways of working that our partners value.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary and Head, Office of the Pacific

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This is a follow-up question from that. How have you and the department then dealt with the key outcomes? Go to the key outcomes of the Pacific Islands Forum leaders meeting in Palau. Could you outline for me those key outcomes and if there has been any other progress to date since that meeting?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I might ask Mr Chittick to answer that.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary and Head, Office of the Pacific

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
Senator, the Pacific Islands Forum is the premiere regional forum for leaders and for ministers. The government's investment in Pacific regionalism is important because a stronger, more resilient and more prosperous Pacific will be easier for the region to secure when its own institutions are strong. It is something that Australia has invested in very heavily in recent years.

As Ms Peak said, the Prime Minister attended the Pacific Islands Forum leaders meeting in September this year. It was his fifth Pacific Islands Forum leaders meeting. It was a very substantive leaders communique which outlines a number of lines of work that are really valuable in securing the region's vision, ambitions and interests. I thought I would mention three.

The first one is the Waqa Moana initiative, which is a counterdrug trafficking initiative. It really directly responds to the call by Pacific leaders at their meeting. In particular, it addresses the maritime drug trafficking that is fuelling drug consumption in the region. This is an initiative that we're really proud to work closely with Fiji in developing. Fiji will form a real centrepiece of the Waqa Moana initiative. The Prime Minister and Minister Conroy announced in Palau funding from Australia of over $600 million over the next decade to support implementation of the Waqa Moana initiative.

The second element I will mention is digital and artificial intelligence. Pacific leaders adopted a set of digital and AI principles that will guide policy development in the region and help PIF members make high-quality selections when it comes to investment. This is something that Australia has been supporting the region in for many years now. I'm also mindful of the announcement by the Prime Minister and Mr Conroy at the PIF of the finalisation of the East Micronesia cable. That now means that all PIF members are connected to the modern world through broadband and undersea cables. The government's capitalisation of the AIFFP to $550 million in additional grants will provide additional support for Australia to be able to help the region with its own vision for its digital and AI future.

Senator, the third point I will mention is women's political participation. We were very encouraged by PIF leaders. I will quote directly from their communique:

Leaders urged members to adopt national policies and laws to increase women's political participation and representation. Leaders welcomed the announcement by Australia on the investment of $195million in the Pacific Women Lead Program, which has supported women s leadership and entrepreneurship and combatted gender-based violence.

This will be phase 2 of this very successful program. There are many other, I think, successes that are contained in the leaders communique, but I might leave it there.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: Deputy Head, Office of the Pacific, and First Assistant Secretary, Pacific Strategy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I appreciate that. I am mindful of time. I want to go back to the first initiative that you touched on. How will it strengthen the regional cooperation when it comes to illicit drug trafficking? Can you unpack that for me a bit more, please?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The region is well-tooled to address illegal fishing through a range of regional institutions such as the Forum Fisheries Agency and the provision of maritime domain awareness to identify illegal fishing vessels. To address the issue of drug trafficking, it is about connecting those existing regional institutions along with the Guardian-class patrol boat program, with which Australia has supported the region over many years. Australia's support will be through additional defence spending, particularly around aerial surveillance. We will be working, including through the AFP, to better join up those regional assets so that we can get actionable intelligence into the hands of law enforcement agencies and they can take sovereign action within their own jurisdictions.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: Deputy Head, Office of the Pacific, and First Assistant Secretary, Pacific Strategy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I will add to that. I think Mr Chittick outlined it very clearly and succinctly. This is really important. I want to acknowledge not just the PIF members, obviously, but the AFP and Defence. There has been and will be a really important exercise in us trying to join up a range of the measures we are already providing and increasing in some areas to try to deal much more effectively with transnational crime, particularly illicit drug trafficking. It will be important because we want to stop drugs and we want to stop the criminal networks that are operating in the region. As Mr Chittick said, we want to get to a much greater capacity in the maritime domain that is joined up, regional and enables countries to make their sovereign choices about how to deal with them. It is a lot of work. I really appreciate the work of the AFP and the ADF as well as the work of the Office of the Pacific in developing this. It was really good that the Prime Minister and Mr Conroy got this agreed at the PIF leaders meeting. It's very important.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thanks, Minister. It goes neatly to my next question, which is about how our support for this initiative translates into much stronger information sharing, the maritime surveillance that you touched on and the capacity to respond to transnational crime.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I jumped the gun there, didn't I?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That's alright.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I half answered that.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm not sure if Mr Chittick wants to add anything else to that. Clearly, it is good cooperation between our police and defence forces.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The AFP, the Department of Defence and the ADF have incredibly deep relationships bilaterally in the region. That addresses some vital security issues. Regionally, we also have a history of working together; the Pacific policing initiative is a fantastic example of that. In a sense, this is a maritime version of that kind of cooperation which ultimately is about, as the minister said, empowering sovereign countries in the Pacific to be able to take the law enforcement action that we know they want to take. It is about getting better maritime domain awareness. It is about having it analysed and transformed and then communicated quickly and effectively to PIF members so that they can take the action that they want to and need to and that benefits the region as well.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: Deputy Head, Office of the Pacific, and First Assistant Secretary, Pacific Strategy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I will skip ahead to the Vuvale Union agreement. I understand that it includes cooperation on transnational crime and illicit drugs. What will that mean in practice? Why is it important, noting what you've also just mentioned? How do the two link or intersect with each other?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you, Senator. In some ways, the Vuvale Union provided the foundation for this broader regional initiative. Fiji has been ringing the bell on transnational crime, drugs and the social implications of that for some time.
