The Vuvale Union provided an opportunity for us to come together to deal with that bilaterally. We were then able to together take that to the Pacific Islands Forum and multilateralise it. The efforts and energy that we have put in to the Vuvale Union helped regionally. I will add one point. Indeed, the unusual philosophy, perhaps, of the Vuvale Union and the Ocean of Peace Alliance is that while they are bilateral treaties, the philosophy is that any investment made under those auspices should help Fiji, should help Australia and should help the region. So that's the frame of reference that our two countries have taken to the investments that we're making bilaterally.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary and Head, Office of the Pacific

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There is a distinction between each of the treaties—the Vuvale Union and the Ocean of Peace Alliance. Are you able to explain briefly the distinction; the purpose of each of those treaties and how they work together; and the main commitments under the Vuvale Union and how progress against them will be tracked?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you, Senator. The Ocean of Peace Alliance is a mutual defence treaty. The core component is a mutual defence obligation elevating our two countries to allies and to an elite level of strategic trust. The Vuvale Union covers the waterfront of our cooperation. As I mentioned, it is a multidecadal treaty that covers all elements of our relationship. That will be tracked and implemented hand in hand. I mentioned earlier the bukmak forum. 'Bukmak' means everyone. We will have a bukmak forum on an annual basis; that is the intention. That will be an opportunity not just for governments to come together but potentially traditional leaders, faith leaders, business leaders and community leaders so that we can have whole-of-nation tracking of the implementation of the extensive commitments we have made to each other.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary and Head, Office of the Pacific

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Is that the purpose of that forum?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That's right.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary and Head, Office of the Pacific

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I have some other questions when it comes to Australia and Vanuatu. I note the time. We might break here and then come back after lunch and continue with questions. Thanks, everyone.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Welcome back, everyone. I will hand the call to Senator Dean Smith.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Good afternoon, Minister and officials. I'm seeking an update to recent media reports and representations made concerning Mr Tran, a dual citizen of Australia and Vietnam, who is currently detained by Vietnamese authorities.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Do you want an update?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes. I was asking for an update rather than providing one. Thank you.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: DFAT continues to provide consular assistance to Mr Tran and his family. Consular officials were able to visit Mr Tran on 15 October and heard directly from him about his welfare, his consular needs and the circumstances of his detention. We're seeking an expeditious resolution of Mr Tran's case and his return to Australia to be reunited with family. We're continuing to raise his case at senior levels with Vietnamese authorities. We're pressing for regular consular access under the terms of our bilateral consular agreement with Vietnam, humane treatment, access to legal representation and a quick process. We're deeply concerned at the report that Mr Tran has given that he was abducted in Cambodia and taken against his will to Vietnam and have sought urgent clarification from both governments about the circumstances of his entry to Vietnam.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you very much, Ms McGregor. Can I confirm that Australian officials have engaged Vietnamese officials?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That is correct.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And a consular visit has taken place?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That is correct.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Has a subsequent consular visit been requested or confirmed?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We have requested monthly consular visits. That is under the terms of our bilateral consular agreement with Vietnam.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Has that request been confirmed? Has the next monthly consular visit been confirmed?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I can confirm that we have requested it. I am not aware that it has been confirmed yet.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thanks very much. Thank you, Chair.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator Cadell, you have some other questions?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I have some questions on treaties.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Is there any particular area of treaty?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It is my doom scrolling. I found a section on the website. I will read it.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Your doom scrolling? We are being asked questions about it.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes. You cannot vouch for the accuracy or completeness of the treaties database. I'm trying to work out how we keep track of how many treaties we've got. On the treaties database, it says that DFAT cannot vouch for the accuracy or completeness of this list of treaties. Do we have a list of how many treaties Australia is currently party to?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's difficult to pin down an exact number. There are over 2,000 entries in the treaties database. That includes not only treaties. Every time there is an amendment to a treaty or an annexe to a treaty is amended, that is recorded as a treaty action because it is a matter that needs to go before JSCOT and, if necessary, before the parliament. The second thing I would add is that the treaties database goes right back to the first treaty that we signed as an independent nation, which was the Treaty of Versailles in 1919. So especially for some of those earlier entries when issues were recorded potentially in a different and not altogether accurate way, we can't vouch 100 per cent for the accuracy of those first couple of decades.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: Chief Counsel and First Assistant Secretary, Legal Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Away from treaty actions, do we have a list of bilateral or multilateral treaties that are still in effect versus those? You mentioned the Treaty of Versailles. Is there a definitive list I can look through for current active multilateral and bilateral treaties?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The treaties database is split into multilateral treaties and bilateral treaties, so they are recorded on two different sides of the one treaty database.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: Chief Counsel and First Assistant Secretary, Legal Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But they are not all valid. The Treaty of Amity between the United Kingdom, Ireland and Columbia in 1825 is on there.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That would not be recorded against our treaties database because we were not any dependent country or a signatory. In answer to your question, the revocation of a treaty is also a treaty action, so it is recorded in the database as well.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: Chief Counsel and First Assistant Secretary, Legal Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I get they're all there. It's quite complicated to go through it and see which are the valid ones. How do I find which ones are still in effect without having to read every one to find the withdrawals? How do I find out what treaties Australia is party to?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There is no central list. The way in which you can identify the status of a treaty would be to, in the case of the database, click on the relevant treaty. You would then be able to identify its status. It will note whether or not it is in force.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: Acting Assistant Secretary, International Law Branch

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. Each individual one; I get that. So, of all the entries on that database, you have to click on each individual one. Is there no-one in the department who can do a review and get the active ones in a separate list?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As Mr McCarthy said, there are thousands of treaties on that database. That database has the full list. There's not a schedule or a separate document that records that list as a list.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: Acting Assistant Secretary, International Law Branch

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Who in the department, on every law we pass or anything, is responsible for finding out that we're not breaching one of these treaties that exists from a long time ago or we're outside the scope of? Who knows whether Australia's actions are in line with everything we're required to be within if we don't have a single list of still active ones?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I will answer in two parts. DFAT has a treaties secretariat. That sits within the international law branch. We are responsible for assisting the foreign minister with her responsibility for treaties and supporting the entry of those treaties through parliament—for example, through JSCOT. Once a treaty is in force, the implementation and ongoing operation of that treaty is managed by the relevant departmental lead.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: Acting Assistant Secretary, International Law Branch

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I should also say that, when legislation comes forth that may engage our international obligations, it is standard practice that that is referred both to DFAT's legal division and to the Attorney-General's Office of International Law. That is to do, if you like, a stocktake and ensure that whatever domestic legislation is being proposed is consistent with our international obligations and to provide advice on that.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: Chief Counsel and First Assistant Secretary, Legal Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Can you just go over it quickly? We mentioned these thousands of entries that go through. How many clicks would I have to go through right down that page to make sure nothing applies? Every treaty action listed in there. My concern is just that you can't say an actual number. You can't say, 'This is how many bilateral. This is how many multilateral.' You can't give me a number of how many actually exist. If we can't have a number of how many are still active and valid—I hope we could—how do I know that they are all being monitored for these things?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The answer that Dr Mitchell just gave you, Senator Cadell.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So someone goes through and clicks?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This portfolio has responsibility—I will make sure I say it correctly—for ticking off on essentially the making of the treaty. The foreign minister sends a treaty to X Co et cetera. But once it is in force—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: DCCEEW takes it or someone else?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, whoever. There would be a department. We have some that we are the lead on. There would be other departments. They are responsible for ensuring that we meet our obligations under those treaties.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So to get that, I should go to every department and ask how many treaties they actively monitor? Would that be the way to do it potentially?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm not sure it's up to me to draft your questions.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No. I'll ask the secretary. How many treaties does DFAT currently actively monitor?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: How many treaties are we the lead department for? We can provide that. We might have to take it on notice.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm happy for that. You mentioned JSCOT. A 2017 paper from the Australian and New Zealand association of parliamentary clerks found that seven treaties were JSCOT against ratifying and five went ahead regardless. I won't make it political by government. How many times in the last 10 years has the government taken binding treaty action against JSCOT recommendations or before JSCOT had recommended?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I would have to take it on notice, Senator. I'm not aware of any recent examples where JSCOT has recommended against binding treaty action.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: Acting Assistant Secretary, International Law Branch

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I can say—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This was all pre-2017. I'm wondering since then.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We'll see if we can help you. I have been shadow trade minister, shadow foreign minister and then foreign minister. The approach that has always been taken is you try to ensure that any issues in the JSCOT are dealt with.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's just interesting.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The approach generally from either side of politics has generally not been a combative one with JSCOT.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I also read that the treaties council was set up a long time ago when COAG existed and it had some meetings. COAG no longer exists. Does the treaties council still exist in any way, shape or form?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I've never heard of the treaties council.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The states used to get a say in some of the treaties. I think that was the basis of it.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Under Australia's treaty practice, we administered through Prime Minister and Cabinet what was previously called the Standing Committee on Treaties. It now exists through the intergovernmental working group with the states and territories. Several times a year we consult with the states and territories on treaties that are currently under negotiation or review.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: Acting Assistant Secretary, International Law Branch

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. So that standing committee on treaties is a group of Commonwealth and state officials now?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes. It's administered through the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet for which we provide secretariat support.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: Acting Assistant Secretary, International Law Branch

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: In your next break, I've got something. Finish this first.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: How many treaties have you referred to that group? How many times has it met in the last 12 months?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'll have to take that on notice.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: Acting Assistant Secretary, International Law Branch

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm advised by my very able staff that the Australian Treaties Database has a filter on its website where you can choose between in force, no longer in force or not yet in force. So that makes it much easier for you, Senator.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I had a really good click. It doesn't work quite that well.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. I'm just told this.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Best-laid plans of mice and men. That was a rough night. That's all I have, thank you.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I want to finish with a few other questions on the Vuvale and maybe the Vanuatu Nakamal Agreement briefly. I will then hand to Senator Collins and whoever else is here from the cross bench. Before I start, I know the deputy chair had one follow-up question from earlier.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You mentioned the $195 million that was going to Pacific Women Lead for the next five years. Can you clarify? You said it was for gender based violence. The Pacific Women Lead program has three core, I guess, programs in it. Is it now just focusing on gender based violence, or is it all of those three? There is leadership. I've forgotten what the other one was, the third one.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It is broader, Senator. I see Mr Mark Tattersall, the first assistant secretary of our Pacific development division, coming to the table. I'm sure he can provide more detail.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary and Head, Office of the Pacific

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As was mentioned by Mr Chittick earlier, the second phase of Pacific Women Lead was announced at the PIF leaders meeting in Palau. That will constitute $195 million from 2026 to 2031. It is essentially a continuation of the first phase of the program. It has several key objectives but is focused in particular on women's political leadership, gender based violence, women's economic opportunities and increasing women's health outcomes in the regions.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Polynesia, Micronesia and Development Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So no change? Just an extension to it. Thank you very much. I appreciate that.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you for that, Ms Peak and Deputy Chair. Ms Peak, what are the practical changes that the Ocean of Peace Alliance will bring in terms of our cooperation between the ADF and the military of Fiji?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The level of cooperation between the two defence forces is already at a very significant level. There are plans to take that again to a new, as I mentioned before, elite level of strategic trust and interoperability. I refer to my colleagues in Defence to speak to the detailed plans that they have in place. I know they are quite detailed.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary and Head, Office of the Pacific

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm sure we'll have time tomorrow. Thank you. In terms of the Nakamal Agreement that was signed in June this year, are you able to go to the key outcomes of the meeting that occurred I think here in Canberra on 15 October?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
Certainly. The Nakamal Agreement, as you say, was signed on 29 June this year. I mentioned earlier that the Nakamal Agreement established a piece of architecture called the Nakamal committee. Despite the Nakamal Agreement not yet being in force, both parties are very committed to progressing the components of the Nakamal Agreement. We held the first meeting of that committee here in Canberra led by the foreign minister and Minister Conroy on our side and the Deputy Prime Minister of Vanuatu on the other. From that meeting, there were a number of key outcomes. The two governments released a joint statement publicly to outline those. One thing that the committee underscored was the centrality of our cultural connections as an important component to elevate. It is also important in how we work together. In the margins of the committee, we were honoured to host the Australian South Sea Islander leaders. We had First Nations leaders. Ambassador Mohamed convened a conversation with the Vanuatu ministers involved to talk about where we can take the cultural connections and what early advancements we could make on that.

Secondly, there were a number of early actions articulated, including moving forward on increasing police support, climate change support and support for El Nino.

Importantly, the Vanuatu side articulated helpfully the status of policing cooperation in Vanuatu. As is articulated in the treaty, they reaffirmed that Australia is the primary policing partner and that other arrangements were time limited and expected to reduce over time. The expectation is that we will move forward with additional policing support as agreed by the two governments in an early phase of implementation.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary and Head, Office of the Pacific

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you for that. In terms of the committee, how will it help operationalise the agreement?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The communique or the joint statement is a list of early priorities. There are a number of commitments in the Nakamal Agreement. There is no time limit on the treaty. It will be an enduring treaty. Our two governments have come together to work out where we will put our energy and effort for implementation in this early phase.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary and Head, Office of the Pacific

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. I have a couple of colleagues behind me who have short blocks of questions of maybe five minutes each.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I want to follow up on Senator Smith's questions about Mr Hiep Tran. I understand that Mr Tran's wife Chloe came to parliament looking for more answers about her husband's alleged kidnapping in Cambodia and transport to Vietnam. Minister, I understand that you have personally been in touch. I thank you for that. Is the department treating this as a kidnapping of an Australian citizen or something else?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We're treating this case as a consular case. I would say it's a complex consular case. It is being considered in accordance with our complex case framework. That means we work with a range of other agencies in developing our responses. We are giving it our full attention.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. That's good to know. How long will it take for you to be able to know if this is in fact a kidnapping of an Australian citizen or something else?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I am unable to speculate on timeframes.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Consular and Crisis Management Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: How does Mr Tran's case differ from other Australian citizens who have been illegally detained overseas, such as Kylie Moore-Gilbert or Cheng Lei?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I will step in here. When we deal with consular cases such as these, our first priority is the interests of the Australian concerned. That informs what we say in fora like this and what we don't say. It informs how we deal with governments and how we deal with other matters. If you want a discussion outside this forum and you have the authority to do so from the family, I'm prepared to do that. But we are going to be cautious about some of what we say here because we are focused on the best interests of the Australian. What I would say is what I think Ms McGregor said in response to Senator Smith. I think you may have been out of the room. We have already dealt with questions on this matter.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No. I was in here.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm sorry. We take any allegation that an Australian may have been deprived of their liberty and moved across an international border against their will very seriously. We continue to seek clarity about the circumstances in which Mr Tran came to be in Vietnam.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you, Minister. I appreciate that there are sensitivities around this. I know in other circumstances there has been far more public comment and clear direction from government as to what is happening.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I will go back to what I first said. When we determine what we say publicly and when we say it, we do so making a judgement about what is in the best interests of the Australian concerned. It is not a political decision. It is not a publicity decision. It is a decision about the best interests of the person concerned. That is the approach I took in relation to Mr Turnell. That is the approach I took in relation to Ms Cheng Lei. That is the approach I have taken in relation to other consular cases where we have been able to assist people in circumstances where they wanted to come back to Australia.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you, Minister. Can you tell the Senate whether the Vietnamese or Cambodian ambassadors have been called in over the incident?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: DFAT did act promptly on the information available to us. We were advised of his disappearance when people were not aware of his whereabouts. Officials made inquiries initially with the Cambodian authorities. Mr Tran had gone missing in Cambodia after failing to board a scheduled flight to Thailand. On 23 September, DFAT submitted a formal request to authorities from neighbouring countries—Laos, Thailand and Vietnam—about his immigration movements. When Vietnamese state media reported Mr Tran's arrest, which was on 28 September, officials repeatedly sought urgent confirmation of his location and welfare and immediate consular access. That access took place on 15 October. Those discussions have been at various levels, both in Phnom Penh and Hanoi and here in Canberra.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, South and Southeast Asia Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you, Ms Chan. That's great to know. I really appreciate your work on that. Thank you, Minister. I will leave it there.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And take it up away from estimates, thanks.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Good afternoon, Minister, and the officials at the table. There are moves internationally to establish an international panel on inequality to coordinate global efforts on inequality similar, I guess, to the way the IPCC does on climate. Is Australia supportive of these moves, which are being driven by a number of other countries? If you are supportive, what have you done on the international forum to advance the proposal?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I wonder if you could tell us a bit more information. We're not aware of the panel immediately. Was it under the auspices of the UN?
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Development, Multilateral and Europe Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I believe that it is. It is an international panel on inequality, as I said, similar to the IPCC. It's at the formative stages. You're not aware of that?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, we're not. Obviously we're very concerned about inequality in the terms of our development program more broadly and international engagement, but we are not aware of that specific panel.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Development, Multilateral and Europe Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. So 30 countries met during the recent UN General Assembly meeting. Obviously, Australia was not one of those countries.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Development, Multilateral and Europe Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Perhaps I could draw that matter to your attention, Minister, and through you to your officials. I suggest respectfully that you have a look at what is being proposed, and perhaps we can discuss it at a future estimates.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We're happy to have a look.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. There are also growing calls for an international tax treaty. It's further advanced than the matter that I just raised. The UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation began in 2025. It will continue until mid-next year. The proposal arose out of frustration that OECD-led efforts to address tax base erosion and profit shifting are too slow and are too, I guess, colonial in nature; that is, they are favouring wealthy countries over countries that are exploited for their wealth and excluding countries in the global south from negotiations. By the way, that's in response to the OECD-led efforts. Are you aware of negotiations to develop a global tax treaty? Has Australia engaged in that process? If so, how?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As you rightly say, Senator, there are a range of efforts underway, including those at the OECD, in which Australia participates actively. As you have said also, those efforts have a range of limitations. Of course, the Commonwealth Treasury leads on these matters. They would be the appropriate place to direct questions on this.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thanks. I will ask Treasury about this a bit later this afternoon. You would be aware of this international work that is being done, obviously?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We're aware of discussions. We're not the lead agency, so we don't track international negotiations. They are quite different from the broader question of whether there's dialogue and discussion on global coordination on tax. Of course we're aware of that. The Commonwealth Treasury is the lead agency on these matters.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Do you advise Treasury on Australia's engagement with negotiations around an international tax treaty?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sorry, did you ask whether we advise?
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Treasury is the lead on matters relating to international tax. They would be the ones that typically would prepare advice on these matters to government.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sure. You could correct me if I am wrong, Minister, or anyone at the table. Surely you don't just let random Australian government agencies kind of blunder around on the international stage.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Oh, my goodness. You are Treasury spokesperson.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No. Minister, you know the point I'm making here.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I don't think they would be thrilled with that.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I withdraw the word 'random'. You know the point I'm making. Surely DFAT exercises some engagement with Australian agencies who are acting on the international stage. I'll put it like that.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The orderly way in which in these international relations are managed and various international issues and policy areas are managed is to ensure that the relevant government department is clearly the government department that has responsibility for it.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sure.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We have certain responsibilities. Mr Mina is going to be very happy to talk to the committee, I'm sure, about why the European FTA should be supported by you and by the coalition and why that will benefit Australian workers. He will do so, I'm sure, eloquently and with a lot of evidence later today. We're happy to talk about the treaties or proposed treaties that we are responsible for. But this area is led by Treasury.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I get that, Minister.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: In fact, the Treasurer and the Assistant Treasurer and the former assistant treasurers have done a lot of work, including by the OECD, on some of the issues you raise. But they are best placed to respond on these issues.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm not seeking to ask you any questions of detail about what Treasury is doing. I'm simply asking what engagement this department has with what Treasury is doing. Do you have any engagement at all or does Treasury just get to stride on to the international stage with no engagement with DFAT at all and conduct negotiations unilaterally? Is there some level of engagement from DFAT?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There are so many things in that. There are so many presumptions that I need to respond to.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's a simple proposition, Minister.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No. It wasn't. It was a whole set of incorrect assumptions first.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I haven't come here for an argument. If you want one, I'm happy to give you one.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No treaties are entered into. There is a process of approval for ministers who are engaging in international negotiations. If you are seeking to engage in and negotiate a treaty, you have to get a mandate from the cabinet. First, on this point that it is willy-nilly, I think, or whatever the phrase was, frankly, that is just not a truthful proposition. The second point is I have no doubt that, as appropriate, departments would engage on issues. The only point we're making is that Treasury is the lead on some of the issues you are raising. If you have other issues, we are happy to assist.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm very aware of the fact that Treasury is the lead because I have been informed about half a dozen times in the last five minutes.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Excellent.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I don't need to be informed of that again.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Good.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm not seeking to ask about that. I'm not seeking to challenge that. I'm simply asking what, if any, engagement does this department have with Treasury's work on this matter on the international stage. That is a simple question.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On which matter?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Actually—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Because there are lots of different issues.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I have been very clear about this. It is the UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation, Minister.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On tax cooperation?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes. What if any engagement does DFAT have with Treasury while Treasury is working on the UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation? I don't think it's a controversial question.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, further to the minister's explanation, when any government department, be it transport, health or Treasury, is engaged in international treaty negotiations, there's, of course, a whole-of-government process behind the original cabinet mandate that is given by government to the negotiators. As relevant, those policy agencies with lead responsibility engage other parts of the Commonwealth government. That would include DFAT sometimes. It would include the Attorney-General's Department sometimes on matters to do with international law. It so much depends on the subject. If there are connections between particular provisions and, for example, our trade law obligations, the WTO or our investment agreements bilaterally, Treasury has responsibility for those. It would depend on the subject matter and how they construct their consultation. I suppose I can say as secretary that where treaty negotiations engage either our international law or our policy subject matter or, for that matter, our bilateral relationship equities, we would be involved.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: PSM, Secretary

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Perhaps I will ask you to take this on notice. Obviously, I'm not going to get it today. Could you please respond specifically in relation to the Department of Treasury and the UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation? What are the governance arrangements, if any, around that? Is there an IDC or a working group of some kind? What kind of engagement has your—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm sorry, but that's actually Treasury. Treasury is running that.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: PSM, Secretary

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I understand that Treasury would have a working group. Is DFAT involved? I'm asking from this ministry what your engagement is with Treasury. You're obviously not going to answer it here. I'm asking you to take it on notice and see if there is anything further you can provide.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sure. If they've said anything further, we will provide it. I am being upfront with you. We may simply be referring the question to Treasury. We will see if there is any further assistance we can provide.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I would like to ask some questions about the PRC missile testing and the PLA Navy's missile test in July. What time and date was Australia first notified of the test, by whom and through which channel? Was it an embassy in Canberra? Was it our embassy in Beijing? Was it military channels? How were we notified of that?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The first date was on 5 July. I will defer to my colleague Ms DeZoeten for details.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Strategic Planning and Coordination Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As deputy secretary Lawson said, a number of Notice to Airmen and closure areas, including temporary exclusion zones, were issued prelaunch on 5 to 6 July. But those notices, from our perspective, lacked some detail. In terms of the bilateral communication, that occurred on 6 July both in Beijing through military channels and in Canberra to DFAT officials.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Defence and National Security Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: To the DFAT officials, was that from your PRC counterparts or was that from our military that had already received that?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sorry not to be clear. That was the Chinese embassy in Canberra.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Defence and National Security Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The Chinese embassy in Canberra?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: To DFAT officials.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Defence and National Security Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: To DFAT officials?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On 6 July.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Defence and National Security Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On 6 July. And how many hours before? The launch was on the 6th. How many hours before the launch did you receive that notification?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Around two hours.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Defence and National Security Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You said that the pre-launch warning lacked some detail. What sort of details was it missing? What sort of details did it include?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'll have to come back to you on the specifics of the formal notification context. My comment around the lack of details in the NOTAMs, which is the Notice to Airmen notices, for example, referred to hazardous operations or space debris. It did not provide specific detail. Obviously, the nature of the discussions from our perspective when we were having the exchanges with the Chinese officials when they conveyed the information to us was to ask about intent, purpose, timing and capability.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Defence and National Security Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Were you told about the direction in which it would travel and where it was intended to land?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'll have to come back to you on the specifics of that discussion. I don't have the details of that in relation to the specific elements of that. From our perspective, the nature of the notifications we were provided with did not provide a sufficient level of detail that we would expect, including under the Hague code of conduct, to which Australia is a party, which sets out things around the flight path and the nature of the capability et cetera. We did not consider that the requirements under the Hague code of conduct were met.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Defence and National Security Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. Pacific islands were under the flight path or near the flight path. Are you aware of any other Pacific islands that were notified prior to the launch?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There have been some public statements in relation to this. I'm not sure we are the ones to indicate when others were notified.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But we can look at what is public.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Reportedly not all Pacific nations were pre-notified. There was a statement by the PIF forum ministers.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Strategic Planning and Coordination Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Just to be clear, you didn't have any indication prior to the formal notification that this was going to happen? It was all a surprise to the Australian government?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That's not a matter I can comment on, Senator.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Defence and National Security Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Did DFAT notify Pacific islands to make sure they were aware that the missile was coming their way?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We're not going to comment on that.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I won't go into the specifics of private bilateral conversations we may or may not have had. I will refer you to the comments the foreign minister made when she was in Suva. There were public comments in which she indicated that China had advised the Australian government of its intent to conduct a sea-based missile. She did make those comments publicly in advance of the test.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Defence and National Security Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But as a member of the Pacific family and for security within the Pacific family, I assume the Australian government would have notified Pacific island governments that this was about to happen in the region.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, I think we've already answered the question.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Strategic Planning and Coordination Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I was in Suva with the Prime Minister to sign the Vuvale Union and the Ocean of Peace Alliance.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So you can draw the inference.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You mentioned the Hague convention. What is DFAT's legal assessment of whether the test was consistent with China's obligations under international law?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There are a few things I would say in relation to the Hague code of conduct. The first thing is that it isn't a legal instrument. It is a voluntary arrangement which states subscribe to, if you like. From our perspective, we see it as a transparency and confidence building measure. There are 145 subscribed states, as I mentioned before, including, of course, Australia. China is not a signatory to the Hague code of conduct. We call on states to sign in and subscribe to the principles. It provides a range of non-legally binding processes. The first is notification to the other subscribing states. Of course, China is not a subscribing state so did not do that. So 145 states that subscribe to that did not meet that.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Defence and National Security Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But they did notify you, just not within the time frame that is expected. Is that what I understand to be correct?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: They did notify all of the Hague code of conduct states as far as we are aware. They notified Australia but they didn't use the Hague code of conduct process. There's actually a process where all subscribing states to the Hague code of conduct have a process by which they are able to notify everybody else of an intention to undertake the test. It sets out a range of requirements, if you like. That includes things such as prelaunch notifications and information such as the generic class of the ballistic missile or the space launch vehicle; the planned launch notification window; the launch area; and the planned direction by which the missile test will take place.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Defence and National Security Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So none of that information was provided?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: From our perspective, those requirements, principles or measures that are outlined were not met.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Defence and National Security Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. The second part of my question is whether the test was consistent with China's obligations under international codes. I know you mentioned the Hague code of conduct. My apologies for calling it the Hague convention. Was the test consistent with broader obligations under international law?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We don't usually get into the specifics of international law advice. I'm not sure if my colleagues from the legal team have anything to add beyond that.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Defence and National Security Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I really don't have a lot to add to Ms DeZoeten's answer. The Hague code of conduct is, of course, non-binding; it's not legally binding. There is actually very little in the way of legal framework that is in this area. Beyond that, we would be getting into the territory of the provision of legal advice. So there's not a lot further I can add to that.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: Chief Counsel and First Assistant Secretary, Legal Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. Just to be clear, the PRC doesn't recognise the Treaty of Rarotonga, does it, or the South Pacific Nuclear-Free Zone? Are you aware of that?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, I'm looking at you wryly because it's a tricky answer. I'm just wanting to get to the right page. Obviously, there are states that are party to the South Pacific nuclear weapon free zone treaty. There are also a series of protocols to which nuclear weapon states can subscribe. If you give me one moment, I will find them. There are three. China, from my memory, is a party to those. Those relate in general terms to things around nuclear weapon states not coercing or threatening signatory parties to the treaty with nuclear weapons. One relates to those nuclear weapon states that have territories within the zone. The third one I'm just trying to remember. If you give me a minute, I can find it.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Defence and National Security Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: More specifically, I think the Treaty of Rarotonga is probably the most important thing here.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So they are not a party. They cannot sign on to the Treaty of Rarotonga itself, but they can subscribe, as I understand it—my legal colleagues will tell me if I am wrong—to the protocols, which they have; I should say that is those that are relevant to them. Sorry to interrupt you.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Defence and National Security Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So they have signed to the protocols, or they have the ability to sign?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, Ms DeZoeten is entirely correct. That accords with my understanding. Maybe we can take that on notice and respond in the course of the session.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: Chief Counsel and First Assistant Secretary, Legal Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I've found the page. There are three protocols. Protocol 1 applies the prohibitions of the treaty with respect to nuclear weapon states in respective territories in the zone. That is not applicable to China. The second protocol to the Treaty of Rarotonga applies to not use or threaten to use nuclear explosive devices against any party to the treaty or each other's territory within the zone. China has ratified that protocol. The third protocol relates not to testing nuclear explosive devices within the zone. Again, China has ratified that protocol.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Defence and National Security Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you very much. I go to the point that the minister raised before about being in Fiji at the time. Was it DFAT's assessment that it was coincidence that the missile test happened on the same day that the minister was there signing and ratifying the Ocean of Peace Alliance?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I can't speculate, Senator, on the intention of China in undertaking this activity.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Defence and National Security Policy Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Was there any advice given to the minister about that at the time?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The focus at the time immediately, from my recollection, was about ensuring the minister was aware that it had occurred and explaining and providing briefing in relation to the Hague code of conduct, for example, and the nature of the information we had received. That was the immediate priority.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. Has DFAT raised the test in any multilateral forums, such as the NPT review conference process, the conference on disarmament or the UN First Committee?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I don't know if officials can add to this. I can say to you at ministerial level the focus was to work with the PIF. There was a discussion, including in the PIF foreign ministers and in the leaders meeting.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
That's right. I will add to the foreign minister's comments. As she said, the PIF leaders meeting communique and the foreign ministers communique both referenced the test. I'm happy to quote it to you if that would be helpful. The leaders meeting communique says that leaders, in recalling the Blue Pacific Ocean of Peace Declaration, registered concern about the recent intercontinental ballistic missile, or ICBM, test which overflew a number of members without adequate notice. Leaders called on all states undertaking ICBM testing to ensure transparency and reassurance, including through the provision of advanced notification of at least 24 hours in accordance with international practice. Leaders emphasised the importance of all states conducting ICBM tests to do so consistently with the Blue Pacific Ocean of Peace Declaration, the Treaty of Rarotonga and in respect of the sovereignty of forum members. I should make the point for completeness that the Republic of Naoero dissociated itself with that paragraph.

The other point to your question, Senator, at the top is, yes, we did make comments about this in multilateral fora as well. We joined a joint statement in the conference on disarmament in relation to the notification of ballistic missile launches. Australia, along with 39 other countries, joined this statement, which was US-led. Inter alia, that statement called on all countries to commit to participate in arrangements for providing advance notification to affected states. It also indicated concern with the recent missile testing activity in the Pacific, which did not follow standard practices. It stated that conducting such tests without submitting advanced notice is dangerous and disrupts the peace and security of relevant nations in proximity to these tests; increases the risk of miscalculation; undermines global stability and security; and is incompatible with the responsibilities that come with possessing long-range missile capabilities.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: My questions go to the official development assistance program. Thanks for being here again. I have a number of lines of questions in this area. In response to my questioning at estimates on 4 June this year regarding conflicts of interest between the design and implementation functions, DFAT stated that processes exist to manage these conflicts and potential competitive advantages as a result. Instead of relying on information sharing through briefings in a two-step tender process that cannot reliably remove competitive advantage for firms with no information or involvement in design, why can't firms simply be banned from doing both design and implementation for the same program in the manner that firms are banned from doing both the implementation and evaluation of the same program?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you for the question and for your interest in this issue. I recall in the hearing back in June we did indicate that there was an additional procurement mechanism coming online that would provide us with some more options in the future for managing and reducing this potential conflict of interest or advantage. We are very close to being in a position where we can actually exclude contractors who have undertaken a design from subsequent procurements. I will ask Ms Shillito to speak to how that's rolling out. In effect, we are establishing a new mechanism through which we can procure design support. It will not only strengthen the robustness of that procurement; it also reduces the opportunity for unfair advantage. It will increase diversity in our market. I will ask Ms Shillito to give you an update on where it is at.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Development, Multilateral and Europe Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As Ms Cohen has mentioned, we are very close to finalising what we're describing as the DEV+ Panel. That's a panel that will provide streamlined access to a more diverse pool of providers in core development functions—namely, design; monitoring, evaluation and learning; due diligence and accreditation; safeguards; probity advice; and procurement evaluation. The panel has been operating since 26 August. We've onboarded 57 providers. It is still a live procurement process so we can't give you final numbers. But we expect to have it fully operational by the end of this year. We also expect that to provide a good mix of small to medium and large providers and providers who have worked for us before and a number of providers who haven't worked with the department before. As Ms Cohen has indicated, it will provide a capability that we can access that will enable us to separate design and implementation procurements. We're hoping to introduce that reform sometime in the 2027 calendar year.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Development Programming Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
I will come back to DEV+ later. I want to go to the question of cooling off and the revolving door issue. DFAT answered on notice my question at estimates on 4 June regarding cooling off and revolving door issues in the sector. QON 203 states, and I quote:

…26 DFAT officials have resigned from their APS job and returned to the Department as a contractor through a Labour Hire Company since 1 July 2023. …The other conflict-of-interest declarations identified through this cohort related to private interests.

What was the conflict in this case? How was it mitigated?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I don't have the detail of that particular matter with us today, but I'm very happy to take that on notice.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary and Chief People Officer, People Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. Why should so many relatively senior DFAT staff leave the APS in this manner and be retained for their expertise through private companies? Why are we seeing this?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What I would say on that is that the use of contractors will depend on needing particular expertise, perhaps for a short period of time. When people leave the Public Service, there are still times when it is appropriate to draw on some of that expertise. We're obviously very focused on making sure that our capability in-house is very strong, so I think our trend is downwards on that. We obviously do quite a bit of work with our policy settings just to make sure that people are taking proper account of the issues that you should think about when you are making a decision about a contractor engagement. Certainly most of the contracting settings and the contracting situations in the department tend to go to where there is a need for a short-term, very specialist set of expertise rather than a pattern of need to do this on a regular basis.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary and Chief People Officer, People Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I would like to know how and in what functions these 26 former APS officials are deployed within the public sector across Canberra and posts. If on notice you could help me with that, I would appreciate that.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes. I'm happy to.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary and Chief People Officer, People Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm very conscious this government has made commitments to reduce its dependence on contractors, consultants and labour hire, but it's not having success. We are at a $20 billion level of expenditure external to the public sector, which is back at the last year of the Morrison government. So I'm curious about this kind of exit and then reemployment as a consultant. Does it point to a structural problem in DFAT's ability to retain expertise and specialisations within the APS ranks? What are your thoughts about that?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
We've obviously been doing a lot of work under the strategic commissioning framework looking at the use of contractors in the department. We've reduced since 2022 the number of contractors from 1,375 in October 2022 to 788 in September 2026. That is a reduction of about 43 per cent. When people in the department are making decisions to engage contractors, we are tracking now the rationale so that we can understand whether it is straying into what we might consider core work for the department and for the APS or whether it is something that it is genuinely difficult to get into the Public Service that we might need for a short period of time. Minister Gallagher mentioned in the finance hearing yesterday or the APSC hearing—one of those; I'm sorry for not remembering which one—that one of the examples for DFAT, of course, is infrastructure financing projects in the Pacific. They are short term and very specialist. They are not core capability for the department. Most of the time, it's a very strong indication. It's a difficulty recruiting that particular skill set in the APS or it's a short-term demand for resourcing. They are the two key reasons. I'm happy to take on notice some of the particulars.

Certainly in the DFAT context, some of the scenarios where we're using contractors is in some of our demand driven parts of the business. We know, for example, that we've got potential peaks coming for passport processing and requests, so we scale that up. But we don't need to keep that all the time, so we scale down. Generally, it's very specialised cyber and ICT skill sets and some very particular security projects. They are very short term, very specific and niche parts of the department's work, not core.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary and Chief People Officer, People Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You mentioned that number from 1,375 in October 2022 to 788 in September this year. Has that been offset by an increase in permanent employment? How has that been managed? The work is presumably still there.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Indeed. There obviously has been a corresponding increase of ASL to the department through several budget processes. Obviously the detail of that is clear in the PBS and elsewhere. We have obviously been doing contractor conversion in some places where it's relevant and appropriate. Where it's core work and that capability needs to be in the department, we are using some of that ASL, obviously, for contractor conversions. There has been, obviously, a corresponding increase in the department's ASL.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary and Chief People Officer, People Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
That same question on notice, No. 203, states, and I quote:

The department has supported four officers who separated since 1 July 2023 who intended to undertake employment with a managing contractor within the exclusion period.

It continues:

Each was assessed and all were approved by the relevant delegate as appropriate in the circumstances.

Can you confirm that in each of these cases the APS employees did not take up a private position to advise in relation to a contract or a grant agreement to which DFAT is or is proposed to be a party for a period of nine months post separation?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I don't have the detail of those particular exemptions and processes here with me. I'm very happy to take that on notice.

witness_position: First Assistant Secretary and Chief People Officer, People Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. As you do that, I would be interested in how the assessment was made by the relevant DFAT delegate that each of these four cases was appropriate in the circumstances. I want to go to for-profit advisers based inside DFAT posts. I understand that several for-profit managing contractors have employed staff that act as 'embedded advisers' at different DFAT posts advising across design, implementation and evaluation functions for a range of programs. AusConnect recruitment material indicates that privately contracted consultants are being embedded long term at posts to provide technical advice. Can you confirm where and how these models are being used across the Australian international development program and what safeguards have been put in place?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It is a model that is used. I can't tell you the exact numbers or where it is now. I can say that we are aware that we need to have a robust system in place to manage that right from the outset of employment. That includes that the individuals sign conflict of interest declarations and deeds of confidentiality. They receive regular briefings and reminders about that. We also have information, particular clauses and requirements inserted into the contracts. They might be managed in different ways depending on the circumstances. Usually those personnel are bringing in unique and specialist expertise that we're looking for in the development program and that address technical or resource gaps. They allow us to really deliver on the government's development priorities, including in terms of surge support in particular. I do acknowledge this can raise challenges around perceived and real conflicts of interest. We continue to look at ensuring that we have the most robust system in place to manage that and to mitigate those risks. That includes some of the things that we talked about a few minutes ago in terms of a separation between different companies involved in the implementation versus the evaluation of a program, for example.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Development, Multilateral and Europe Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Do you think this is a good way to manage conflicts of interest and a good model to be managing work around?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The model of using contractors embedded in this way is working well for us in terms of being able to deliver on what is a very complex development program. It enables us to access the expertise that we need. I wouldn't say it's a model used widely or broadly. It's used in very specific circumstances, as I said. It's often related to very specific subsectors or the technical expertise we need. In those cases, it does allow us to get access to that expertise, have it incorporated into the broader work we are doing in the delivery of a program and, thus, improve the effectiveness of that delivery.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Development, Multilateral and Europe Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Are these mostly working for US owned managing contractors? Are these embedded firms in any way precluded from future contracting that they may be influencing due to their role at the posts?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I couldn't tell you off the top of my head which firms they are. The same approach applies in terms of conflict of interest, probity and separation. Ms Shillito might want to add to that.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Development, Multilateral and Europe Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I think, in addition to that, where we identify that there is an unmitigable conflict of interest, we would put in place physical measures—either restricting access to systems and information that those particular contractors have and sometimes even physical separation from the team they are advising. So we're very conscious of the perceived conflict of interest that creates and seek to manage that in all instances, including through things such as non-disclosure agreements and things such as that and confidentiality agreements.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Development Programming Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: When did you last have a blow-up around a conflict of interest? One measure of a system working well in that policing is that bad behaviour is ratted out and dealt with. When did you last have to do that? Fill us in on the rigour of what you're doing.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I can give you a recent example from the past two weeks. I have not been in this job for too long. I can look at that in more detail. Advice is often sought from us on how to manage conflicts of interest related to procurement processes. My division is responsible for overseeing the probity of the broader development program. There was one instance where an embedded contractor was asked to do some design work. We advised against that and said it is an unmitigable conflict of interest and that they would need to seek a procurement from the market for that.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Development Programming Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you. I asked questions in December last year about the market concentration in the managing contractor ecosystem. It was QON 304. DFAT's answer on notice mentioned that ODA procurements are open and not restricted to organisations and companies in Australia in line with the OECD principle of untied aid. Is that sufficient justification for DFAT allowing market concentration in the hands of a few large firms, many of which are headquartered in the US?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I recall that discussion and the question on notice. I think what we've discussed before in these sessions is that we acknowledge that there is in some cases concentration in the market in the delivery of the development program. We have been conscious of that for several years now. We have worked to try to address that issue. That has included things such as doing a lot of proactive outreach to potential bidders and firms of all sizes to make sure that we have as level a playing field as possible. It includes things such as the two-step tender process you mentioned before and briefing throughout the tender processes and a range of other mechanisms. We have seen a large increase in the number of different companies bidding for our work since USAID closed and, then again, when the UK development program also reduced its funding. So we have in some cases a doubling or a tripling of the number of responses to tenders. I think it will take a bit of time for the data to show the concentration being affected by that spreading out of the number of different bidders and tenders. We are watching that closely and monitoring it.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Acting Deputy Secretary, Development, Multilateral and Europe Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Isn't it also the case that there have been mergers and increasing concentration occurring at the same time? Is that also a concern? You have people who are missing out on business over there coming here. There is a concentration that is increasing, is there not?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The mergers were quite frequent probably four to five years ago. They've been less in recent years.

text: I would add in relation to Ms Cohen's comments that we have been very proactively reaching out to potential new entrants to the market. text: Good afternoon. I have a question about a contract that was awarded to Wild Pacific Media to make a documentary. I have the contract number here, if that's helpful. It is CN4243289. Mr Nankervis, I will direct my question to you. Can you tell me what that contract was for?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. This is about the diplomatic part. There are two more runways in our Antarctic territory. Has DFAT reached out diplomatically to China about these insertions on our territory?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, I would not characterise them as insertions, Senator. Under the Antarctic Treaty, Antarctic Treaty parties, which include Australia, China and 27 other countries, commit to certain undertakings. Most importantly, article 1 is the non-militarisation objective. That is the peaceful uses objective. Article 4, if you like, freezes and preserves the claimant system, including our claim for 42 per cent of the continent in the Australian Antarctic Territory. Article 7 allows for the inspections regime with respect to Antarctic bases. It's a deal. It's a compromise. Provided any country, any one of the treaty parties, complies with the obligations of the treaty, we will recognise any Antarctic Treaty party's right to establish stations where it so wants to do. That was the nature of the original, if you like, deal that was struck between the United States and then Soviet Union many years ago. It still applies. We call on all Antarctic Treaty parties to comply with their obligations, including, most significantly, article 1, which, as I said, is about non-militarisation and peaceful use. Beyond that, we recognise that the treaty provides a right for any treaty party to establish a station.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: Chief Counsel and First Assistant Secretary, Legal Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

text: I have one more very quick question on the NRL expansion and then we're done with me.
