I wonder if we can have an update, please, on the progress towards securing Australian government funding for the Veimoana rugby partnership. Given the significant investment in rugby league, I want to make sure that we are advancing both sports equally. Especially for the national sports, I want to make sure that we're developing world-class players that come from the islands and we are strengthening the local institutions and teams there.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thanks for your ongoing interest in this topic. As we discussed last time, we've received the Veimoana Partnership proposal that was developed by Rugby Australia and has the endorsement of the three relevant governments. We've been in discussions with each of those governments and Rugby Australia during the intervening period. You may have seen under the Vuvale Union with Fiji there is a commitment to sport under that framework. We are continuing discussions with the government there about the exact constituent nature of that funding and the proportion that will be directed to rugby. We haven't reached a conclusion in those discussions yet. As Ms Peak mentioned earlier, we're also in discussions with the government of Tonga under the Kaume'a Ofi framework. It's yet to be determined what the outcome of those negotiations will be. But sport is certainly an interest of that country, as you would appreciate. In Samoa, we've also been discussing both with government and rugby union authorities the relevance of rugby union investment there. As you may appreciate, there are some ongoing governance challenges around the game there that we're watching with interest and in conversations with Rugby Australia. So at this point, I have nothing more to add to what I said a number of months ago other than saying that we are in further discussions with those governments and we'll have more to say in due course.

We knew that they were discussing their ongoing interest in the Greater Sunrise project with Timor Leste, including Timor Gap. It's really a decision for them to make on the timing. We knew that Greater Sunrise was part of an overall global review.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's not really for me to project that far ahead. These projects are, as you know, very complex. They involve a whole lot of decisions by commercial operators. I'm reluctant to really make an assessment about its viability. Woodside, in their statement, did comment about the quality of the asset. On their statement that they released when they made that decision, they did talk about the quality of the asset. But it's not really for me to talk about its viability.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I want to add to what Mr Marcelo has said. Obviously, a project of this scale is a massive project. It's a commercial decision, as he said. A project such as this is a multibillion-dollar investment, so it is not surprising that it has a very long lead time, often taking many years from discovery to first production. It's not unusual in cases like this for those involved to look at changes in their corporate strategy, their capital allocation or their risk appetite. It does not change the Australian government's very strong commitment to the development of the Greater Sunrise gas fields. We recognise the importance of this to Timor Leste, as was confirmed in the Parseria declaration between Prime Minister Albanese and President Gusm o in January. What is clear, though, is that it's really for the commercial partners for the Sunrise joint venture to bring forward a proposal that is technically feasible and commercially viable. agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, can I first say—I really would encourage you to do this—when we deal with these issues, it's not about publicity or media attention. It is about the interests of the Australian citizen. That is how I approach these matters. I would urge you to do the same.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I do.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I do.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You have not asked for a briefing. If you wish to have a briefing and you are willing to deal with it in those circumstances, I will provide one provided the family gives consent. The family, the next of kin, has to give consent. That is the first point. I would really encourage you to bear that in mind. Secondly, we will say what we said before. We take seriously any allegation that an Australian may have been deprived of their liberty and moved across an international border against their will. As Dr Webster and Ms McGregor have said in response to a number of questions—I think this is the third or fourth tranche—we are seeking information from both governments.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The family have asked me to ask you here whether you will call on the Vietnamese ambassador and seek a direct explanation one to one. That seems the minimum that you would expect. It would match the statement that we got from Dr Webster that the government treats this with the utmost seriousness. You could make that direct request to the ambassador to come in and provide an explanation. I don't understand the resistance to you doing that.

I am still at a loss as to why in these circumstances you resist calling in the Vietnamese ambassador. agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
Thank you for this opportunity. The global trading environment is as complex and contested as it was last time we appeared before this committee, in June. The department has continued to work deliberately and effectively across our international network and with partner agencies to strengthen Australia's economic security and resilience in the face of these headwinds. As the secretary said this morning, we continue to invest in new rules and relationships, support the resilience of critical supply chains, advance multilateral trade reform at the WTO and beyond and expand opportunities for Australian exporters. Our strong trade performance demonstrates the value of this approach, with two-way trade reaching a record $1.3 trillion. We've also supported the government's efforts to bolster and diversify economic partnerships, including through a comprehensive free trade agreement with the European Union. This agreement will open a market of 450 million consumers, with a GDP valued at $30 trillion. It has been effectively closed to many Australian exporters for decades. It will deliver billions of dollars in trade and economic benefits to Australia, including nearly a billion dollars in preferential red meat access every year. At a time of uncertainty, this is a strong outcome for Australian agriculture, a strong outcome for Australian producers and exporters, and a strong outcome for our consumers.

Australia secured market access outcomes that are comparable to and, in many cases, better than those obtained by major agricultural exporters. For beef, we secured one of the most commercially valuable outcomes the European Union has ever granted to a competitive beef-exporting nation. The agreement levels the playing field with one of the world's most protected agricultural markets and provides our producers with commercially meaningful opportunities that would not exist under the status quo.

Let me be clear: the agreement does not compromise our sovereignty. It does not give the European Union authority over our domestic policies, emissions targets or climate settings. Australia retains the right to regulate in its own interests and to determine its own policy settings, consistent with its international obligations. Nor does the agreement lock Australia into net zero. Our commitment to net zero arises from our own nationally determined contributions under the Paris Agreement, not from any free trade agreement. Australia retains the right to determine and update its own contributions under that framework.

What this agreement does do is support greater trade, investment and job creation in clean energy, critical minerals and environmental goods and services. It will help Australia secure the benefits of the global transition to a lower emissions economy while maintaining full control over our domestic policy choices.

We are not immune to the disruption that's challenging the rules based system on which our prosperity relies. In July, the United States imposed section 301 tariffs on 60 of its trading partners, including Australia. The government has made clear that these tariffs are unjustified and unwarranted and should be removed. The government has advocated with the United States at all levels, including through leader-level engagement, ministerial advocacy, officials-level consultations and sustained efforts through our embassy in Washington. Even in the face of these measures, Australian exporters continue to access the US market, with non-gold exports growing by 7.5 per cent in 2025-26.

As a trading nation, our interests are best served by continuing our engagement with partners, pursuing new opportunities, strengthening our partnerships and continuing to support an open, stable and predictable trading system. The department will continue to advance these interests. As always, none of this work would be possible without the dedication, professionalism and expertise of DFAT staff here in Canberra and across our overseas network. I thank them for their efforts. Thank you, Chair. I've got copies for the secretariat.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The European Union, in 2025, was one of Australia's largest sources of foreign investment, with that number being in the vicinity of $966 billion. How will this trade agreement affect investment both from Australia into the EU and from the EU into Australia?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This deal will have a major impact on two-way investment flows. As you have mentioned, the EU, as a single entity, is our second-largest investor. We've made provisions for facilitated investment screening arrangements for the European Union. We have made a range of improvements to goods sectors in which the EU wants to invest, including, as the minister has already made clear, in critical minerals, in green energy and in a whole range of energy resources infrastructure and related sectors. We would hope for and expect a continued uplift in that critical investment partnership with our European colleagues.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Wonderful. You're speaking my language, Mr Mina, when you talk about critical minerals, energy and resources. It's an enormously important part of the Western Australian economy, and trade revenues from those industries are vital to both Western Australia and Australia as a whole. Are you able to shed some light on access and the impact of the Australia-EU free trade agreement in relation to Australia's seafood industry?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Gina Rinehart also supports the critical minerals element, if I'm not mistaken, Minister.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The Australia-EU FTA will eliminate EU tariffs on Australian seafood at entry into force, subject to rules of origin on that Australian seafood qualifying under those rules of origin.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Are you able to summarise very quickly the rules of origin, or that condition?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The rules of origin differ, depending on where the seafood is caught. Seafood that is farmed or caught within Australia's territorial seas, up to 12 nautical miles from the coast, qualifies as originating. Seafood caught further offshore, in Australia's EEZ, or on the high seas, qualify subject to certain additional rules relating to the registration of the vehicle, the flag under which it's sailing and the ownership of the vehicle. So those rules are a little complicated.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you very much for that summary. I think the services sector accounts for, give or take, roughly two-thirds of Australia's GDP. Are you able to offer some insight into the impact of the EU trade deal on Australian service provider access to European markets?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, Senator. The agreement will definitely open up opportunities for Australian service suppliers into the European Union. It will make it easier and more accessible for a range of Australian professionals to enter into the EU—intra-corporate transferees, contract service suppliers, independent professionals and so forth. It also contains a recognition of qualifications for Australian professionals. Under the free trade agreement, once an Australian professional qualification is recognised in one EU member state, it will be recognised in another EU member state without a need to requalify. We also have a particular provision in the free trade agreement called the innovation mobility pathway, which will also make it easier for researchers and technicians to travel to and work within the European Union.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Wonderful. Australia has increased the number of bilateral trade agreements that we've entered, probably in the last two decades, and the importance of them has probably never been higher, as the global trade system comes under pressure and faces some significant barriers. How do the outcomes in this negotiation compare to other free trade agreements that we've concluded in the past? I'm thinking, front of mind, of the United States, Japan or China.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
The first two points you made, Senator, I can only wholeheartedly agree with. This is a very consequential agreement. It lifts our coverage from 79 per cent of Australia's trade covered by free trade agreements to 88 per cent. It puts us effectively in the position of having one of the best, if not the best, free trade networks on the planet, in terms of both coverage and quality. In respect of your point, Senator, about the significance of the moment and the turbulence in global trade, I tried in my opening statement to point to the significance of this deal in that context. Again, I wholeheartedly agree that this deal allows for a new commitment by both these major rules based players to the rules based system at a time when it's under major stress. It is a joint reaffirmation and reconfirmation of our commitment to rules based trade.

In respect of the comparative assessment that you've asked me for, Senator, there are a number of comparisons one could make. Even the US FTA, which was a very high quality FTA, did not cover all agricultural sectors and did not liberalise all agricultural sectors. Of course, famously, sugar was not a part of that final FTA deal. That's not the case here with the European Union. We have managed an uplift in every agricultural sector.

In respect of other developed country free trade agreements, such as Japan, Japan started with a coverage of 76 per cent of tariff lines at the entry into force. We're starting here with 89.7 per cent of tariff lines covered at entry into force. We know we are dealing with countries that are traditionally protectionist on agriculture. We understand that. But even with respect to another major agricultural protectionist country, Japan, this deal is leagues ahead. It's a high-quality deal by all of those measures.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This is just an area of interest to me, which is in a slightly different direction: the Australian government's policy is now to exclude investor-state dispute settlement provisions from new trade and investment agreements. How do these fare in the EU trade deal?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Can I go back to some of the issues that you were answering questions on earlier. It relates to the 'affirmation'—I think that was the word you used, Mr Mina—of Australia's Paris accord and net zero commitment. Just to clarify that, does the EU FTA lock Australia into net zero in any way?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, it doesn't.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Does it create any new obligations in respect of net zero?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Is it a fixed-in-time proposition? If our obligations under our climate goals change, how does the EU trade agreement deal with that?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
The individually and nationally determined contributions under the Paris framework are just that—individual and nationally determined. We retain the flexibility to change those commitments under the Paris accord and we retain them under this free trade agreement. In fact, this free trade agreement explicitly recognises that flexibility. Article 18.2 of the agreement says:

… recognise the right of each Party to determine its sustainable development policies and priorities, to establish the levels of domestic environmental and labour protection it deems appropriate and adopt or modify its relevant laws and policies in a manner consistent with its commitments under the international agreements and labour standards referred to …

Even in the agreement text itself there is that explicit recognition of the flexibility we have under the Paris accord.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This is my final question. It is taking advantage of the expertise we have at the table. We've discussed the services sector a little bit, we've discussed the resources sector a little bit and we've discussed agriculture. Are there sectors in the Australian economy that we haven't discussed yet that you are particularly excited about in relation to this deal or that are particularly game changing or groundbreaking?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There are a whole range of those sectors. You've mentioned many of them. What we also mentioned earlier is the enormous potential, as the minister has already referenced, for us to work together with the EU on energy, critical minerals and the resources sector more generally, where the EU clearly has both the capabilities and capital to contribute to our economy and to our jobs and investment, and we have the resources that can seriously contribute to that partnership. There are big opportunities for us in the green economy sector, including the tens of billions of dollars of potential investment that's available. In respect of the goods and services related to the green economy, the agreement specifies, in the sustainable development chapter, a whole range of commodities which would be now subject to zero tariffs and a big part of the outcome of this deal.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Some of those items or materials—critical minerals being front of mind—also have strategic implications. There has been this concept, as we try and secure global supply chains for strategically important materials, of friendshoring or ally-shoring. It seems to me that this represents an example of that. Are you able to elaborate on that at all?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Absolutely. In respect of our broader interests in critical minerals, what we want to do is work with all of our friends and partners globally to build resilient supply chains, diversify those supply chains and make sure that we're not overly reliant on one supplier or one set of suppliers, and to ensure that in Australia we can capture as much as possible of the exports relating to this sector and the uplift in processing that would be associated with this sector. What we need is capital—capital that invests in our processing of critical minerals, and markets, offtake partners. The enormous needs of European industry and European manufacturing, including not only the high-tech sectors but also the more downstream sectors, are only forecast to grow massively. So we have an opportunity there not only to attract the capital and expertise but also, as an export partner, to work with the European Union on these issues.

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

text: No, before my questioning tonight. Before that, had you ever actually indicated in a footnote, with asterisks, 'Actually, these figures don't necessarily reflect the deal as signed'?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As I said, and as in Ms Raper's evidence earlier, we have referenced the report to which you refer and we have referenced in that footnote where one can access that report, including, to the extent that it was available in 2020-21, what those assumptions were. Senator, that's why—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It took me a couple of hours to read through it this week, preparing notes.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That's why we're doing this updated assessment.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And it's very disappointing to see the Australian government mislead the Australian people. It erodes trust in our institutions when departments and others sign off information which is clearly misleading—it is clearly misleading—to the Australian public. All of this information is publicly available and easy to access. The report also claims, under this scenario you've relied on, that Australia's rice exports will increase by 113 per cent, sugar exports to the EU will increase by 123 per cent and dairy exports to the EU will increase by 86 per cent. Do you stand by those increases? Will that happen under the EU free trade deal?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I first make the point, as I have many times already, that this modelling is getting updated. In respect of dairy, what we can do is talk to the outcomes. We had a sector that had miserably low access into Europe. We have—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Can I just bring you back to the question. The question was—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Do we accept—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You said in the fact sheet that it could increase—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Chair.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Australia's GDP by up to $7.8 billion.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Chair.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That relies on an 86 per cent increase in dairy exports. Is that going to happen?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Minister, do you want to add something there?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This was a week in which we were trying to improve respect in the parliament. The witness is trying to give a genuine and honest answer to the question that Senator Canavan has raised. Can I request that we try and maintain that respect and at least give the witness an opportunity to answer the question.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On the point of order, respect is earned, not given. It is not helped when public officials and the government present misleading information. That is why people are disrespecting our parliament—because there are lies being told—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You've still got to give respect.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Order!

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: time and again about all sorts of things.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Order! As chair I'll enforce the standing orders, as required by the Senate and as adopted by the Senate. Mr Mina, did you have anything else to add to your evidence?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I did. The senator has just made some comments about dairy. We had an average dairy tariff of 2.4 per cent. The European Union had an average dairy tariff of 27 per cent. Now that's largely gone to zero. So we have a massive levelling of the playing field on dairy. We are going to eliminate 87 per cent of the European Union's dairy tariffs. One can draw one's own conclusions about the benefits that would provide to our dairy sector. The predominant point is that this is a massive uplift in dairy.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Do those tariffs include the tariff equivalents, including the subsidies that the EU provides to its dairy industry?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Neither are climate agreements. Neither are labour agreements.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The Australian government has been consistent—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That wasn't a constraint.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The Australian government has been a consistent supporter, on both sides of politics, of agricultural subsidy reform. We have been continuing to press our European counterparts for subsidy reform, including in dairy, for many years through the Cairns Group.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On the topic of dairy, are you aware that, with the EU Commission modelling, under its conservative scenario—which does not include the removal of agricultural non-tariff barriers; it's more accurately describing the agreement—the dairy industry in Australia would be one of six to see production fall, as a result of the agreement? Our production would fall. Are you aware of that?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You are citing, I take it, the European Union's analysis?
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That might explain why the dairy industry is ropeable about this. I might leave it there, given the time, and move on to another issue with this deal. Is the government aware that a Dutch environmental organisation, known as Both ENDS, has lodged a formal complaint with the European Commission, alleging that New Zealand has breached its climate obligations under the EU-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement? They lodged this on 29 September.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We are aware of that report.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What's your awareness of the basis for their claim?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This is a complaint made under a private mechanism of the European Union. It is not directly related to any mechanism in the EU-New Zealand FTA. Certainly, there is no means under the Australia-EU FTA for a private person or organisation, including an NGO from the EU, to bring any dispute against Australia under our FTA.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The complaint specifically challenges New Zealand's decision to reduce its 2015 methane reduction target from 24 to 47 per cent to 14 to 24 per cent. What's stopping a private group making a similar complaint on the EU-Australia free trade deal?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Because there is no mechanism for them to do so under the Australia-EU FTA deal.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Is there such a mechanism under the New Zealand free trade deal with the EU?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That would be a matter for the New Zealand government. As I said, it is under a commission domestic mechanism that this complaint has been brought.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Both ENDS have also identified New Zealand's reversal of its offshore oil and gas exploration ban. It has cited the New Zealand government investing $200 million in a gas security fund. It's also challenging New Zealand's decision to remove the legal requirement that its ETS align with the Paris Agreement targets. I've been assured time and time again that Australian laws can't be used or weaponised by climate activist groups, and we've seen them do that. Surely, there's a risk here that, similarly, what we're doing here is giving licence to European courts to make rulings on Australian government decisions.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This is a matter within European processes, unrelated to our FTA.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Both ENDS have publicly identified that their next target will be Australia, after New Zealand. Are you aware of that?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, Senator.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: They are going to pursue this. How can you give a guarantee about what European courts will decide on these matters? Can you give such guarantees?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There is no connection between this process and the dispute settlement provisions in our FTA. They are completely unrelated processes.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But it's a treaty and an agreement that the EU has signed up to. I am no international lawyer, but quite often these international agreements are weaponised through international law courts and through European courts. We've seen that in the past. A European court is beyond the purview of the European Commission, presumably, and/or our own government, and it can decide what it may on the details of this agreement.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Is there a question there, Senator?
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We, presumably, cannot dictate or control what a European court may decide here.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But they have no jurisdiction over us.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: How do we know? They have potential jurisdiction over the agreement, though.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, they don't.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Why couldn't they rule that the EU has to enforce its deal, as those international courts have ruled that the Paris Agreement—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Chair, the witness is attempting to answer the question.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I don't think I was interrupting. I thought she had finished.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The witness was attempting to honestly answer the question, Senator Canavan. You continued to talk over her.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I apologise for that. I wasn't intending to.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We are getting closer to dinner. Let's keep marching on.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: If I could add something, as was given in evidence previously, there are no investor-state dispute settlement provisions in the EU FTA at all, which means that only the EU, as the state, can take a state-to-state dispute settlement process. All the provisions regarding enforcement need to be done on a state-to-state basis. The reasons that motivate a country to take a dispute vary, but the actual dispute action can only be taken between the two states.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Trade Law and Economic Security Division, and Chief Trade Law Officer

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What's stopping a European court directing the European Commission to take that action?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The basis on which a government may take a dispute, or not, is independent of the FTA.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Trade Law and Economic Security Division, and Chief Trade Law Officer

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I am not sure that answers my question. European governments are subject, presumably, to European courts, just as we are to Australian courts. What would stop a European court ruling that the European Commission, European officials, have to take that state-to-state action that you refer to as being available to them under this agreement?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The point is that it's not something that is covered in the FTA. The basis on which the state in question in relation to a dispute action takes that decision is not addressed in the FTA. That is a matter for the Australian government or the—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Trade Law and Economic Security Division, and Chief Trade Law Officer

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That doesn't reassure me at all, particularly given our own experience. Just recently, a New South Wales court stopped a coal mine. We've been assured time and time again that these provisions wouldn't affect scope 3 emissions. It happens all the time in our own system. I don't see what would stop it happening in Europe, particularly given, probably, their activist class is even more weaponised than ours. Moving on to the provisions of the Paris Agreement, at the June estimates, when I asked about this, DFAT referred to the exceptions available in chapter 23 that would potentially provide the Australian government with flexibility in regard to things like climate agreements. On notice, it would appear DFAT has confirmed that article 23.1 does not apply to the trade and sustainable development chapter. Is that true?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That's correct, Senator.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We can't rely on the general exceptions of 23.1 to defend ourselves against any potential breach of chapter 18?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, there are other exceptions that apply, but not that one.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: With the other exceptions, 23.2 relates to national security, and it really focuses on things like arms control, fissionable materials and wartime. You've identified 23.3, which is taxation, particularly taxation agreements with other countries. 23.4 is about the treatment of information that may or may not be confidential under the agreement, and 23.5 relates to waivers of WTO agreements. I'm struggling to see how any of those subsections or subclauses of chapter 23 would give us an exception to chapter 18. Can you take me through how that would work?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It would depend on the circumstances of the particular issue, in analysing whether any of those exceptions that you've just referred to apply. Of course, we have to look at the agreement in its entirety. As Mr Mina said earlier, the environment chapter, the trade and sustainable development chapter itself, already provides that flexibility very clearly in article 18.2 for a party to adapt or modify its environmental policies.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: 'Adapt and modify' is different. Say we decided we'd pull out of the Paris Agreement—that's it, we're out—which of those exceptions would give us protection in that event?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Once again, this agreement simply reaffirms Paris. In that respect, the—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Does it lock us into it, though? That's my question.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: If your question is whether it locks us into the particular targets under Paris, of course not.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, it wasn't my question.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But if it—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'd appreciate it if my questions aren't reframed.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No; if it's relating to enforcement in relation to whether to be a member of Paris, the answer there is simply that there are enforcement provisions here, quite evidently. That's the purpose of the relevant provisions relating to Paris. But the important point there is that the enforcement action can only take you back to where you were before the FTA. In other words, the enforcement action is only a denial of the benefits of the FTA. You don't go backwards from where you were before the FTA.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As the government has said, and as you have said, it binds us, then; it's a binding situation. 'Binding' is the verb you used, when announcing this deal. Obviously, if we are in a war, we can get out of Paris then, and we can rely on section 23.2. But that's a fairly extreme scenario. I don't see how any other provisions—the taxation provision, the information-sharing provision, the WTO waiver provision—provide any defence from having flexibility around our agreement to Paris or not.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As to membership of Paris itself, we're already bound. This is a repetition of that, and nothing more than that.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But there are no penalties to get out of Paris. We've seen that with the US. There are no—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sorry, Senator; can you repeat that?
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There are no ramifications to the Paris Agreement. There are to this. That is how this is different. This is binding Australia in a way we haven't been before.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What I am trying to explain is that the only consequence under this agreement is a denial of the benefits under this agreement. In other words, you go back to where you were before the FTA was signed.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But it's fundamentally different from what we signed up to when we signed up for Paris. I was there at the time. Full transparency: I have never said, and now maintain, that we should be okay to stay in Paris, but only if it doesn't bind us in a legal fashion, which this now does, which you've admitted to.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, Senator, it is not fundamentally—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This is the core problem we have with it. It goes well beyond what we signed up to under the Paris Agreement.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, Senator, it does not fundamentally differ from the Paris commitment, nor does it go substantially beyond the Paris commitment. We were bound before—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I disagree with that.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We were bound before the FTA. We reaffirmed, and repeated that Paris commitment in the FTA, so we were bound before and through this FTA.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I've outlined how I disagree with your—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It is not a fundamental difference.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Unless you can tell me—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's in fact a simple reaffirmation of that.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You have established that there is a penalty, the denial of the benefits of this free trade agreement, if we get out of Paris. That is something that you have established. What is the denial of benefits to Australia under the Paris Agreement if we remove ourselves from that?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, on the first part of your question, that is accurate. On the second, we would need to refer that, as I said earlier, to experts on the Paris accord.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That's the difference. That's why we are fundamentally against this, because it is not—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, you go back to where you were before you signed the FTA; in other words, you don't access the significant uplift in economic opportunity here.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I don't think we should be binding ourselves on something—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What you don't do—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: as important as energy security.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, if I can finish; it is quite important.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Let the witness finish, please.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What we do not do is impose any penalty on Australia beyond that which is contained in this free trade agreement. It is contained to the uplift—the economic uplift—that this deal provides to us. Yes, we wouldn't be able to access those benefits. That's an important reason why we are taking advantage and taking the full opportunity of this package.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I have a few questions. Mr Mina, could you talk us through the engagement in this deal around Horizon? I know there are a lot of interested people, particularly in the national security space, defence space, and even in academia. Could you or one of your officials talk to us about the benefits that arise out of this free trade deal with respect to Horizon?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
European Commission President von der Leyen, when she visited in March, made three important announcements. One was the conclusion of negotiation of this free trade agreement between Australia and the European Union, one was around Australia's association with Horizon Europe, and the other one was the Security and Defence Partnership. All of these three pillars of the advancement of the Australia-Europe relationship are complementary. The free trade agreement will help operationalise the other two parts of this relationship uplift. Specifically, the free trade agreement will provide the mobility provisions that will enable academics and researchers to travel to the European Union and live and work in order to access those research and development opportunities and funding under Horizon Europe. It will also allow our services professionals to do similar, and to be able to take advantage of those benefits.

Relating to the Security and Defence Partnership, we see provisions such as the investment improvements that we've referenced and the elimination of tariffs. The government procurement opportunities from the FTA will also help complement the other benefits in these arrangements between Australia and the European Union.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: With respect to the funding pool that's available, could you elaborate on the access that we will all be able to have in terms of advanced computing, space, supply chain security and critical minerals? What will it mean in practical terms for the sectors in Australia that would benefit from having access to that pool, which I understand is quite substantial?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The funding package for Horizon Europe at the moment, for 2021-27, is around 95 million euros. It's the largest innovation and research scheme of its kind in the world. Australia is going through the process of entering into that Horizon Europe scheme.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Europe Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What does that mean for innovation or productivity gains here?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'd probably have to defer questions on particular innovation uplift to colleagues at the Department of Industry, Science and Resources. But it is a large scheme with huge potential.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Europe Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You'd expect to see a much greater engagement and stronger research collaboration between academia and the Europeans in terms of the greater investment in space, for instance.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Absolutely. One of the other elements that Australia's entered into is the Security and Defence Partnership, which goes to some of those areas, like the defence industry, innovation, space dialogue and critical minerals. A range of those innovative sectors would be encompassed.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Europe Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What value are you expecting that would also add, with our national security agencies having access under this deal? What are they expecting to gain?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Under the Security and Defence Partnership that the government announced earlier this year, there would be opportunity, as there has been already, in economic security. There's been a security dialogue that officials have held. There will be a range of opportunities to progress economic security, space and other areas with the EU.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Europe Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Have you got more examples? What are the things that will come out of this? Surely you've got some practical examples you are able to provide to us.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We will enter into the first phase from January next year, so we are still going through that. For any other concrete examples, we would have to defer to the Department of Industry, Science and Resources.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Europe Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator Ghosh mentioned critical minerals. There would be a number of businesses in Western Australia, and obviously across Australia, that would stand to benefit immensely. Arafura, the rare earth miner, has publicly supported the deal, as has the Minerals Council of Australia. Why is it that they are so supportive of this free trade deal?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
It goes precisely to the reasons you've set out, Senator. The first is the innovation pathways this provides Australia. We have a very fast-growing sector in space and high-tech exports, which has huge potential through our research collaborations, industrial partnerships and, indeed, university partnerships to take advantage of European expertise in this area. Secondly, with the resources that we have and the opportunity this deal presents for companies like Arafura and for other players associated with the Minerals Council to find partnerships for both offtake and investment to diversify those supply chains we've been talking about, we have a major opportunity here to embed our resources industry in one of the fastest-growing industrial sectors anywhere.

Thirdly, of course, is the investment that comes with the above two features. If you like, the Horizon package and the free trade agreement nestle together to provide big opportunities for the Australian resources sector.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: In terms of the science innovation grants, did you say it was A$95 million?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Euros.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I was under the impression it was billions.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Do you want us to convert it to Australian dollars?
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Europe Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What is that in Australian dollars?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It would be around A$130 million.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Europe Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Would that then allow not just universities but others to tap into that research or pool the money for research and development? Is that your understanding on how that would operate?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It would give access to Australian researchers to access that.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Europe Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Will that be managed through the department or one of the agencies that fall within DFAT, or is it a direct application to the Europeans?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The point of contact within the Australian government to manage that interaction would be the Department of Industry, Science and Resources.
witness_organisation: Office of the Pacific
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Europe Division

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Then fast forward. What are the next steps that will make sure that we do end up having access to funding like this? What are the next steps to ensure that the trade deal is in force?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We need, on both sides, to bring this deal not only to signature but through our domestic ratification processes. We need to do that as soon as possible. We need to make sure that we have in place a treaty entering into force as soon as possible so that the tariff reductions, which are done over a period of years, as always is the case with free trade agreements, can kick in. The investment facilitation I spoke about earlier can kick in and the benefits of these industrial partnerships under Horizon can also start to flourish. Those benefits are available to us as soon as ratification commences.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: In terms of that process, I think we all understand it will go to our committee that looks after treaties. Before that process starts, is it correct that the Europeans need to sign off and then it comes to us for signature? Is that how that works?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, Senator. Both sides need to complete domestic processes to get to signature, which is the next step that we're working towards. On the European side, a Council of Europe vote is required in order to approve European signature of the FTA.

text:
As Ms Raper has said, article 25.5 of the EU-Australia FTA then refers to the Australia-EU Framework Agreement, which is a high-level agreement that sits broadly with our bilateral area. But it specifically refers to clarifying that, for the purposes of that agreement, the EU-Australia FTA is considered one of the agreements that qualifies as a specific agreement under article 55.1. That then means that, in those cases referred to in 25.5.2, the relevant provisions of article 57 of the framework agreement can be invoked. Those provisions relate to matters of special urgency and then simply refer back to the agreements that may be relevant. So it's really a mechanism to clearly link the two agreements: the framework agreement and the specific references there, back to the FTA. The mechanisms under the framework agreement for resolving disputes are not as comprehensive as the mechanisms under the free trade agreement. I also might say that, in the same chapter that you were referring to, it's also relevant that article 25.7 goes to 'no direct effect of the FTA'. It states:

Nothing in this Agreement shall be construed as conferring rights or imposing obligations on persons, other than the rights or obligations created between the Parties under public international law, nor as permitting this Agreement to be directly invoked in a Party's legal system.

So they're just elements to the mechanism by which obligations or commitments can be challenged and enforced. As I said earlier, it's a state-to-state-only mechanism that would then be implemented in the free trade agreement. I think article 25.5 is simply linking that to the framework agreement, and article 25.7 is making clear that it is not creating a direct effect or giving any direct rights for any other body or group to directly enforce the obligations in the free trade agreement. So, if a breach were considered to have occurred, including a breach related to materially defeating the objects and purposes of the Paris Agreement, it would only be the mechanism under the dispute settlement chapter of the free trade agreement that would be invoked.
