In cases of urgency, it's a referral to the joint committee structures, under the framework agreement, and then potentially for ministerial consideration. There's not a tribunal or panel established but, as I've said—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Trade Law and Economic Security Division, and Chief Trade Law Officer

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You mentioned earlier that the framework agreement seems to deal with issues of human rights, and I think it also deals with weapons of mass destruction. I can under that there would be urgency in those cases and perhaps the need to obviate an independent panel process. Why then is anything that materially defeats an object or purpose of the Paris Agreement put on the same level as human rights breaches or issues around weapons of mass destruction?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I hesitate to provide more-specific legal advice, in relation to the framework agreement, because it's not a trade agreement and I'm the chief trade law officer.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Trade Law and Economic Security Division, and Chief Trade Law Officer

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But I'm referring to what's in the trade agreement.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Trade Law and Economic Security Division, and Chief Trade Law Officer

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The evidence that I'm hearing on the other side of the table is, 'Oh, don't worry about it, Matt; we can do whatever we like under the Paris Agreement,' yet time and time again—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: My evidence—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Trade Law and Economic Security Division, and Chief Trade Law Officer

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: May I finish?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm sorry.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Trade Law and Economic Security Division, and Chief Trade Law Officer

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The evidence that I'm hearing is, 'Don't worry about it, as it's fine; we can do whatever we like under the Paris Agreement,' yet we have a provision here in this trade agreement that gives the EU the right to take action in a seemingly fairly urgent manner, without the need to go through independent panel processes to resolve a dispute, equivalent to what they could do regarding human rights and weapons of mass destruction, for anything that defeats the objects and purposes of the Paris Agreement. That provision does not seem consistent with your overall conclusion that this deal would not impose significant constraints on how we handle our commitments under the Paris Agreement.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I would make a few points. Article 57.4 states that the parties 'recognise that such a case of special urgency may serve as a ground for taking appropriate measures outside this agreement'—that is, the framework agreement—'in accordance with the rights and obligations of the parties under other agreements between the parties or under general international law'. That then means you turn back to the provisions of the free trade agreement. My evidence is certainly not that there is absolutely no relevance or commitment; the commitment is to refrain from actions that materially defeat the objects and purposes of the Paris Agreement.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Trade Law and Economic Security Division, and Chief Trade Law Officer

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Absolutely.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On that basis, the EU, as the state, could potentially take a dispute and then, if it were established that whatever action the Australian government had taken did do that, through a panel process there would then potentially be scope to impose retaliation, which would have to be proportionate to the breach. Also, as Mr Mina has said, that takes you back to the position before the FTA, so it's contained in the FTA. So no one is saying that there are no consequences. We are saying that they are contained to the FTA and require that high bar, and we are able to change our nationally determined contribution. I think it's clear how it works.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Trade Law and Economic Security Division, and Chief Trade Law Officer

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I think you've just laid it out clearly: yes, the objects and purposes of the Paris Agreement are now going to be binding on us in a way they weren't previously. They're clearly not binding under the Paris Agreement proper, but now they will be—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: They are legally binding.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Trade Law and Economic Security Division, and Chief Trade Law Officer

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There will be serious, real consequences, which weren't there before if we act in a way which materially defeats the objects and purpose of the Paris Agreement. That is clear.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We have to reject that proposition again. This is not fundamentally different to the position we have at the moment. We are bound to the Paris Agreement. Currently, before the estimates—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You can't answer these questions when I ask them, so I don't know how we get to the conclusion. If I ask—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: If I can finish, we are bound currently, and we will be bound after the FTA, so that is not a fundamental difference. We want to meet this very high bar. As Ms Holmes just explained, yes, there are enforcement consequences, and they are limited to the FTA—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Under the Paris Agreement, do we face real consequences for doing something which materially defeats the objects and purposes of that agreement?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This is the counterfactual. At the moment, we have no economic benefits from this FTA. We also don't face that enforcement risk of losing those economic benefits. So it is contained to the FTA—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We've established that pretty well here. This does bind us seriously, in a way, and it's very clear to me.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's very important that that distinction is made clear.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We're moving the call around. Senator Dowling.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I want to ask some questions in relation to Australia's red-meat market access issues, if I can. For context, what's the volume of beef that we sell internationally, and how has that number changed over recent years?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We've had an extraordinary uplift in the last five or six years in Australia's beef exports internationally, from something like $8 or $9 billion five or six years ago to $20.8 billion in 2025-26. Our beef trade is strong.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What would be the causes of that growth? What's the main driver there?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There are a variety of reasons for that. Part of it relates to herd sizes and sustainability in major producing countries. Part of it relates to our relative market access in relation to other major exporting parties—for instance, in the United States, our beef exports enter tariff free. I would hesitate to get into the climatic and other production conditions related to the expansion of the Australian herd, but clearly the success of our own production factors and capabilities is a big part of this. Economists at the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics would no doubt be well placed to talk you through those. Trade is a big feature, obviously, and the success is down to the trade environment and to the access we've been able to win.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There's been a lot of commentary around how the proposed EU free trade agreement would affect beef. Could you give us any clear numbers on precisely what is the outcome for beef in the trade agreement?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, of course. I guess the important comparator is our current access to the EU market for Australian beef. Our only current guaranteed access is 4,400 tonnes. Under this free trade agreement we'll be able to increase that access to guaranteed preferential access of 35,000 tonnes. That is split into a number of different buckets, which I can go into, if you wish.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: If I may add to Ms Raper's evidence, the comparative outcomes here, with reference to competitor exporters into the EU, are extremely strong. Our access, which is now eight times higher under this FTA for beef into Europe, is more than individual Mercosur countries. We're able to win three times more in fact than New Zealand was able to achieve, three times more than Mexico was able to achieve and equivalent to the quantum of fresh and chilled access that Canada was able to achieve. But we also know that Canada has been unable to use its full access, which is larger than ours in theory. But their ability to use has been restrained. So this stacks up as, if not the best, one of the best outcomes anyone's able to achieve on beef into the EU market.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The conditions attached to our access are also better. For example, we have no frozen only requirement, whereas, in the Mercosur deal, roughly half of their access is reserved for frozen beef. The Mercosur countries also continue to be subject to a 7.5 per cent tariff, whereas almost two-thirds of Australian beef under this deal will be duty free.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: To summarise that, to be clear, the outcomes for beef are superior to the status quo and superior to the outcomes negotiated for the Mercosur countries.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That's right. And these were both on the quality of the outcomes that Ms Raper has just set out and the quantum of the access we achieved. These were extremely hard-fought negotiations. We've been at this deal to get access to EU agriculture for 20 years in various fora—the World Trade Organization, and then in this bilateral free trade agreement. Our negotiators, led by Ms Raper, achieved some extraordinary results, and this access is highly usable. It'll allow us to access that high premium price market in the EU of 450 million consumers. It will allow us to keep pace with and beat competitors who are moving ahead in their own access. Again, the counterfactual, stand still, gain nothing and worse, see our market share taken by other competitors.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As a very experienced negotiation team, the idea that there was something better on the table, or there's some mythical superior outcome, that's just not the case.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I was in various rooms with the minister who of course who had led a very difficult negotiation with both commissioners for trade and agriculture. We left nothing on the table.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
Thank you. Could I also focus now on an issue that I'm passionate about: Tasmanian vegetables. The industry body, AUSVEG, has strongly backed the trade agreement. I saw a quote where they've warned:

… a populist stampede to stop this Free Trade Agreement risks severe collateral damage to Australian vegetable growers, and our national food security.

I know in Tasmania, for example, Premium Fresh at Forth, which employs about 150 people and exports vegetables to Europe, they currently face a situation when a carrot arrives in Europe— if you could confirm this—it's greeted with a welcoming gift of a 3.6 per cent tariff. I think an onion arrives with about a 9.6 per cent tariff. Can you confirm if, under this deal that's been negotiated, those tariffs would actually disappear immediately. And what does that actually mean for the competitiveness of our vegetable growers, such as Premium Fresh at Forth.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On entry into force, the vast majority of EU tariffs will be eliminated. That includes tariffs on vegetables and vegetable products. For example, under this FTA, on entry into force, we will see the 9.6 per cent tariff on onions to the EU eliminated. We will see the 13.6 per cent tariff on carrots eliminated, and tariffs of up to 11.5 per cent on potatoes will be eliminated.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I've also seen some disturbing reports about losing market share to New Zealand. Charlton Farm Produce in north-west of Tasmania previously exported as much as 1,200 tonnes of onions to Spain, but that trade has fallen to zero since New Zealand secured preferential access under its own agreement with Europe. So can you explain the competitive disadvantage Australian growers have faced since that New Zealand free trade agreement came into effect, and how our agreement would help to address that?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, New Zealand has had those tariffs eliminated. We have not, and we will not have them eliminated until this treaty enters into force. So we are currently at a significant tariff disadvantage, and, as a result, New Zealand has obtained that market share. This free trade agreement offers an opportunity to level that playing field with our competitors.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The longer that we stay with the status quo and don't achieve this agreement the longer our growers face that disadvantage?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Correct.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Tasmania is also a very important producer of cherries, apples and pears. As I understand it, under the agreement, European tariffs that are up to 12 per cent on fresh cherries would be eliminated. Could you outline some of the opportunities this agreement creates for our fruitgrowers, particularly including that staged removal of tariffs on apples and pears as well?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Certainly. Yes, the current EU tariff of 12 per cent on Australian cherries will be eliminated on the entry into force of this agreement. Tariffs on pears of up to 10.4 per cent will be eliminated after three years following entry into force. Tariffs on apples of up to nine per cent will be eliminated at seven years, which is the term for the full implementation of the agreement.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Reflecting the comprehensive nature of the agreement beyond horticulture, I also understand that there are removals of tariffs on Atlantic salmon, aluminium, zinc and wood products. Can you explain how the agreement improves market access, particularly for things like Tasmanian seafood producers and our established manufacturing and minerals processing industries?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes. We also see tariffs removed on several seafood products. Importantly, the tariff on Atlantic salmon of two per cent will be eliminated under this agreement. In addition, there are other important tariff eliminations also on seafood, such as 12 per cent on prawns and 11 per cent on abalone.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Your department figures show that Tasmania exported $4.6 billion in goods globally in 2025. But, of that $4.6 billion, only $95 million went to the EU. Does this suggest there's considerable scope for Tasmanian exporters to diversify now into that wealthy European market, given the additional opportunities for agriculture, seafood and manufacturing?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That's absolutely right. As Mr Mina said earlier, the European market has been largely closed to Australian exports of agricultural products due to their very high tariffs. As a result, we've not been able to get our product into the EU market, because it's not being competitive with other countries that have got preferential access—you referenced New Zealand there. Because this agreement will remove those tariff disadvantages, we would expect our exports to increase accordingly.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you for that insight. That sounds like a pretty good deal to me, Chair, so I'm done.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You're sold! Good. I'll see if the coalition have any other questions. Senator Canavan, you have the call.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: With this beef situation, what has happened to our quota to the EU of beef exports over the past decade? What was it 10 years ago, what is it today and what is it meant to be under this agreement?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The major event in that period, in what was quite low access to begin with, was, as you've already said, the decision by the UK to leave the European Union. In that context, there was a further reduction by the EU 27 and the available access to beef. We can go into more detail if you wish.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Prior to Brexit, Australian exporters could export 9,300 tonnes of beef to the EU, including the UK. But, once the UK left the EU in 2021, this quota was split roughly in half to 4,900 tonnes for the UK and 4,400 tonnes for the EU, which is where we're still stuck.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Didn't we have access to some other global quota as well?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We do have access to a global quota.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What was that 10 years ago?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That was established by the EU but has been reduced following US dispute action.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That's right.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And now it's a share of a global quota of, I think, 10,000 tonnes. But that is shared amongst all countries who wish to access it, so it's not guaranteed.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: When I speak to beef producers—and this is the reason they're ropeable about this deal—in their view, the access we get under this deal really, at best, re-establishes what we had before the EU side deal with the first Trump administration. What do you say to that claim?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Based on the numbers I've just read out, I think this access will be higher.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But that 9,000 doesn't include the access to the global quota, does it?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But that's not guaranteed access.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay, it's not guaranteed, but we had it and we were able to—I've seen some figures showing we exported around 30,000 tonnes to the EU a decade or so ago, and this deal does 35,000. This is where people get really upset about being gaslighted. Beef producers aren't fools; they know the EU sold us down the river in 2019 when they did a side deal with the Trump administration. That's their right and they did it, and, effectively, we're being asked to now get out the champagne corks for a deal that goes back to what we had before the first Trump administration. It doesn't seem like a great deal for us on those terms.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As we explained, those earlier figures were based on EU28. You have to look at both the EU FTA and the UK FTA outcomes as being the equivalent of that pre-Brexit number.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Do you have the figures for what we exported in tonnes to EU27 over the past decade?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We will have that number but I'll have to take that on notice today.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That's the relevant thing. You're here saying it's such a great deal. I would like to see how much better it is relative to before the EU decided to do a side deal with the Trump administration. That was their right, but for us to turn around and celebrate the unwinding of that seems a bit rich.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On the points you're making about historical access to the EU market, over the last several years—effectively, a decade—it has been quite low, as Ms Raper said. You are right that not only Brexit but also the US-EU negotiation after the beef hormones case was taken at the WTO have impacted significantly on our ability to access the EU market. In fact, over successive decades we have seen a tightening of access. With both the UK and EU deals, we are restoring and boosting significantly beyond the kinds of access levels we have had historically. The choice is not rewinding to a period before the US and the EU negotiated their bilateral deal, or of whether we could control the conditions with respect to Brexit. What we can control is negotiating our way to guaranteed new access, and doing that in a way that is comparable or better than all of our competitors. The point you're making about some historical erosions is a fair one, noting the point that we have control over these negotiations only bilaterally, and we've achieved an outcome that is comparable or better and which, in our view is one we should be taking. We left nothing on the table for both quantity and quality.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The problem here is I don't think our benchmark should be inferior deals that other countries have signed up to the EU with. Our benchmark should be the high standards that the Australian government has always demanded for free trade agreements, including the former coalition government. We signed the UK free trade deal where, eventually, we had unlimited access to export beef to the UK. With this deal, weakening our high standards on these matters weakens our long-term bargaining position. Clearly, the government has been a pushover here on this—they walked away from the same deal three years ago and now they've walked back and signed it. That is the definition of a pushover. It puts us in a weaker position going forward to negotiate strong access with other countries. I think it's very unfortunate. It's not a point that just I am making—the National Farmers Federation made this specific point in their media release the day after. If the access is so great, it's a little bit surprising that no beef representative group like the NFF, no sugar group and no dairy group has come out in favour of the deal. That's why they haven't, because—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's a fact that our current guaranteed access is 4,400 tonnes of beef to the EU, and that's all it will ever be unless we take this—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This is a repeated game; it's not just a one-off. We're looking at it a little bit too narrowly, in my view. I'm an economist who's been around these things for a long time. There was a period of time—when I was very young—when economists used not to look very kindly on bilateral free trade agreements because, notionally, they were in contravention of the most favoured nation status and the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. Did we get legal advice on whether this agreement has met the provisions of GATT and the need to substantially cover all trade?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: First, to address a couple of those assertions that we can't leave unanswered, this does not weaken standards or weaken access.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, it's a judgement call, but yes.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Of course it is not a pushover—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And if they've disagreed—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: and there were substantial improvements from the deal that was on offer in 2023. All of that has to be corrected, I'm sorry. On the question of the GATT standards, article XXIV substantially all trade standards, as Ms Holmes and Ms Raper have made clear, our public international lawyers have been integrally involved in the negotiation of this deal, and, yes, we are confident that this deal meets those high standards. It's one of the highest standards FTAs we have ever negotiated. I made clear earlier that it, unlike the US-Australia FTA, left no agriculture sector uncovered, and, in respect of another major FTA—that with Japan—substantially higher coverage on the tariffs coverage. So it's obviously consistent with provision.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. These are all judgements. As I say, it's not just me but almost all farm groups are coming to the same conclusions about these issues.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Can I also add—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay but quickly, because I want to move on.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There is a review clause after five years on the tariff rate quotas for beef and sheepmeat. That was a key request of Australian industry and one we've met in this agreement.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I want to turn back to this Both ENDS group. The deal gives some special rights to civil society groups or organisations. Is that correct?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I think, on previous occasions, Senator, you and I traversed the reference in the agreement to the involvement of civil society in consultation with civil society, business, industry groups and other groups, as part of the way in which the agreement interfaces with the community.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

text: Is there anything stopping the EU appointing Both ENDS to the domestic advisory group—or any organisation like that that might be very opposed to Australia's second and third largest exports?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, I think we've traversed that issue before. These are provisions that need to be worked through. Again, we traversed that last time as to the institutional arrangements relating to the agreement.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'll just ask again: is there any restriction on the EU appointing non-governmental organisations that are opposed to Australia's coal and gas exports to the domestic advisory group that's referred to in article 22.7 of the agreement?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I repeat, again, that is still being worked out, and it would be part of the institutional arrangements that are being agreed once the agreement comes into force. So we're not in a position to speculate about who the EU may or may not wish to appoint to these groups.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

text: I want to quickly touch on the modelling. You said you're going to do some modelling on this deal.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

text: I know CIE well. It's CGE modelling. Do you know what CGE model they're using?

witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA
