agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It will be factoring in all of the outcomes that are contained in the agreement.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'll ask again. Does that include looking at the impacts of the Common Agricultural Policy?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We have explained before and will explain again that the free trade agreements, bilaterally, are not the venue, not the forum, in which to make changes to policies. The modelling will look at changes to policy prior to and then after the agreement is in force.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I understand that. But a key concern, particularly for the dairy industry, is that we are removing a tariff we impose on the EU in part to offset the distortive impacts of their massive subsidies to their dairy industry. Is the dairy industry's concern going to be looked at in this modelling? The dairy industry is concerned—quite rightly, in my view—that subsidised EU dairy production will be able to undercut Australian production under this agreement and force them out of business. Will that be modelled in the CIE's work?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You're aware these issues were not part of the negotiations, so you will be aware that as I've said before the policy changes will not be modelled unless there are policy changes.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Right, so it won't be.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What I also want to say about the dairy sector is that despite what have been very high levels of producer support—you're right on that, 16 to 18 per cent producer support in dairy—we both fought that in the WTO and improved where we could in the FTA context on the tariff and access outcomes, and 87 per cent of the lines are now duty free. They had tariffs up over 120 per cent. They're going to zero in most cases.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's not the tariffs that they're concerned about.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This is a massive levelling of the playing field. Admittedly, as you continue to point out, that does not address the subsidy issue. But nobody has expected it to, because this is an FTA, not a subsidy package. We would dearly like to get to those subsidies, and we're very—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We're always free not to sign. We can always say, 'If you're not going to deal with it, we don't have to.' If it's a non-tariff barrier, it's clearly—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We're doing something more than complaining.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I always say that's it's their sovereign right to do these things.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We're doing more than complaining. We are indeed taking these issues up at the WTO with the Cairns Group, and EU dairy subsidies are absolutely in our sights.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We're giving away all of our leverage now, so I don't think we're going to have any impact on the EU if we sign up to this deal. Are we locked in to removing the $1.22 per kilogram dairy tariff under the deal? Is there any way we can keep the tariff?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Part of the deal was to eliminate that tariff over three years.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Is there a safeguard mechanism or something? Could we reimpose it if needed?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There is a safeguard provision built into the agreement that, should there be a sudden surge of exports that is damaging our industry, we can suspend that tariff elimination for a certain period of time.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We'd have to wait.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: To add to that point, in addition to the FTA specific safeguards we also have access to the ongoing WTO safeguards agreement. That is a continuing feature of the trade policy landscape between us and the EU.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But we'd have to wait for the influx of imports to take safeguard action.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As with all safeguard action, one needs to tie the allegation of injury to a rise in imports.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Is there anything stopping us, say, giving our dairy industry $1.22 per kilogram subsidy just like the EU does? Could we do that?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You are aware that this deal massively improves the balance towards our—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We don't want to be here all night. Is there anything in this deal that would stop us?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But it is relevant to your question because your question goes to whether we should be subsidising for a tariff reduction, but if you are levelling the playing field in our favour there's no rationale for a—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, there is, because the EU continues to subsidise. We're not levelling the playing field in any way, shape or form because as you said earlier the EU producers get 16 to 17 per cent—the dairy industry says 30 per cent—of their income from taxpayer support. It's not a level playing field at all.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I've been clear—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: My question is—it's a simple question—is there anything in this agreement that would stop us providing equivalent subsidies to our dairy industry to level the playing field?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm afraid I don't agree with the proposition.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm not asking for your policy opinion, though. Indeed, it's not usually—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's embedded in the question that there would be a requirement to restore—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No. I'm asking whether there is anything in the deal that would stop us providing a subsidy to our dairy industry.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: To the dairy industry, writ large, no.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm not asking whether it's a good or bad thing.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This deal is not a subsidies deal.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Can I just get a clear answer. Is there anything in this deal which would stop us providing subsidy support directly to our dairy industry?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, I just said no. There is no such—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay, thank you. That's all I was wanting to get to. I wasn't asking for a policy opinion on whether it was good or bad. But I do dispute that it's levelled the playing field. It's certainly not doing that. Moving on to steel, will the CIE model the EU's steel tariff at 50 per cent, 25 per cent or some other level?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It will model the current EU tariff, which is at 50 per cent.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That'll be the baseline?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It's a 50 per cent out-of-quota rate. There is, of course, a quota that applies before that, but they will model that current EU measure.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: They've also reduced the quota, haven't they.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: They have reduced the quota, yes.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What's been the change there?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, there are different quotas for different countries on different steel products. For Australia, our annual duty free quota under this new EU measure is 47,320 tonnes.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Does that impact some of our exporters?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It does. It is less than we were exporting to the European Union before the measure was introduced.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What was it before?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: About 300,000 tonnes.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Whoa! Was the 300,000 tonnes the quota—we were exporting and paying the tariff rate on top of sometimes?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We were exporting and paying the then EU tariff rate, which I think was 25 per cent.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I think you're right.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That increased under this measure. But we do have a side letter to this FTA on steel which allows us to come back and have a conversation, and that includes being able to seek an additional quota as an FTA partner, because our current quota is as a non-FTA partner.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm very disappointed in this part of what the EU has done. I don't see how this in any way could be the act of a friend or someone who wants to do a deal with us. We're not a major threat to their steel industry; we hardly produce any steel relative to them. What has been their rationale for singling us out to double our tariff and to significantly reduce the tariff-free access that we previously had?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The EU's rationale is that it had a safeguard measure in place under WTO rules for eight years. Safeguards are required to be implemented on a global basis. They're not directed at one partner; they're directed to the whole world. That measure expired, and they were not allowed to renew it under WTO rules. The EU believed that its industry was still under threat and has introduced this new measure. Under this measure it has given countries country-specific quotas. We have one. We hope to get more. But it's a response to the global problem of structural excess capacity that we are not responsible for. The side letter to the agreement makes very clear that we are not the source of that problem.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But if we're not the source of that problem, how can the EU under international law be justified in taking safeguard action against our steel?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Because safeguards are required to be applied on a global basis.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But you said they're providing country-specific quotas.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: They've got to apply the measure across the board, but then they can provide quotas within that measure on a country-specific basis.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Are we planning to take any action against the EU about this through the WTO processes?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As I said, we have a provision in the FTA, on entry into force, that we can come back and have a conversation—via this side letter, I should say, not a provision—to seek an FTA partner-specific quota which would allow us to increase our actions—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Coming back to my question, are we considering WTO action?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: At the moment we have provisions in place that we will seek to access. That's where we are tracking our policy at the moment.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So we're not taking WTO action?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We are not currently planning to do that.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We just lost our last blast furnace for structural steel. We do export a significant amount of hot-rolled coils to the EU. You said it's 300,000 tonnes. That's not immaterial in the context of our production. It's possibly getting around 10 per cent of our production once Whyalla goes. I don't understand how we're copping this. I can understand what the EU is doing, and you're right; there's a structural oversupply of steel. I wish we took a little bit more action, perhaps, against the people that are contributing to this. But we are clearly not the party contributing to this issue, yet we are facing EU action on it.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We are taking action to work with other partners to try and address this problem of global excess steel capacity. We are members of the global forum on excess steel along with the European Union. And just three weeks ago—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes, I saw that.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: when the minister was in Milwaukee, we adopted a comprehensive framework for joint action to address this very issue. So Australia and the EU, together with other partners, are working together to try and solve this problem at its root cause. Measures like the EU's, at the moment, are a bandaid while we work on that larger endeavour.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: What's the root cause?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: GFSEC—the Global Forum on Steel Excess Capacity.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And the root causes, of course, under those auspices are distortions in domestic markets that lead to excess subsidies and lead to distortions on global markets. We, I think, are all aware of those pressures, particularly in the steel industry—globally, I mean.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Alright. Does this side letter constrain us to maintain our tariff on EU steel at a maximum of five per cent?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I believe that's our WTO bound rate, but we can check that.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Would we, though, have safeguard provisions under the WTO to increase above five per cent?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Safeguard is a very particular mechanism where you need to do an investigation and show threat et cetera, but those provisions do remain available to us.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. And they remain available regardless of the side letter with the EU?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. The EU apparently exported $785 million worth of iron and steel to Australia last year. We exported $285 million. If there's someone contributing to the excess supply, it's not us—yet we're facing further risk to our industry. Have we done any work on whether or not the EU's increased tariffs—which are significant, as we've gone through—put at risk our steel industry any further?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: This is a question relating to the impact of trade on domestic performance, and, no, we have not done any modelling or analytical work. But, quite clearly, this is not going to be helpful. Neither is the rise in steel safeguard actions, in fact, worldwide. It's precisely why we're investing in this cooperative effort with the European Union and the United States and others.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It doesn't sound very cooperative!

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Certainly, there are measures being taken unilaterally, which is precisely why we want to get ahead of this trend. Of course, Minister Farrell, in his capacity as our representative to that global forum, has been advocating strongly for these outcomes—as has Minister Ayres, in his work with countries on excess capacity.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So the CIE work won't look at this issue at all then, in terms of the impact of the EU's increased steel tariffs.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It will model the outcomes of the agreement, so the current EU measure will be part of that model.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We're letting our steel industry wither.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator Ghosh has a few questions. I'll move the call on and then come back to you.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: My questions relate to the impact of the EU free trade agreement on Western Australian trade. I appreciate we don't always talk about it in state-by-state terms, but WA is an externally facing economy and the current environment is, therefore, particularly volatile for the Western Australian economy. Trade is a pretty essential enabler for our success and continued prosperity. As a state, we exported something like $237 billion worth of goods globally last year, but about $4 billion—or, as I do it on the back of an envelope, about 1.6 or 1.7 per cent only—to the EU. So I see this market, given its size, as an opportunity area for Western Australia. I really want to explore what this agreement means for certain WA industries, and I want to start with agriculture. Western Australia has some of the best wine regions in the country—although, just at the minute, Western Australian winemakers are struggling a little bit. I want to know what's going to be the effect of the EU free trade agreement on WA wine exports into Europe.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Currently, the European Union charges Australian wine a tariff of $56 per 100 litres of wine. On entry into force of this agreement, that tariff will be eliminated.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: In lay terms, the practical effect of that is it makes Western Australian wine more price competitive in the EU?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Absolutely, and compared to our competitors as well. Remember, New Zealand already has an FTA with the EU, so it has that tariff advantage—we don't—and so do other competitors. Mercosur includes wine-producing countries as well, even Canada, and we're behind all of those because we're paying the tariff and they are not.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Obviously, we export a tremendous amount of wheat and related products from Western Australia. What's the impact on wheat exports to the EU in terms of tariffs out of this EU free trade agreement?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Currently, Australian wheat and meslin to the European Union are paying up to $166 per tonne. Under this FTA that will be eliminated over five years. Also tariffs on durum wheat of up to $259 a tonne will also be eliminated.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Are you able to effectively do that comparison with our competitor nations—that is to say, the countries that otherwise export wheat to the EU nations in competition with Australian wheat, but Western Australian wheat from my particular interest?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes. Again, competitors who are wheat-producing, wheat-exporting countries who have FTAs with the EU will have a significant tariff advantage on Australian wheat exporters at the moment, which will be eliminated under this FTA.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: And is that the same for barley?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes. For barley, we are currently paying $163 a tonne. That will be eliminated within five years after entry into force of this agreement.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Obviously, there's the Western Australian cattle industry and there's the Western Australian sheep industry. Can you talk to me about those exports to the EU and the impact of this free trade agreement?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes. As we discussed a short time ago, currently our access to the European Union for both beef and sheepmeat is extremely limited. It's 4,400 tonnes currently for beef. At full implementation, that will increase to 35,000 tonnes with commercially favourable conditions attached. Our sheepmeat access will increase to 25,000 tonnes.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: If I can add to Ms Raper's evidence, we did achieve a five-fold increase on sheepmeat. Neither the Mercosur countries nor Mexico achieved any increase in their deals with the European Union on sheepmeat. Of course, New Zealand did achieve a very big increase, but we judged that that will not have a meaningful impact on their export performance given that they've substantially underutilised their existing quotas. So our deal on beef is not only a 500 per cent increase but it stacks up very well in comparative terms.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I understand the agreement contains a commitment to provide equal treatment between Australian service suppliers and European service suppliers in terms of the export of our services into the EU. Can you unpack that for me a little bit practically. What are the things that stand in the way currently of equal treatment that are going to be removed as a consequence of this agreement?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We're talking about temporary entry for professionally qualified service suppliers. Currently, it's difficult for them to be able to travel and deliver those services within the EU market, so this agreement will give temporary entry to the EU for Australian citizens and permanent residents across several categories of service providers—business visitors, investors, intercorporate transferees, graduate trainees as well as contractual service suppliers and independent professionals. So particularly looking at Western Australia, key sectors of interests that we've included that access for in the free trade agreement include education services, tourism, communication services, financial services and environmental services.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There's an obligation as well on the parties to this agreement to develop new standards and reduce regulatory barriers on an ongoing basis. I don't want to say it's expressed in terms that are aspirational because it suggests that they won't get done. But how does that actually work in practical terms? What does that obligation look like in terms of what Australia needs to do and what the nations of the EU need to do?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Are you referring to professional qualifications or are you referring to what we call technical barriers to trade?
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm referring to technical barriers to trade.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The first thing to say is that under the agreement both sides reserve the right to set their own standards. It's an important sovereign right under the agreement, recognising that we both have systems and expectations for our consumers around product safety and so forth. But, under the agreement, it sets up ways to try and remove some of the friction between the trade related to those different standards and barriers. For example, it encourages acceptance of each other's testing and certification results. That helps to avoid unnecessary duplication. It provides greater transparency over the development of new standards before they take effect, which enabled us to have extra conversations about how to shape them. It establishes cooperation between our regulators who are setting those standards. It also promotes the use of international standards. These are important extra mechanisms for taking forward those interests with the European Union under this free trade agreement. They will be in addition to other dialogue processes that we have, but these are an important addition to those issues.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: If a European regulator decides that they want to change the standards that apply to a product that would fall within the scope of this free trade agreement or that would otherwise apply to an Australian provider, is there an obligation under the agreement for that regulatory body to reach out to our regulatory body and consult in relation to those changes? Or is it more that it sets up the relationship pathways and then, in effect, that will lead to greater cooperation as a consequence of the relationship?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The focus of the chapter is very much on process and cooperation. Through those processes and those cooperative practices, as I said, it aims to reduce the friction in the trade relationship.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'll end on this—and maybe this is an aspirational question. I started with the volume of exports from Western Australia to the EU overall and noted that it's a relatively small percentage. Particularly in the agricultural space, what are the non-tariff related barriers that might be assisted by this agreement or might assist Western Australia to export more to the European Union?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: In addition to this big uplift in protected markets in agriculture, both tariffs and tariff-rate quotas, you've got, as Ms Raper has already said, provisions on technical barriers, provisions on cooperation on other forms of non-tariff barrier and provisions to help cooperate on SPS and biosecurity matters. There are a variety of means by which both sides' regulatory authorities can communicate and support that trade. On services, we know this is 70 per cent of our economy and a very fast growing area of international trade, and once again regulatory cooperation is at the core of effective access on many of these sectors as well.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you very much.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator Roberts.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you for appearing tonight. My question is regarding the European Union free trade agreement and its chilling effect on Australian sovereignty. Others have unpicked the way in which this government, in order to get the deal done, has agreed to provisions it opposed in 2023. I won't go there again. My concern is this: Minister, why was implementing the Paris climate change agreement included in the European union free trade agreement?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Who was your question directed to?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The minister.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Could you repeat the question?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Sure. Why was implementing the Paris climate change agreement included in the EU FTA—the free trade agreement?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Australia, under Malcolm Turnbull, signed up to the Paris Agreement. That was a commitment. The Labor government supports that agreement, and the agreement simply reflects that we have entered into that agreement.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The UK free trade agreement also included an environmental section which uses the same words international agreements always use—non-binding words, also called weasel words. There's nothing binding in these agreements on Australia. Minister, did the United Kingdom free trade agreement make the Paris Agreement legally enforceable in Australia? And, if so, please specify the wording which had that effect.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The Paris Agreement is a separate agreement, Senator Roberts, and we have freely entered into that agreement, and it's the intention of the government to honour the commitments that we entered into. As I indicated before, that was entered into by Prime Minister Turnbull. The Australian government, the Albanese government, supports that provision, and we intend to honour our obligations under the Paris Agreement.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Minister, the European Union free trade agreement requires Australia to implement the Paris accord and creates a dispute resolution process, including penalties, if we fail to comply—true or false?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Those questions were all answered earlier in the proceedings, but—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: One word—true or false?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I can only repeat what I've already said, Senator Roberts. Australia has freely entered into the Paris Agreement. It's the Paris Agreement that requires us to do certain things in conjunction with what we have agreed to do. It's the Paris Agreement, and our international obligations on that, that impose requirements on Australia to act in a certain way, and it's the intention of the government to honour those proceedings.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Minister, are you aware that the Paris Agreement was stitched together in a way that makes it not an agreement? After the embarrassment of the UN's COP at Copenhagen, at the next COP—in Paris—they signed an agreement that said, 'You can do basically whatever you want.' China said, 'We'll think about it in 2050.' India said, 'We'll think about it in 2060'—no commitment whatsoever. Australia is one of very few countries that signed their life away and wants to destroy their economy. That's not an agreement; that's a suicide note. The European Union free trade agreement requires implementation of the major pillars of the Paris Agreement, which you helpfully list out on your website. It's a bloody long list. Any failure to implement any one of these will trigger the dispute resolution functions of the agreement, resulting in trade sanctions or penalties against Australian produce, meaning you've sold out our farmers. You've lured them into a trap. You've promised very slight benefits from the trade agreement, and then they'll be sanctioned—they'll be cut off—if anyone dares go against the Paris Agreement. Minister, how is that not making the Paris Agreement legally binding? You haven't denied it, I suppose?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I beg your pardon?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You haven't denied that it's legally binding. You're just saying why that's necessary.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
I disagree with a lot of what you've said there, Senator Roberts. If you've got an interest in finding out more about this—the practical application of the EU free trade agreement, including all the benefits under the agreement—then I would be happy to provide expert advice from many of the people at the table here so that you get a full briefing on the implementation of this agreement. The agreement does represent significant advances for Australian businesses, and that's why almost all of the Australian business community is supporting this agreement.

A little bit earlier, I talked about the fact that Mr Craig Emerson, an eminent economist, has valued the early operation of the free trade agreement to provide benefits to the Australian economy at about $10 billion. That very quickly rises to a figure of $30 billion as a result of the provisions that relate to critical minerals. Your state and Western Australia, of course, and now the Northern Territory have been making significant progress on the development of critical minerals. One of the key provisions here is that, for the first time, our critical minerals go into the European Union tariff free. None of our competitors don't get that same advantage, so that gives us a very significant advantage in terms of our access to the European Union.

I understand that certain parts of the Australian economy haven't been happy with everything that they have received out of this agreement. Beef producers, in particular, have made some adverse comments about the agreement. Fortunately, my job is to represent the national interest, and overwhelmingly Australian business support this agreement. The BCA came out again, I think today or yesterday, in support of it. ACCI is very strongly in support of it. The AiG is very strongly in support of it, as are the seafood council and wine and spirits Australia. I can go through all of these organisations that very strongly support it.

I have to make a decision in the national interest and I have to make an assessment as to whether, on balance, this agreement is good for the Australian economy. Right now, the world is falling into two camps—the camp of tariffs and protectionism or the camp of free and fair trade. This government, the Albanese government, has nailed its colours to the mast, and we support free and fair trade. If you do that and a country comes to you and says, 'Look, we would like to reduce tariff barriers on Australian goods into our economy', firstly, I think we have an obligation to negotiate with that country, as we have done. If, on balance, the agreement is in the national interest, we have an obligation to recommend to the Australian people and to the Australian parliament that it is worth doing. If you don't do that in those circumstances and you reject the offer of that country—or region—to reduce tariff barriers, you're not just sending a message to that country; you're sending a message to all of the countries with whom you have reduced trade barriers that Australia no longer believes in reducing tariffs. The prosperity of your state, Senator Roberts, is very much linked to the removal of tariffs. Australia's prosperity has been built on the fact that we've been able to reach these agreements with all of these countries around the world.

Why is the European agreement so important to Australia? Well, at the moment we have about 30 trade agreements with countries around the world. The European free trade agreement is not one new agreement; it's effectively 27 new agreements, because there are 27 countries in the European Union. So, in one fell swoop, we double the number of countries with whom we have a free trade agreement. We're talking about the second-largest economy in the world. This is a region with 450 million consumers, mostly middle-class consumers. Compare that to the population of Australia, Senator Roberts, of 28, 29 million people, so many times larger than us. More importantly, they have a GDP of something in the vicinity of $33 trillion. So this represents a great opportunity. It hasn't been easy, Senator Roberts, to negotiate an agreement with the Europeans. Former coalition ministers tried. Steve Ciobo had a crack, Simon Birmingham had a crack, Dan Tehan had a crack. And on two occasions we rejected offers from the European Union to their great disappointment. But they made a significant improvement in the offer on the last occasion in a whole string of areas where, under the previous negotiator, Valdis Dombrovskis, they weren't prepared to give us a better offer. Under the current Trade Minister, Maros Sefcovic, significant improvements were made in just about every area of the agreement.

As I say, these agreements are a balance of judgement. I had managed to get the UK Free Trade Agreement through the parliament. I managed to get the Indian Free Trade Agreement through the parliament and to negotiate the UAE trade agreement. In that process, Senator Roberts, last year was a record year for Australian trade. We hit $1.37 trillion. Never in the history of Australia have we done so much trade, and in a circumstance where trade was really unstable right around the world for a whole range of reasons. But, Senator Roberts, we can't stop there. If we are going to grow the Queensland contribution to trade, we need to find new markets to export our goods to. So if, as 27 European countries have said to us, 'We want to buy more of your products, and, in the process, we're going to significantly reduce the tariffs,' I don't believe we can say, as a matter of national interest, that we're going to reject that offer. As I say, if we send a message to the rest of the world, 'We're not interested in the removal of tariffs,' that will have consequences on all of our other agreements. All of the other countries will say, 'Australia is moving away from free and fair trade. Perhaps we ought to be doing the same.' And that in my view, has real consequences for your state. You can focus on one relatively small part of the agreement. Obviously, you're focusing on the climate change provision—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The ability to put sanctions on our country is not a small issue.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator, I just don't think you're looking at the totality of the agreement. I'd urge you to take advantage of my offer of getting a full report and your colleague there is also welcome to attend. I'd ask you, for the moment, to keep an open mind on the agreement, and have a look at the totality of the agreement. I believe when you do that, Senator Roberts, you will come to the same conclusion that I have come to, namely that, on balance, the national interest is served by us continuing to process this agreement, sign this agreement and implement this agreement.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Firstly, you raised many issues that I have to respond to. You asked them in the form of questions. I will happily accept your offer of a briefing, but please tell your people to bring their bloody data.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I will ensure they bring everything that you require. If you give me a list of things you particularly want, I'll make sure it's available for you at the meeting.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Bring their data on Paris and on trade.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Yes. Would your colleague like to attend that meeting as well?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Absolutely.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. I will ensure you get the best advice. I myself will attend in case you've got any questions for me.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We need some staff to be able to listen to you.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Don't worry, Don's alright. He'll manage on his own.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You've got to have staff. You laugh about it.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No, I'm sorry, I shouldn't laugh.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Secondly, farmers under the European union free trade agreement are being held to ransom to basically force people to implement the Paris Agreement. The third thing is that we want to discuss sovereignty. That's very, very important—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'll get—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: your simplistic portrayal—by the way, China has nothing like the health and safety regulations that we have, nothing like the workplace relations legislation that we have to protect workers, nothing like the environmental regulations and nothing like the consumer protection legislation. I could go on and on and on. They're not factored into it. China also doesn't have the bloody Paris Agreement, which drives the price of our electricity through the roof, and we subsidise their solar and wind. They're making a killing out of us. Mr Farrell, I advance the interests of 28 million Australians. I'm not terribly interested in the interests of 450 million Europeans. But I think the best message to send to the world for us is 'Australia first'.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I understand the position that you're putting to me, but, as I say, the offer is there to get—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I accepted it.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I understand.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Data on Paris, data on trade.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The only thing I'd ask you to do is to keep an open mind. I'll provide you with all of the information, and you can make an assessment yourself as to whether, on balance, this agreement is good or bad for the Australian economy.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I always keep an open mind—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: but I'm heavily governed by data.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I understand and will provide as much information as I'm able to.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Thank you, Minister.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm very pleased with your response there.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We look forward to something on our staff.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Senator Canavan.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You mentioned there were significant improvements in the deal from the last time you rejected it to the time you accepted it. What were they?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'll get a list of them for you and send them through.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You can't just give us the top three or so right now?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I can give you a range of them, but I'd like to give you an absolutely accurate response.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The claim from others that saw the deal is that it barely changed.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: That simply is not true.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: If the improvements are significant, I'm not so sure why, having been given the floor, you can't tell us what they are.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm happy to supply you with a complete list of them.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I am astounded that has to be taken on notice. You're the one selling this deal, telling us it's worth $10 billion on dodgy figures, and you're saying 'significant improvements', yet you can't even list a single one.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I'm astounded that you would be opposing this agreement.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Given that you can't even outline one improvement in the deal made from the one you rejected three years ago, it's pretty explainable why I would be against it, just like you were against it three years ago. Moving on—I want to get off the free trade deal because we only have an hour or so left and there are some other issues—I want to ask about the consultation DFAT do before entering into agreements. Could you outline what that consultation is and to what extent, Deputy Secretary, you think it's effective at the moment?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We have an extensive process of consultation before entering into new free trade agreements. We typically open for submissions. We often will do extensive outreach. We will place as much information as we can on our websites. We do extend quite a lot of information and request quite a lot of information.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Given you already do those things, do we need a trade advisory group established under legislation?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The purpose of a more structured process of consultation would be to do that—to provide greater structure to our consultation efforts. We've just been through about 18 months of a very structured consultative mechanism in the minister's Trade 2040 Taskforce, which included representatives from business, peak bodies, unions and companies. The value of that was made very clear through the high-quality report that that group produced just a couple of months ago looking at the future of Australia's trade settings, considering all the major trends that are occurring in our trade landscape. That experience has informed the government's interest in taking forward a more structured approach to trade consultation, as has a longstanding request from many parts of the community to contribute in a more structured way to the trade negotiations agenda.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Would the consultation of the last 18 months have been improved by a legislated trade advisory group?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Just to add a little bit of context: the recommendation for a more structured and, indeed, legislated process flowed from the Joint Standing Committee on Trade and Investment Growth inquiry on areas of improvement to existing processes for trade and investment agreements and negotiations. All their recommendations are on the inquiry homepage—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Free Trade Agreements and Stakeholder Engagement Division, and Chief Negotiator

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I was on the committee.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Exactly. I remember discussing this—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Free Trade Agreements and Stakeholder Engagement Division, and Chief Negotiator

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Did that recommendation come from DFAT? Did DFAT recommend to the minister the need for a legislated trade advisory group?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The recommendation came from the Joint Standing Committee on Trade and Investment.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Free Trade Agreements and Stakeholder Engagement Division, and Chief Negotiator

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Has DFAT recommended or provided advice to the minister that there is a need for a legislated trade advisory group?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: We are currently in the process of working through the range of the government's response and providing advice on that. The government has introduced the legislation on the basis of part of the response to the group.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Free Trade Agreements and Stakeholder Engagement Division, and Chief Negotiator

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Do members of the proposed trade advisory group require security clearances?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The intention is that they would sign nondisclosure agreements but not the full security clearance process, as is the case with some other systems.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Free Trade Agreements and Stakeholder Engagement Division, and Chief Negotiator

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Is there anything stopping the establishment of a trade advisory group without legislation?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The Trade 2040 Taskforce that Deputy Secretary Mina was referring to was not set up by legislation—so, in that sense, yes.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Free Trade Agreements and Stakeholder Engagement Division, and Chief Negotiator

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: So it can be done.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As I said, this was responding to a specific—
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Free Trade Agreements and Stakeholder Engagement Division, and Chief Negotiator

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: At that inquiry you referred to earlier, assistant secretary Ms Holmes stated that legislation was not essential to have a consultation process. That remains DFAT's position?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Do you mean in terms of consultations in general on trade?
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Free Trade Agreements and Stakeholder Engagement Division, and Chief Negotiator

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: On trade agreements. It's not essential to have it legislated?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: As Mr Mina was saying, right now, before any agreement, we usually call for submissions, engage with stakeholders and go back and forth through a range of consultations. All that does not need legislation.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Free Trade Agreements and Stakeholder Engagement Division, and Chief Negotiator

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: At that parliamentary inquiry, associate secretary Tim Yeend warned that a legislative approach could lock negotiators into particular approaches and constrain the Australian government's ability to respond to changing circumstances in the negotiation. Has DFAT provided advice to the government or the minister about those concerns with a legislative approach?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The legislation which was tabled by the minister earlier this year seeks to strike that balance between ensuring flexibility and ensuring that a clear voice that will be providing advice is legislated. That was a dynamic that was considered in the drafting of the bill.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Free Trade Agreements and Stakeholder Engagement Division, and Chief Negotiator

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The legislation mandates the appointment of trade union representatives on the group. Did DFAT recommend that?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: First of all, it's a bill; it's not yet legislation. We worked very closely with the government in providing advice on drafting the bill. I think that's probably as far as I can go.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Free Trade Agreements and Stakeholder Engagement Division, and Chief Negotiator

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Moving on: a few weeks ago, Minister, you raised the prospect that Australian super funds could invest in the US lamb industry. What's the status of that proposal?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
I was talking with two groups about that very issue today. We have a circumstance where the United States government has made a reference to its trade authorities to review Australian exports of lamb into the United States. Australia, on some occasions, represents somewhere between 50 and 70 per cent of all lamb that's eaten in the United States. I want to put lamb exports into perspective. For every lamb chop that an American eats, they eat 10 pork chops, 50 beef patties and 80 buffalo chicken wings—so lamb is a very small part of the protein in the American diet. In discussions with all our major exporters to the United States, it became very clear to me that there is an opportunity to work with the American industry to try and increase the level of lamb exports into the United States. Many companies, including some great South Australian companies like Thomas Foods, are already investing in additional provisions into the United States.

Last week, our ambassador, Ambassador Moriarty, led the argument against America increasing restrictions on Australian lamb, whether that comes in the form of a higher tariff or quotas or some combination. In the next 10 days or so, the American committee—six individuals—looking at this will make a determination as to whether or not we are in breach of export obligations into the United States. If that happens, then we will need to provide a response or a remedy in a certain period of time. It's my view that we should have an all-of-government and all-of-Australia response to the American decision. It's not beyond the realms of possibility that the United States applies, say, a 50 per cent tariff on top of the 12½ per cent tariff that they're applying. So, in discussion with the industry, we need to come up with a formal response in the event of an adverse result. I've had discussions with my counterpart, Ambassador Greer, and agriculture minister Rollins, about whether or not there's an opportunity to lift the level of consumption of lamb into the United States. I'll continue to work in conjunction with, in particular, the people I met today, our government representatives over there, the ambassador and industry generally about how we might make a positive contribution to increasing the appetite of Americans for lamb, particularly Australian lamb. In the process, we'll perhaps try and build the supply chain of lamb into the American consumer market.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay. Just can I confirm, though, that the Australian government's not proposing that there'd be any obligation on super funds to invest in the US lamb industry or any foreign markets.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: No. Nobody has ever suggested that.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Okay.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I was a member of a superannuation for fund for 15 years. I'm well and truly aware of the fiduciary obligations of super funds and was never suggesting that there should be any breach of our fiduciary duties. Currently, lamb exports represent about a $1.5 billion export to the United States. It's not a big figure in terms of the United States, but it is a significant figure for Australian lamb exporters. I want to do everything I can to assist the Australian lamb exports. If the Americans were to apply the sort of tariff that is being bandied about in the United States, it would almost certainly end Australian lamb exports to the United States. An immediate impact of $1.5 billion on the Australian lamb export industry would be as significant as when, under the Morrison government, China imposed 220 per cent tariffs on Australian wine. It would have that very same impact. I think for the Americans to proceed with this the way they might is actually completely counterproductive to their own interests because, in the absence of fantastic Australian lamb into the US market, that market itself will collapse. So I think there's the potential here of economic self-harm by the American lamb producers to their own industry if they proceed with these extra tariffs. I want to engage and I will engage Ambassador Greer on this topic, as I have already. I think we should engage Secretary Rollins, and I think we have to have an all-Australian response to this because lamb exporters don't deserve to lose this market. The lamb industry and the Australian government have to work together to find a solution to this problem: a solution which ensures that Americans eat more lamb and we get our wonderful product to continue to go into the American market.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Well, look, I agree with all of that. Moving on. You did just, as you have done many times, berate the former coalition government for China making a decision about their tariffs. Given that—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: All I did, Senator, with due respect, was point out that the wine industry lost more than $1 billion worth of trade.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: But you blame us for that. And with that in mind—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I never blamed you for that. I simply made the observation that, if the Americans proceed with this, the effect on the Australian lamb industry will be exactly the same as what happened to the Australian wine industry.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: You have blamed the coalition many times for those Chinese tariffs. That being said, then, why haven't you been able to prevent the US from imposing higher tariffs on Australia under the forced labour provisions than they have on other developed countries? If the coalition is to blame for the China situation, why aren't you then to blame for these high tariffs from the US?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: There is a significant difference between what is occurring in the United States and—you might not like the answer, Senator Canavan, but at least give me the respect of listening to me without—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I have.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
making those funny little comments that you make. There is a significant difference between what's occurring now in the United States and what was occurring in China. When China imposed those $20 billion worth of bans on Australian products, we were singled out for treatment, and so, for instance, when the bans were imposed on beef our quotas were being filled by other countries—Brazil, Argentina and so forth.

What's happening in the United States is this: on so-called Liberation Day in April of last year, the United States government decided to impose a range of tariff regimes on every country that basically traded with the United States. Those tariff regimes range from a figure of 10 per cent, which is at the lowest, to anything up to 50 per cent or a figure even higher. Consumers in United States took a case to the American Supreme Court to challenge the implementation of those tariffs, and they were successful in overturning the tariffs. In response to that, the American government then imposed an across-the-board tariff of 10 per cent. So while we had had an advantageous provision originally, when the original decision was made by President Trump, all of a sudden we were returned to the average of all of the countries. Under American law that could only have been applied for a period of six months, and that six months—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: It was 150 days—five months.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
I've just been corrected; it was 150 days. At the end of that, when that provision was coming to an end, the United States government then had to find another way of keeping the tariffs. They chose to go down the path of examining the responses of countries to modern slavery. Again, they made an almost universal application of modern slavery against every country in the world and lifted the tariff to 12½ per cent. Countries like Australia, the United Kingdom and New Zealand were all lumped in a similar category. Interestingly, countries like Pakistan and Bangladesh were exempted from that higher increase.

We continue to argue against that uniform application. The point I make on the distinguishing factor between what happened in China and what is now happening in the United States is that the United States are applying these tariffs right across the board as a policy position to reintroduce tariffs. That wasn't what was happening in China. But, Senator Canavan, despite all of those tariffs being applied, our exports to the United States have gone up by 67 per cent. Despite the application of these tariffs, Australia has managed to increase our exports to the United States.

When I was talking to Senator Roberts a bit earlier, I referred to the fact that last year's was a record figure for trade, at $1.37 trillion. One of the reasons for that higher increase in our trade figures is the fact that we have been able to increase our exports to the United States. How have we done that? Well, Senator Canavan—I know you're looking a bit bored there—the reason that we have been able to do that is our three largest exports, in terms of both volume and value, are beef, gold and copper, and all of those three products enter the United States tariff free. Whereas the other products that we sell into the United States are subject to a 12½ per cent tariff or higher—as in the case of steel or aluminium, 50 per cent—those products, which represent both higher value and higher volume, have given us that figure of 67 per cent.

Why is beef such a significant contributor? The American beef stock, because of drought, is very low. They've in fact even invited other countries to increase the amount of beef exports. You'll have seen a figure of 300,000 tonnes made available to, particularly, the South Americans. The net result is that we are increasing our exports to the United Kingdom. I met CSL, one of the companies that export significant amounts of product into the United States. They believe there's an opportunity to increase exports in their space. We're doing everything we can—and I think, having met with the meat industry today, they're appreciative of the efforts the Australian government is going to—but there's certainly more work to be done in that space, and we don't resile from that for one moment, Senator Canavan.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I was looking a bit bored because you've described what happened but you haven't answered my question. Why haven't you been able to get the same lower tariff that the UK and other countries have got on these across-the-board tariffs on forced-labour issues?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
I think here we have to talk about the US's approach to the test and the thresholds they were applying in respect of what they wanted to see from partners on dealing with modern slavery in their supply chains. The US was very clear they opposed a binary test. Either one has a blanket import ban or one doesn't. What we've been trying to argue to them—and we're continuing to press this case—is that we have a different approach. We have the same policy objective to remove modern slavery from supply chains. As I think we discussed last time, we are emphasising to them that we have a different approach which relies on business-based accountability mechanisms. In fact, there are many aspects of our approach that are more effective, because you can reach higher up supply chains, identify risks and deal with them at their source.

We've also in the last couple of months—and, again, this is at the highest levels; the Prime Minister and the minister have been making these points—introduced a legislative reform package that goes to higher and more serious civil and criminal penalties for offences, particularly for companies with revenues over a hundred million dollars. We've introduced that into the discussion with the Americans. Minister Farrell was able to do that in his last discussions, not only in Milwaukee but actually back in August. We have been continuing to advocate on the effectiveness of our reforms, which are obviously yet to be brought into force, but we will be pressing for the Americans to recognise those reforms, as the Prime Minister has done.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: Deputy Secretary, Trade and Investment Group

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: To make it clear, I don't blame the minister or the government for not getting a better deal. The primary blame for these tariffs is with the United States administration, clearly. But I think the last 10 minutes or so that we're not going to get back demonstrate how absurd it is to blame the former, coalition government for China's actions. The people responsible for increasing protection are the countries that do it, and I'm not going to run down our country or our officials by making these sorts of things political. We should stand together when action like this is taken. That's the point I was making. Thank you. We might move on, given the time.

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: I have one or two questions with respect to the EU deal and Victoria, given I'm a very proud Victorian. How will the agreement support the European investment in Victoria's priority sectors such as life sciences, renewable energy and defence industries?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text:
Many of the benefits we talked about earlier will, of course, also benefit Victoria, but, to drill down a little bit on key Victorian exports, we will see under this FTA the elimination of tariffs on key Victorian exports, such as 12.8 per cent on chemicals and pharmaceuticals, 14 per cent on machinery and electrical parts, 12 per cent on textiles and 4.5 per cent on auto parts. On agriculture, the outcomes that we referred to earlier on beef, sheepmeat, wine, wheat and barley will also benefit Victoria. We haven't talked too much about tree nuts, but there is an almond tariff elimination of up to 5.6 per cent. On seafood, Victorian mussels will benefit from the elimination of a 10 per cent tariff, and 11 per cent for abalone.

Of course, we have one market access for Australian cheese into the European market, which is often overlooked in the discussion on dairy and the FTA. So we will see the elimination of EU tariffs on cheese—which are extraordinarily high, as I think Deputy Secretary Mina referred to earlier—with $3,872 a tonne eliminated within three years, which is an amazing opportunity for Australian cheese exporters. We also have benefits, of course, for the Victorian services exporters, particularly priority areas there. Some of them I referred to before, such as education and tourism, but also digital services, financial services and environmental services will benefit Victorian services exporters. Those are a few of the highlights that I think will be particularly interesting to the state of Victoria.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Victoria is also Australia's second-largest service exporter. How will the agreement, including the new Innovation Mobility Pathway, help Victoria's universities, researchers and service providers grow in the EU market?

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: The Innovation Mobility Pathway is a new mobility initiative under the agreement that will make it easier for researchers and technicians to travel to and work within the European Union. It is particularly directed at people with experience in areas such as advanced manufacturing, AI, computing and communications, biotechnology, gene technology and vaccines, energy, the environment, quantum sensing, robotics and space. There are quite a few industries there that are important in the Victorian market. What it will mean is that they will be able to travel to and work in the EU in order to undertake their research. Our researchers will be able to stay in the EU for up to nine months while they get that started and be able to travel across the European Union states. Also, importantly, they will be able to have their qualifications recognised throughout the EU. As I mentioned earlier, recognition of qualifications in one EU member state will mean that they won't need to be requalified in another European Union member state.
witness_organisation: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Are degrees recognised or—

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade

witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Office of Global Trade Negotiations, and Chief Negotiator for AU-EU FTA

agency: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
text: Excellent. I'll finish on this one then. Victoria, as we know, has a very strong and proud pharmaceutical and advanced manufacturing base.
