text: We also have the PALM scheme in this country. The PALM scheme has a lot of limitations that don't make it enthusiastically embraced by the tourism industry—like minimum hour obligations, where the employer continues to pay the costs of the PALM scheme visa holder even if they can't give that visa holder work, because our tourism industry is so heavily reliant on casual workers during the warmer and busier months. So it's correct, isn't it, that the tourism industry does not embrace the PALM scheme?

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: I think there are a variety of views from the sector about the PALM scheme. I don't have the exact figures in front of me, but from my last recollection there are over 600 workers working in the accommodation sector under the PALM scheme. We'd have to get advice from the department of employment, which I think runs that program, for the precise figure for you.
witness_organisation: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
witness_position: General Manager, Office of Tourism and the Visitor Economy

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: The unfairness that would be attached to using UK working holiday-makers to meet the needs of our tourism industry and the unhelpful way that the PALM scheme applies to our tourism industry takes us back to needing to keep the current rate of backpackers, doesn't it, to be able to properly support our thriving tourism industry in this country? You agree with that, don't you?

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: I think you're asking me to express an opinion on various aspects of government policy.
witness_organisation: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
witness_position: General Manager, Office of Tourism and the Visitor Economy

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: Having regard to those facts, you'd be aware of how reliant our tourism industry is on backpackers and you'd be aware of the unfairness and the limitations to which I've referred to other options that might otherwise be available. So doesn't that take us back to the fact that our tourism industry depends on backpackers and needs to continue to do so?

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: Certainly, the tourism industry does utilise backpackers for aspects of its labour force. I'm happy to take you through what our data says about that.
witness_organisation: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
witness_position: General Manager, Office of Tourism and the Visitor Economy

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: Go ahead.

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: What our data from the international visitor survey suggests is that around 86 per cent of first-year working holiday-makers undertake some form of work when they're in the country. Our survey also says that, of those that do work, approximately 40 per cent work in the tourism sector.
witness_organisation: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
witness_position: General Manager, Office of Tourism and the Visitor Economy

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: Speaking of surveys, are you aware of ATIC's survey, the Australian Tourism Industry Council's survey, that was undertaken in September this year, which was an opinion poll of 1,000 Australians, where 72 per cent considered working holiday-makers to be not migrants but tourists travelling around Australia and earning money to put back into our regional communities to pay their way through their holidays and 76 per cent supported working holiday-makers staying longer to travel and work across regional Australia. Only eight per cent supported the changes that are intended to be made to decrease the rate of backpackers to almost 50 per cent. Are you aware of that poll?

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: I think this is going into matters that are really for the Department of Home Affairs, not for the tourism portfolio.
witness_organisation: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: You play an advisory role to the decision-maker, being the government.

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: Indeed, and, as Mr Dowie indicated, we're happy to be helpful in providing you with information on the labour force impacts of the changes.
witness_organisation: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: I'm very grateful for the advisory role that you play on behalf of our tourism industry for our government, so I'm interested to understand if you are aware of this poll, because of course polls like this would inform the advice that you give to our decision-makers in this country.

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: But, fundamentally, the question is going to matters for the Department of Home Affairs rather than for the tourism portfolio. As I mentioned a moment ago, the principal impacts from our perspective are on labour supply.
witness_organisation: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: When you give advice to government, is it motivated by the best interests of the tourism industry in this country?

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: We're a Public Service agency, so we're motivated by the public interest. One of the reasons why we created, within Austrade, the Office of Tourism and the Visitor Economy was precisely to ensure that there was a strong capability within the Australian government to provide advice on the tourism industry and to liaise closely with industry. We take that very, very seriously—indeed quite passionately—but we are very mindful of the fact that, as public servants, our focus is on the public interest in general.
witness_organisation: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: The public interest, from all of the matters to which I have referred this evening, clearly supports keeping the rate of backpackers at its current rate so we can properly support our tourism industry, doesn't it?

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: I'll take that as an expression of opinion. As I said, we're here to assist you with matters relating to tourism.
witness_organisation: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: And matters that are in the public interest, so I was then testing what you consider to be in the public interest if that's your motivation—

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: It's well established that it's not the role of officials to be providing matters of opinion before estimates committees.
witness_organisation: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
witness_position: Chief Executive Officer

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: That's not what I was asking. They're my questions, Chair; I'll give someone else a chance in the next five minutes. Thank you very much for answering my questions.

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: We have one more witness, don't we, Chair?

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: We do, but I doubt we'll get to them.

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: I've just got one question then. On the follow-up from Senator Bleyer, you mentioned that most of the visas are year 1. The problem, though, is—this is the feedback I've got from employers; I've spoken to quite a few backpacker workers themselves—without the incentive of year 2 and year 3, either they're not going to come here or, if they do, they won't go to the rural and remote areas, because there's not the same guaranteed incentive for them. Have you looked at the effect of the ballots and caps on whether or not people come here for year 1 in the first place?

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: We've been able to look at the changes about what our—let me rephrase. We've been able to provide what we think the impact of these changes is, based on what our data tells us about what people are currently doing at the moment. So, in terms of any behavioural change that there might be as a result of this—for example, as you've mentioned, are fewer people going to work in regional areas as a consequence of this?—we've not been able to model or to estimate that with any degree of certainty, because there hasn't really been a benchmark for us to use, because this is—
witness_organisation: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
witness_position: General Manager, Office of Tourism and the Visitor Economy

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: Certainly, the colloquial feedback I'm getting—but alright. Sorry to cut you off, but, given the time, I think we—if it's okay, Chair, I've got some similar questions for Tourism Australia.

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: Okay. Thanks, Paul and team. We'll now welcome Tourism Australia. Hurry up! Sorry, we've only got four minutes. Mr Mack, if you have an opening statement, could you please table it. It will be circulated to the committee. Senator Canavan.

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: First of all, following on from that discussion, which I think you were in the room for, the tourism industry is up in arms about these changes to working holiday-maker visas. Have you done any work on assessing what the impact will be and whether their claims are correct?

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: For us at Tourism Australia, we're a demand-generating agency, so it's not our role to work on modelling. That's what our other agency partners will do for us, in that sense. We focus on marketing and what we can do to create demand. We do liaise with our industry quite extensively in our work, through conferences, events and one-on-one engagement. We share feedback we get from our industry with our stakeholders, yes.
witness_organisation: Tourism Australia
witness_position: Managing Director

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: Tourism Australia has previously identified that working holiday-makers are among Australia's highest-value visitors, contributing $3.2 billion back in 2019. If fewer of them come here, what's going to be the impact on our local tourism industry?

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: In terms of the modelling, that's not, as I said, something that we do. For us, it's about demand generation. We talk to a number of high-yielding traveller cohorts. Working holiday-makers are one of those, as are business events and as are leisure travellers—those that are coming for a holiday or visiting friends and relatives. So it's a broader group that we put under the umbrella of high-yielding travellers.
witness_organisation: Tourism Australia
witness_position: Managing Director

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: Did the government ask Tourism Australia for any advice on the impacts of a ballot and a cap system?

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: Our role as an agency is not to advise on policy. But, as I said, in terms of when we get feedback from industry, that's what we share.
witness_organisation: Tourism Australia
witness_position: Managing Director

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: Did the government ask you for any advice in this case?

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: I guess we might have shared it ahead of being asked, but we certainly have continual dialogue between our minister's office and ourselves.
witness_organisation: Tourism Australia
witness_position: Managing Director

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: Another issue for the tourism sector I'm hearing about is that the fuel crisis has made it very difficult for those exposed to international tourism, given that the costs of getting here have gone up. Do you do any work on trying to help or promote that Australians holiday at home as a cheaper alternative?

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: From our perspective, we don't focus on domestic tourism. We're solely focused on international, inbound tourism, so we leave the domestic work to our states and territories.
witness_organisation: Tourism Australia
witness_position: Managing Director

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: Has Tourism Australia ever done work on inbound tourism or domestic tourism?

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: Domestic tourism—we have in the past, yes.
witness_organisation: Tourism Australia
witness_position: Managing Director

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: There's been no reflection on there being maybe a shift to that, given the high transport costs since the Iran crisis?

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: The last time we were involved in it was during COVID, when borders were closed. We were looking at it then. Our state and territory partners do a great job in that space for us. While costs are going up—you're right about the impact on fuel prices and airfare costs—the demand is still there. People are still wanting to travel. We're trying to grab that share of international visitors because, when they come, they support our industry in a greater way than domestic travellers. They'll stay longer, they'll spend more, they'll stay mid-week and they will disperse widely. So that's solely our focus, and we maintain that focus.
witness_organisation: Tourism Australia
witness_position: Managing Director

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: Is that a decision you can make—about domestic tourism—or are you directed by government on where to focus?

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: We'd be directed on that.
witness_organisation: Tourism Australia
witness_position: Managing Director

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: Okay. Thank you, Chair.

agency: Australian Trade and Investment Commission
text: Thank you, Mr Mack, and thank you to your team. That concludes today's proceedings. The committee is due to recommence its examination of estimates tomorrow, with the Department of Defence. I want to thank ministers Wong and Farrell; all the officers; the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and their agencies; and all the witnesses. Thank you also to Hansard, Broadcasting and the secretariat.
